source_paragraphs: The Tale, the Parable, and the Fable are all common and popular modes of conveying instruction. Each is distinguished by its own special characteristics. The Tale consists simply in the narration of a story either founded on facts, or created solely by the imagination, and not necessarily associated with the teaching of any moral lesson. The Parable is the designed use of language purposely intended to convey a hidden and secret meaning other than that contained in the words themselves; and which may or may not bear a special reference to the hearer, or reader. The Fable partly agrees with, and partly differs from both of these. It will contain, like the Tale, a short but real narrative; it will seek, like the Parable, to convey a hidden meaning, and that not so much by the use of language, as by the skilful introduction of fictitious characters; and yet, unlike to either Tale or Parable, it will ever keep in view, as its high prerogative, and inseparable attribute, the great purpose of instruction, and will necessarily seek to inculcate some moral maxim, social duty, or political truth. The true Fable, if it rise to its high requirements, ever aims at one great end and purpose—the representation of human motive, and the improvement of human conduct, and yet it so conceals its design under the disguise of fictitious characters, by clothing with speech the animals of the field, the birds of the air, the trees of the wood, or the beasts of the forest, that the reader shall receive advice without perceiving the presence of the adviser. Thus the superiority of the counsellor, which often renders counsel unpalatable, is kept out of view, and the lesson comes with the greater acceptance when the reader is led, unconsciously to himself, to have his sympathies enlisted in behalf of what is pure, honourable, and praiseworthy, and to have his indignation excited against what is low, ignoble, and unworthy. The true fabulist, therefore, discharges a most important function. He is neither a narrator, nor an allegorist. He is a great teacher, a corrector of morals, a censor of vice, and a commender of virtue. In this consists the superiority of the Fable over the Tale or the Parable. The fabulist is to create a laugh, but yet, under a merry guise, to convey instruction. Phædrus, the great imitator of Æsop, plainly indicates this double purpose to be the true office of the writer of fables.

Duplex libelli dos est: quod risum movet,
Et quod prudenti vitam consilio monet.

The continual observance of this twofold aim creates the charm, and accounts for the universal favour, of the fables of Æsop. “The fable,” says Professor K. O. Mueller, “originated in Greece in an intentional travestie of human affairs. The ‘ainos,’ as its name denotes, is an admonition, or rather a reproof, veiled, either from fear of an excess of frankness, or from a love of fun and jest, beneath the fiction of an occurrence happening among beasts; and wherever we have any ancient and authentic account of the Æsopian fables, we find it to be the same.”[1]

The construction of a fable involves a minute attention to (1), the narration itself; (2), the deduction of the moral; and (3), a careful maintenance of the individual characteristics of the fictitious personages introduced into it. The narration should relate to one simple action, consistent with itself, and neither be overladen with a multiplicity of details, nor distracted by a variety of circumstances. The moral or lesson should be so plain, and so intimately interwoven with, and so necessarily dependent on, the narration, that every reader should be compelled to give to it the same undeniable interpretation. The introduction of the animals or fictitious characters should be marked with an unexceptionable care and attention to their natural attributes, and to the qualities attributed to them by universal popular consent. The Fox should be always cunning, the Hare timid, the Lion bold, the Wolf cruel, the Bull strong, the Horse proud, and the Ass patient. Many of these fables are characterized by the strictest observance of these rules. They are occupied with one short narrative, from which the moral naturally flows, and with which it is intimately associated. “’Tis the simple manner,” says Dodsley,[2] “in which the morals of Æsop are interwoven with his fables that distinguishes him, and gives him the preference over all other mythologists. His ‘Mountain delivered of a Mouse,’ produces the moral of his fable in ridicule of pompous pretenders; and his Crow, when she drops her cheese, lets fall, as it were by accident, the strongest admonition against the power of flattery. There is no need of a separate sentence to explain it; no possibility of impressing it deeper, by that load we too often see of accumulated reflections.”[3] An equal amount of praise is due for the consistency with which the characters of the animals, fictitiously introduced, are marked. While they are made to depict the motives and passions of men, they retain, in an eminent degree, their own special features of craft or counsel, of cowardice or courage, of generosity or rapacity.

These terms of praise, it must be confessed, cannot be bestowed on all the fables in this collection. Many of them lack that unity of design, that close connection of the moral with the narrative, that wise choice in the introduction of the animals, which constitute the charm and excellency of true Æsopian fable. This inferiority of some to others is sufficiently accounted for in the history of the origin and descent of these fables. The great bulk of them are not the immediate work of Æsop. Many are obtained from ancient authors prior to the time in which he lived. Thus, the fable of the “Hawk and the Nightingale” is related by Hesiod;[4] the “Eagle wounded by an Arrow, winged with its own feathers,” by Æschylus;[5] the “Fox avenging his wrongs on the Eagle,” by Archilochus.[6] Many of them again are of later origin, and are to be traced to the monks of the middle ages: and yet this collection, though thus made up of fables both earlier and later than the era of Æsop, rightfully bears his name, because he composed so large a number (all framed in the same mould, and conformed to the same fashion, and stamped with the same lineaments, image, and superscription) as to secure to himself the right to be considered the father of Greek fables, and the founder of this class of writing, which has ever since borne his name, and has secured for him, through all succeeding ages, the position of the first of moralists.[7]

The fables were in the first instance only narrated by Æsop, and for a long time were handed down by the uncertain channel of oral tradition. Socrates is mentioned by Plato[8] as having employed his time while in prison, awaiting the return of the sacred ship from Delphos which was to be the signal of his death, in turning some of these fables into verse, but he thus versified only such as he remembered. Demetrius Phalereus, a philosopher at Athens about 300 B.C., is said to have made the first collection of these fables. Phædrus, a slave by birth or by subsequent misfortunes, and admitted by Augustus to the honours of a freedman, imitated many of these fables in Latin iambics about the commencement of the Christian era. Aphthonius, a rhetorician of Antioch, A.D. 315, wrote a treatise on, and converted into Latin prose, some of these fables. This translation is the more worthy of notice, as it illustrates a custom of common use, both in these and in later times. The rhetoricians and philosophers were accustomed to give the Fables of Æsop as an exercise to their scholars, not only inviting them to discuss the moral of the tale, but also to practice and to perfect themselves thereby in style and rules of grammar, by making for themselves new and various versions of the fables. Ausonius,[9] the friend of the Emperor Valentinian, and the latest poet of eminence in the Western Empire, has handed down some of these fables in verse, which Julianus Titianus, a contemporary writer of no great name, translated into prose. Avienus, also a contemporary of Ausonius, put some of these fables into Latin elegiacs, which are given by Nevelet (in a book we shall refer to hereafter), and are occasionally incorporated with the editions of Phædrus.

Seven centuries elapsed before the next notice is found of the Fables of Æsop. During this long period these fables seem to have suffered an eclipse, to have disappeared and to have been forgotten; and it is at the commencement of the fourteenth century, when the Byzantine emperors were the great patrons of learning, and amidst the splendors of an Asiatic court, that we next find honours paid to the name and memory of Æsop. Maximus Planudes, a learned monk of Constantinople, made a collection of about a hundred and fifty of these fables. Little is known of his history. Planudes, however, was no mere recluse, shut up in his monastery. He took an active part in public affairs. In 1327 A.D. he was sent on a diplomatic mission to Venice by the Emperor Andronicus the Elder. This brought him into immediate contact with the Western Patriarch, whose interests he henceforth advocated with so much zeal as to bring on him suspicion and persecution from the rulers of the Eastern Church. Planudes has been exposed to a two-fold accusation. He is charged on the one hand with having had before him a copy of Babrias (to whom we shall have occasion to refer at greater length in the end of this Preface), and to have had the bad taste “to transpose,” or to turn his poetical version into prose: and he is asserted, on the other hand, never to have seen the Fables of Æsop at all, but to have himself invented and made the fables which he palmed off under the name of the famous Greek fabulist. The truth lies between these two extremes. Planudes may have invented some few fables, or have inserted some that were current in his day; but there is an abundance of unanswerable internal evidence to prove that he had an acquaintance with the veritable fables of Æsop, although the versions he had access to were probably corrupt, as contained in the various translations and disquisitional exercises of the rhetoricians and philosophers. His collection is interesting and important, not only as the parent source or foundation of the earlier printed versions of Æsop, but as the direct channel of attracting to these fables the attention of the learned.

The eventual re-introduction, however, of these Fables of Æsop to their high place in the general literature of Christendom, is to be looked for in the West rather than in the East. The calamities gradually thickening round the Eastern Empire, and the fall of Constantinople, 1453 A.D. combined with other events to promote the rapid restoration of learning in Italy; and with that recovery of learning the revival of an interest in the Fables of Æsop is closely identified. These fables, indeed, were among the first writings of an earlier antiquity that attracted attention. They took their place beside the Holy Scriptures and the ancient classic authors, in the minds of the great students of that day. Lorenzo Valla, one of the most famous promoters of Italian learning, not only translated into Latin the Iliad of Homer and the Histories of Herodotus and Thucydides, but also the Fables of Æsop.

These fables, again, were among the books brought into an extended circulation by the agency of the printing press. Bonus Accursius, as early as 1475–1480, printed the collection of these fables, made by Planudes, which, within five years afterwards, Caxton translated into English, and printed at his press in Westminster Abbey, 1485.[10] It must be mentioned also that the learning of this age has left permanent traces of its influence on these fables,[11] by causing the interpolation with them (as a κτῆμα εἰς ἰει) of some of those amusing stories which were so frequently introduced into the public discourses of the great preachers of those days, and of which specimens are yet to be found in the extant sermons of Jean Raulin, Meffreth, and Gabriel Barlette.[12] The publication of this era which most probably has influenced these fables, is the “Liber Facetiarum,”[13] a book consisting of a hundred jests and stories, by the celebrated Poggio Bracciolini, published A.D. 1471, from which the two fables of the “Miller, his Son, and the Ass,” and the “Fox and the Woodcutter,” are undoubtedly selected.

The knowledge of these fables rapidly spread from Italy into Germany, and their popularity was increased by the favour and sanction given to them by the great fathers of the Reformation, who frequently used them as vehicles for satire and protest against the tricks and abuses of the Romish ecclesiastics. The zealous and renowned Camerarius, who took an active part in the preparation of the Confession of Augsburgh, found time, amidst his numerous avocations, to prepare a version for the students in the University of Tübingen, in which he was a professor. Martin Luther translated twenty of these fables, and was urged by Melancthon to complete the whole; while Gottfried Arnold, the celebrated Lutheran theologian, and librarian to Frederick I., king of Prussia, mentions that the great Reformer valued the Fables of Æsop next after the Holy Scriptures. In 1546 A.D. the second printed edition of the collection of the Fables made by Planudes, was issued from the printing-press of Robert Stephens, in which were inserted some additional fables from a MS. in the Bibliothêque du Roy at Paris.

The greatest advance, however, towards a re-introduction of the Fables of Æsop to a place in the literature of the world, was made in the early part of the seventeenth century. In the year 1610, a learned Swiss, Isaac Nicholas Nevelet, sent forth the third printed edition of these fables, in a work entitled “Mythologia Æsopica.” This was a noble effort to do honour to the great fabulist, and was the most perfect collection of Æsopian fables ever yet published. It consisted, in addition to the collection of fables given by Planudes and reprinted in the various earlier editions, of one hundred and thirty-six new fables (never before published) from MSS. in the Library of the Vatican, of forty fables attributed to Aphthonius, and of forty-three from Babrias. It also contained the Latin versions of the same fables by Phædrus, Avienus, and other authors. This volume of Nevelet forms a complete “Corpus Fabularum Æsopicarum;” and to his labours Æsop owes his restoration to universal favour as one of the wise moralists and great teachers of mankind. During the interval of three centuries which has elapsed since the publication of this volume of Nevelet’s, no book, with the exception of the Holy Scriptures, has had a wider circulation than Æsop’s Fables. They have been translated into the greater number of the languages both of Europe and of the East, and have been read, and will be read, for generations, alike by Jew, Heathen, Mohammedan, and Christian. They are, at the present time, not only engrafted into the literature of the civilized world, but are familiar as household words in the common intercourse and daily conversation of the inhabitants of all countries.

This collection of Nevelet’s is the great culminating point in the history of the revival of the fame and reputation of Æsopian Fables. It is remarkable, also, as containing in its preface the germ of an idea, which has been since proved to have been correct by a strange chain of circumstances. Nevelet intimates an opinion, that a writer named Babrias would be found to be the veritable author of the existing form of Æsopian Fables. This intimation has since given rise to a series of inquiries, the knowledge of which is necessary, in the present day, to a full understanding of the true position of Æsop in connection with the writings that bear his name.

The history of Babrias is so strange and interesting, that it might not unfitly be enumerated among the curiosities of literature. He is generally supposed to have been a Greek of Asia Minor, of one of the Ionic Colonies, but the exact period in which he lived and wrote is yet unsettled. He is placed, by one critic,[14] as far back as the institution of the Achaian League, B.C. 250; by another as late as the Emperor Severus, who died A.D. 235; while others make him a contemporary with Phædrus in the time of Augustus. At whatever time he wrote his version of Æsop, by some strange accident it seems to have entirely disappeared, and to have been lost sight of. His name is mentioned by Avienus; by Suidas, a celebrated critic, at the close of the eleventh century, who gives in his lexicon several isolated verses of his version of the fables; and by John Tzetzes, a grammarian and poet of Constantinople, who lived during the latter half of the twelfth century. Nevelet, in the preface to the volume which we have described, points out that the Fables of Planudes could not be the work of Æsop, as they contain a reference in two places to “Holy monks,” and give a verse from the Epistle of St. James as an “Epimith” to one of the fables, and suggests Babrias as their author. Francis Vavassor,[15] a learned French jesuit, entered at greater length on this subject, and produced further proofs from internal evidence, from the use of the word Piræus in describing the harbour of Athens, a name which was not given till two hundred years after Æsop, and from the introduction of other modern words, that many of these fables must have been at least committed to writing posterior to the time of Æsop, and more boldly suggests Babrias as their author or collector.[16] These various references to Babrias induced Dr. Richard Bentley, at the close of the seventeenth century, to examine more minutely the existing versions of Æsop’s Fables, and he maintained that many of them could, with a slight change of words, be resolved into the Scazonic[17] iambics, in which Babrias is known to have written: and, with a greater freedom than the evidence then justified, he put forth, in behalf of Babrias, a claim to the exclusive authorship of these fables. Such a seemingly extravagant theory, thus roundly asserted, excited much opposition. Dr. Bentley[18] met with an able antagonist in a member of the University of Oxford, the Hon. Mr. Charles Boyle,[19] afterwards Earl of Orrery. Their letters and disputations on this subject, enlivened on both sides with much wit and learning, will ever bear a conspicuous place in the literary history of the seventeenth century. The arguments of Dr. Bentley were yet further defended a few years later by Mr. Thomas Tyrwhitt, a well-read scholar, who gave up high civil distinctions that he might devote himself the more unreservedly to literary pursuits. Mr. Tyrwhitt published, A.D. 1776, a Dissertation on Babrias, and a collection of his fables in choliambic metre found in a MS. in the Bodleian Library at Oxford. Francesco de Furia, a learned Italian, contributed further testimony to the correctness of the supposition that Babrias had made a veritable collection of fables by printing from a MS. contained in the Vatican library several fables never before published. In the year 1844, however, new and unexpected light was thrown upon this subject. A veritable copy of Babrias was found in a manner as singular as were the MSS. of Quinctilian’s Institutes, and of Cicero’s Orations by Poggio in the monastery of St. Gall A.D. 1416. M. Menoides, at the suggestion of M. Villemain, Minister of Public Instruction to King Louis Philippe, had been entrusted with a commission to search for ancient MSS., and in carrying out his instructions he found a MS. at the convent of St. Laura, on Mount Athos, which proved to be a copy of the long suspected and wished-for choliambic version of Babrias. This MS. was found to be divided into two books, the one containing a hundred and twenty-five, and the other ninety-five fables. This discovery attracted very general attention, not only as confirming, in a singular manner, the conjectures so boldly made by a long chain of critics, but as bringing to light valuable literary treasures tending to establish the reputation, and to confirm the antiquity and authenticity of the great mass of Æsopian Fable. The Fables thus recovered were soon published. They found a most worthy editor in the late distinguished Sir George Cornewall Lewis, and a translator equally qualified for his task, in the Reverend James Davies, M.A., sometime a scholar of Lincoln College, Oxford, and himself a relation of their English editor. Thus, after an eclipse of many centuries, Babrias shines out as the earliest, and most reliable collector of veritable Æsopian Fables.

Having thus given a complete synopsis of the origin, descent, and history of these fables, it only remains to explain the reasons which have induced the Publishers to prepare a new edition of Æsop, and to state the grounds on which they hope to establish a claim for support and public approval in their undertaking. They boldly assert that the new light thrown upon these fables by the discovery of the metrical version by Babrias, renders a new translation an inevitable necessity. The two chief existing English versions of Æsop are those by Archdeacon Croxall, and by the late Rev. Thomas James, canon of Peterborough. The first of these deviates so very far from the text, that it degenerates into a parody. The fables are so padded, diluted, and altered, as to give very little idea to the reader either of the terseness or the meaning of the original. The second of these is an improvement on its predecessor, but Mr. James, either out of compliance with the wishes of the publishers, or in condescension to the taste prevalent some twenty years ago, has so freely introduced as the point of the fable conventional English sayings which are not sanctioned by the Greek, and which in many instances are scarcely equivalent to it, that his version frequently approaches a paraphrase rather than a translation.

The Publishers therefore ground their first claim for public approval on the necessity of a new translation. They trust further that their present work will have met that necessity in a satisfactory manner. They have sought to give as nearly a literal translation as possible of the Greek text; and they hope that if the reader should miss the smoothness and thoroughly English tone which characterized the previous version of these fables, he will be more than repaid by gaining a nearer approach to the spirit, thoughts, and (in some cases) to the epigrammatic terseness of the original. The Publishers trust to vindicate, on another ground, their claims to a share of public patronage. They have inserted a hundred new fables, and they have the satisfaction of knowing that this edition, on which they have spared no pains nor cost, will afford a larger choice, and greater variety, to the numerous and increasing circle of the admirers of Æsopian Fables. Whatever be the result of their labours, they will be content to have contributed towards promoting a wider acquaintance with fables, the wisdom, excellency, and wonderful suitableness of which to every condition of humanity has been attested and confirmed by the experience of so many generations; and which in all ages, amidst the ever changing fluctuations of human opinion, are adapted alike to amuse the young, and to instruct the thoughtful, and are well fitted to teach all who study them lessons useful for their guidance in every position of political, social, civil, or domestic life.

The Editor must claim the privilege of adding a few words on a matter personal to himself. He has already within the last few months been connected with one edition of Æsop, and it may seem strange that he should be willing to undertake the superintendence of another. His answer is, that the two works on which he has been engaged were totally distinct, and entirely independent of each other. The first was a request to furnish new morals and applications to a definite number of fables; Ihe other was a commission to add a large number of additional fables and to make a wholly new translation. The necessity of a new and improved translation the Editor then recognized, and would have willingly undertaken. It was a wish he had much at heart, and when the proposal was voluntarily made to him by the present Publishers, to undertake the task of a new translation of an enlarged number of Æsop’s Fables, he saw no reason for refusing the offer because of his prior discharge of a totally different design; and he resolved to comply with the request submitted to him, and to do his best towards the attainment of so desirable an object as a purer translation and more literal rendering of fables so justly celebrated.
The following are the sources from which the present translation has been prepared:—

translated_paragraphs: 故事、譬喻和寓言，都是常用而又受人欢迎的施教方式，三者各有自己的特点。故事单讲一段经历，可以有事实依据，也可以全出于想象，不一定非教给人一条道德训诫。譬喻则是有意运用言辞，使所说的话在字面之外另有一层隐含的意思。这层意思可能特指听者或读者，也可能没有这样的特指。寓言与这两者都有相似之处，也都不尽相同。它同故事一样，有一段短小却切实展开的叙事；它同譬喻一样，要传达一层言外之意，实现这一点，主要靠巧妙地引进虚构的人物，而不单靠言辞本身。寓言又有一项有别于故事和譬喻的特有权利，也是它不可分离的禀性：它始终把教益这个重大的目标放在心上，力求使读者领会某项道德准则、社会义务或政治道理。真正的寓言，如要不负这样的高要求，总有一个目的，就是写出人的动机，改善人的行为。然而它让一切意图藏在虚构人物身后，叫原野上的牲畜、天空的飞鸟、林间的草木、森林的猛兽都能开口。读者听进了劝告，却不曾察觉身边有个劝告者。劝人的人一旦显得高人一等，劝告往往叫人难以下咽。现在那种居高临下的姿态被遮掩了，读者不知不觉开始同情纯洁、正直、值得赞许的事物，开始为卑下、可耻、不值得称道的事愤慨，那堂课也就更容易叫人接受。由此看来，真正的寓言家承担着甚为重要的职责。他既不只是个讲故事的人，也不只是个用比喻说话的人。他是重要的教师，匡正风俗，谴责恶行，称许美德。寓言胜过故事和譬喻之处正在于此。寓言家要惹人发笑，又要透过欢快的面貌给人教益。伟大的伊索效仿者费德鲁斯把这双重目的说得很清楚，认为这正是寓言作者的本职。

这本小书有两样赠礼：一是叫人发笑，
二是以明智的忠告，指点生活之道。
伊索寓言始终兼顾这两个目标，其魅力正在这里，也正因此，它才处处为人喜爱。K. O. 缪勒教授说：“希腊寓言有意把人间事务换一身装扮。希腊语 ainos，顾名思义，是一番劝诫，或者更确切地说，是一番责备。人们或是不愿失于直露，或是爱开玩笑，便虚构动物间的一场遭遇，把它藏在里面。古时凡有可靠记载说到伊索式寓言，我们都可见到同样的做法。”〔1〕

构造寓言要精心顾及三件事。第一是叙事本身，第二是从中引出的寓意，第三是认真保持虚构角色各自的特点。叙事宜围绕一个简明的行动，自始至终讲得通，不叫过多细节压住，也不叫太多枝节分散。一篇的寓意应该足够清楚，同叙事紧紧交织，且必然依赖于叙事，以至于每一位读者读到那里，都会得到同一个不容置疑的解释。引入动物或其他虚构角色时，对它们天生的属性以及人们公认加给它们的性情，也应该有无可指摘的细心。狐狸应当狡猾，野兔胆怯，狮子勇猛，狼残忍，公牛强壮，马骄傲，驴有耐性。这部书的许多篇章都极谨严地守着这些准则，只写一件小事，寓意便自然流出，两者紧密相连。多兹利说〔2〕：“伊索的独到之处，使他胜过其他一切借虚构故事说理的作者的，是他用那么朴素的方法，把道理织进故事。《大山产下一只老鼠》，故事本身便嘲弄了装腔作势的夸口者；而他的乌鸦，奶酪从嘴上一掉，几乎像出于无心，竟一并落下了最有力的警告，说尽奉承的厉害。不必添一句话解释。人们惯爱把感想一层叠一层地压在故事后面，那也绝不能叫它留下更深的印象。”〔3〕书中那些虚构入场的动物，性情能自始至终保持一致，也同样值得称道。它们用来刻画人的动机与激情，同时又鲜明地保有自己的机诈或谋略、胆怯或勇气、慷慨或贪婪。

必须承认，这些赞美之辞并不适用于集子里所有的寓言。其中不少篇缺乏统一的构思，叙事和寓意没能密切相扣，动物也选得不够恰当，而这些恰是伊索式好寓言的魅力和长处。考察它们的起源与流传，有的篇章不如别的篇章，便完全说得通了。大多数并非直接出自伊索之手。许多取自生活在伊索之前的古代作家。例如《鹰和夜莺》是赫西俄德讲过的〔4〕，《鹰被缀着自己羽毛的箭射伤》见于埃斯库罗斯〔5〕，狐狸向欺负它的鹰报仇的故事则见于阿尔基洛科斯〔6〕。另有许多篇起源较晚，可追溯到中世纪的修士。不过，这本集子虽然由伊索时代之前和之后的寓言共同构成，仍有充分理由冠上他的名字。他自己写下的数目如此之多，又全都出于同一个模子，式样相同，仿佛钱币上铸着相同的轮廓、面貌和铭文，他因而有资格被视作希腊寓言之父和这一文类的创立者。从那时起，这种文体一直以他为名，他也在后来的各个时代享有道德教师中第一人的地位。〔7〕

伊索最先只是把这些故事讲给别人听，此后很长时间，它们都借不很稳定的口头传统流传。柏拉图提到〔8〕，苏格拉底在狱中等待一艘自德尔福返回的圣船，那艘船一到，便是他死期已至的信号。他利用这段时间把几则寓言改成诗，只写他还记得的那些。据说，约在公元前300年，雅典的哲学家法勒隆的德米特里乌斯第一次把这些寓言收集成册。费德鲁斯或生来就是奴隶，或因后来遭遇不幸而失去自由，后来得到奥古斯都的准许，获得自由民身份。他在公元纪元之初，用拉丁短长格诗仿作了许多寓言。公元315年前后的安条克修辞学家阿弗托尼乌斯写过一篇论述，又把其中一些寓言改写成拉丁散文。这批译作特别值得关注，因为它反映出当时以及此后各时代的一种普遍习俗。修辞学家和哲学家常拿伊索寓言给学生当练习，不仅请学生讨论故事的教益，还要求他们把同一则寓言改作种种新版本，借以锤炼文风，熟习语法。奥索尼乌斯〔9〕是瓦伦提尼安皇帝的朋友，也是西罗马帝国最后一位有声望的诗人。几篇寓言靠他的诗保存下来，和他同时代、名气不大的作者尤利安努斯·提提亚努斯把它们改写成散文。与奥索尼乌斯同时代的阿维埃努斯，也曾把几篇改作拉丁挽歌体。内韦莱在下文会讲到的书中收入这些小诗，它们有时也编入费德鲁斯的集子。

再往下，隔了七个世纪，才又见到关于伊索寓言的记述。在这片漫长的时光里，那些故事似乎被阴影遮蔽，从人们的视野和记忆中消失了。直到十四世纪初，在拜占庭皇帝大力扶助学术的时代，在一座东方宫廷的辉煌之中，伊索的名字和留给后世的记忆才又受到尊崇。君士坦丁堡的博学修士马克西穆斯·普拉努德斯汇集了大约一百五十则寓言。他的生平所知不多。不过普拉努德斯并不是闭门隐修的人，他积极参与公共事务。公元1327年，老安德罗尼库斯皇帝派他出使威尼斯，他因此得以直接接触西方教会的宗主。此后他热诚维护对方的利益，以致招来东方教会当权者的猜忌和迫害。普拉努德斯遭受过两种指责。其一说，他手边有一部巴布里阿斯的抄本（本序结尾还要详论此人），竟然趣味如此之差，把诗本“移置”为散文。其二又说，他根本没见过伊索寓言，冒用这位希腊名家之名，把自己杜撰的故事拿出来充数。实情介于两端之间。普拉努德斯也许自编了少数篇目，或收入一些当时流传的故事；不过书内有充分而难以驳倒的证据，证明他熟悉真正的伊索寓言。由于他接触到的版本大概收在修辞学家和哲学家的各种译写与论说练习里，传本很可能已有讹误。他这部集子之所以既有意思又重要，不只因为它是早期伊索印本的母本或基础，更因为学者的目光由此直接转向了这些寓言。

不过，最后使伊索寓言重新在基督教世界的文学中占有崇高地位的，却要往西方去找，不能只到东方去找。东罗马帝国的灾难接踵而至，公元1453年君士坦丁堡陷落，这些事和其他事件一道，推动了学术在意大利的迅速复兴。人们对伊索寓言兴趣的复苏，与这场学术复兴密不可分。事实上，在重新引起关注的上古著述中，这些寓言便属最早的一批。在那一代大学者心目中，它们同《圣经》以及古代经典作者的作品并列。意大利最著名的学术倡导者之一洛伦佐·瓦拉，不仅将荷马的《伊利亚特》、希罗多德及修昔底德的史著译为拉丁文，也翻译了伊索寓言。

借印刷机而广泛流传的书籍之中，同样有这些寓言。早在1475至1480年间，博努斯·阿库尔西乌斯便把普拉努德斯辑成的寓言集印行了。此后五年之内，卡克斯顿又将它译成英文，1485年在威斯敏斯特修道院的印刷所付印。〔10〕还应指出，这个时代的学术给寓言留下了持久的印记〔11〕。那些年大布道家们常在公开讲道中穿插诙谐故事，一部分便作为可永久保存的东西混入了寓言集。今天在让·罗兰、梅弗雷特和加布里埃尔·巴莱特留下的讲道辞里，仍可看到这类例子。〔12〕这一时期最可能影响过寓言集的出版物，是著名的波焦·布拉乔利尼收集一百则笑话和故事而成的《笑谈录》〔13〕，刊于公元1471年。《磨坊主、儿子和驴》以及《狐狸和樵夫》这两篇，无疑取自此书。

关于这些寓言的知识迅速由意大利传播到德国。宗教改革的几位奠基人对它们的欣赏与认可，使寓言更受欢迎。他们常借这些故事讽刺和抗议罗马教士的伎俩与弊端。声望很高、热心学术的卡梅拉里乌斯积极参与了《奥格斯堡信纲》的起草，还从繁多的职务中挤出时间，编写了一个版本，供自己任教授的蒂宾根大学的学生使用。马丁·路德翻译了其中二十则，梅兰希通还催他把整部译完。著名路德宗神学家、普鲁士国王腓特烈一世的图书馆员戈特弗里德·阿诺德曾提到，在这位大改革家心中，伊索寓言的地位仅次于《圣经》。公元1546年，罗贝尔·埃蒂安的印刷所出版了普拉努德斯寓言集的第二种印本，又据巴黎王家图书馆的一份手稿增收了几篇。

然而，推动伊索寓言在世界文学中重新占有一席之地的最大进展，还在十七世纪初。1610年，一位学识深厚的瑞士人伊萨克·尼古拉·内韦莱编印了这些寓言的第三种印本，题为《伊索寓言汇编》。这是向伟大寓言家致敬的一项壮举，也是当时出版过的最完备的伊索式寓言集。除了普拉努德斯收集、较早几种版本一再重印的篇目，它还收入一百三十六则取自梵蒂冈图书馆抄本、此前从未刊印的寓言，四十则题作阿弗托尼乌斯所作的故事，以及四十三则巴布里阿斯的寓言。书里还有费德鲁斯、阿维埃努斯及其他作者的拉丁文版本。内韦莱这部书构成了一套完整的《伊索寓言文集》。有赖他的辛劳，伊索重新普遍受到喜爱，被尊为人类明智的道德教导者和伟大的教师之一。从内韦莱这本书出版至今的三个世纪里，除了《圣经》，再没有一部书流传得比伊索寓言更广。它们已译成欧洲及东方的大部分语言，犹太人、古代异教徒、穆斯林、基督徒一样在读，也将一代代继续读下去。今天，它们不但融入了文明世界的文学，而且进入各国居民的日常往来与闲谈，熟悉得如家常用语一般。
在伊索式寓言重振声名的历史上，内韦莱的集子是个高峰。它的序言里还包含一个构想的萌芽，后来竟由一连串奇特的机缘得到证实，这也使它值得留意。内韦莱隐约提出，现存形态的伊索式寓言，真正的作者或将证明是一个名叫巴布里阿斯的人。这个暗示后来引出一系列考察。今日要充分理解伊索本人和那些冠他之名的作品究竟是什么关系，不能不对这些考察有所了解。

巴布里阿斯的身世奇特有趣，列入文学掌故也毫不勉强。通常认为他是小亚细亚某个伊奥尼亚殖民地的希腊人，但他生活和写作的确切年代至今没有定论。一位批评家〔14〕把他推到公元前250年亚该亚同盟立盟之时，另一位却把他推迟到公元235年去世的塞维鲁皇帝时代，还有人认为他和费德鲁斯一样生活在奥古斯都治下。无论他的伊索版本写于何时，那些作品似乎因某个奇怪的缘故全部消失了。阿维埃努斯提过他的名字；十一世纪末著名的评论家苏伊达斯也提过，并在词典里引了他所写寓言的若干零散诗句；生活在十二世纪后半叶君士坦丁堡的语法家兼诗人约翰·采采斯同样谈到过他。在上述那本集子的序言里，内韦莱指出，普拉努德斯的寓言不可能是伊索当年写下的原文。书里有两处提到“圣洁的修士”，还有一篇拿《雅各书》里的一句经文作篇末点明寓意的结句。他提出作者可能是巴布里阿斯。法国博学的耶稣会士弗朗索瓦·瓦瓦瑟〔15〕更详尽地讨论了此事，提出进一步的书内证据。书里称雅典的港口为比雷埃夫斯，这个名字却在伊索之后两百年才出现；还用到了其他一些后起的词。由此可知，至少有许多篇是在伊索身后才被写定。他更大胆地推测，巴布里阿斯就是它们的作者或辑者。〔16〕有关巴布里阿斯的种种线索，促使理查德·本特利博士在十七世纪末仔细检视现存各版伊索寓言。他主张，许多篇只须略换几个词，便能还原为巴布里阿斯惯用的跛行短长格诗〔17〕。他更进一步，说这些寓言全是巴布里阿斯一人所作；这就超出了当时证据所能支持的范围。如此直截了当地断言这一看似过分的理论，激起了不小的反对。本特利博士〔18〕遇到一个有本事的对手，牛津大学的查尔斯·博伊尔阁下〔19〕，即后来的奥雷里伯爵。双方围绕这一题目往还的信札与论争，处处见学问和机智，在十七世纪的文学史上将永远占有醒目的位置。若干年后，博学的托马斯·特怀特进一步为本特利的论据辩护。他为了更专心研究文学，放弃了崇高的公职。公元1776年，他发表了论巴布里阿斯的专著，并刊出牛津博德利图书馆手稿里以跛行短长格写成的寓言。意大利学者弗朗切斯科·德·富里亚从梵蒂冈图书馆的手稿里印出数篇从未发表的寓言，进一步佐证了巴布里阿斯确曾编辑过寓言集。1844年，这个问题上又有了出人意料的新发现。一部真正的巴布里阿斯抄本现身了。发现的奇特程度，不亚于公元1416年波焦在圣加仑修道院找到昆体良《演说术原理》与西塞罗《演说集》手稿。在法国国王路易-菲利普的公共教育大臣维尔曼的倡议下，梅诺伊德斯先生受命寻找古代手稿。他奉命搜访，在阿索斯山的大拉夫拉修道院发现一份抄本，正是学者们长期猜想其存在、又殷切寻觅的巴布里阿斯跛行短长格寓言本。抄本分两卷，一卷一百二十五则，一卷九十五则。它不仅出人意表地印证了历代批评者的大胆猜想，还让珍贵的文学遗存重见天日，有助于确立大部分伊索式寓言的声誉，证实其古老和真实。这一发现引起了极其广泛的注意，复得的寓言很快就出版了。已故的著名学者乔治·康沃尔·刘易斯爵士担当编辑，实至名归。译者詹姆斯·戴维斯牧师同样胜任，他是文学硕士，曾为牛津林肯学院的学者，又与这位英国编辑有亲属关系。经过好几个世纪的黯淡无闻，巴布里阿斯终于重现光辉，成为已知真正的伊索式寓言最早而又最可靠的编集者。

上文既已全面概述这些寓言的起源、传承和历史，接下来只须说明出版者为何要另备一版《伊索寓言》，以及他们希望凭什么得到公众的支持和认可。他们愿意大胆地说，巴布里阿斯韵文本的发现，使人们对这些寓言有了新的认识，另做一次翻译已势所必然。目前主要有两种英译，一种是克罗克索尔副主教所译，一种是已故彼得伯勒座堂教士托马斯·詹姆斯牧师所译。第一种偏离原文太远，以致近于仿作。寓言被铺张、稀释、改动到这般地步，读者不大看得出原本的简劲，也摸不到本意。第二种比前者好些，但詹姆斯先生也许是迁就出版者的意思，也许是屈从大约二十年前盛行的口味，时常把英格兰惯说的俗谚拿来替代故事的要旨。那些话在希腊原文里没有依据，不少在意义上也相去甚远，他的译本遂往往更接近意述。

因此，出版者首先以重译的必要为理由，盼望获得公众认可。他们也相信，新作已经妥善满足这项需要。他们力求尽可能按字面翻译希腊文本。先前的英译有一股流畅而十足英国式的语调，读者若怀念它，新译本对原作精神、见解，以及个别篇章警句般凝练语气的靠近，想必足以补偿这点缺憾。出版者还希望用另一个理由争取公众支持。他们增入了一百则新寓言。这一版不惜工本、不辞辛苦，使日益增多的伊索寓言爱好者有更多、更丰富的篇目可挑选，这令出版者感到欣慰。无论这些劳作最终得到何种结果，只要能使更多人认识这些寓言，他们就已满足。许多世代的亲身经验一再见证了其中的智慧、长处，以及它们对于各种人生处境的奇妙适切。在见解不断变动的所有时代，它们都能给年轻人乐趣，给愿意思考的人教益；无论在政治、社会、公民还是家庭生活里处于什么位置，认真研读它们的人都能得到有助于行事的启发。

编者还得请求容许，就自己说几句私事。前几个月，他已经参与另一项伊索寓言的出版工作，现在还愿意主持新的一项，也许叫人奇怪。他的答复是，两项工作完全不同，也彼此独立。先前的一项，是为数目确定的一批寓言补写新的寓意和应用说明；后一项则是要大量增补篇目，重做一部全新的译本。在做前一项工作时，编者就已经意识到有必要重译，好把原作译得更好，也乐于承担。那原是他的一个心愿。如今的出版者主动提出，请他重译数量更多的伊索寓言。他既然只是执行过一个全然不同的计划，就看不出非得因此回绝这份邀请的道理。他决心应允所请，竭尽全力，让这些理所当然广受赞誉的寓言，获得一种更纯正、更接近原文字面的译法。
本次英译所依据的文献如下。
《巴布里阿斯所作伊索寓言》，乔治·康沃尔·刘易斯编，牛津，1846年。
《巴布里阿斯所作伊索寓言》第二部，乔治·康沃尔·刘易斯据手稿编订，伦敦，帕克出版，1857年。
《伊索寓言汇编》，伊萨克·尼古拉·内韦莱编著，法兰克福，1610年。
《普拉努德斯以前流传的伊索寓言》，弗朗切斯科·德·富里亚整理，莱比锡，1810年。
《伊索寓言集》，卡尔·哈尔姆校订，莱比锡，1851年。
《费德鲁斯所作伊索寓言》，王太子古典丛书，1822年。
乔治·法伊勒·汤森

source_paragraphs: The Life and History of Æsop is involved, like that of Homer, the most famous of Greek poets, in much obscurity. Sardis, the capital of Lydia; Samos, a Greek island; Mesembria, an ancient colony in Thrace; and Cotiæum, the chief city of a province of Phrygia, contend for the distinction of being the birthplace of Æsop. Although the honour thus claimed cannot be definitely assigned to any one of these places, yet there are a few incidents now generally accepted by scholars as established facts, relating to the birth, life, and death of Æsop. He is, by an almost universal consent, allowed to have been born about the year 620 B.C., and to have been by birth a slave. He was owned by two masters in succession, both inhabitants of Samos, Xanthus and Jadmon, the latter of whom gave him his liberty as a reward for his learning and wit. One of the privileges of a freedman in the ancient republics of Greece, was the permission to take an active interest in public affairs; and Æsop, like the philosophers Phædo, Menippus, and Epictetus, in later times, raised himself from the indignity of a servile condition to a position of high renown. In his desire alike to instruct and to be instructed, he travelled through many countries, and among others came to Sardis, the capital of the famous king of Lydia, the great patron, in that day, of learning and of learned men. He met at the court of Crœsus with Solon, Thales, and other sages, and is related so to have pleased his royal master by the part he took in the conversations held with these philosophers, that he applied to him an expression which has since passed into a proverb, “μᾶλλον ὁ Φρύξ.” “The Phrygian has spoken better than all.”

On the invitation of Crœsus he fixed his residence at Sardis, and was employed by that monarch in various difficult and delicate affairs of State. In his discharge of these commissions he visited the different petty republics of Greece. At one time he is found in Corinth, and at another in Athens, endeavouring, by the narration of some of his wise fables, to reconcile the inhabitants of those cities to the administration of their respective rulers Periander and Pisistratus. One of these ambassadorial missions, undertaken at the command of Crœsus, was the occasion of his death. Having been sent to Delphi with a large sum of gold for distribution among the citizens, he was so provoked at their covetousness that he refused to divide the money, and sent it back to his master. The Delphians, enraged at this treatment, accused him of impiety, and, in spite of his sacred character as ambassador, executed him as a public criminal. This cruel death of Æsop was not unavenged. The citizens of Delphi were visited with a series of calamities, until they made a public reparation of their crime; and, “The blood of Æsop” became a well-known adage, bearing witness to the truth that deeds of wrong would not pass unpunished. Neither did the great fabulist lack posthumous honours; for a statue was erected to his memory at Athens, the work of Lysippus, one of the most famous of Greek sculptors. Phædrus thus immortalizes the event:—

Æsopo ingentem statuam posuere Attici,
Servumque collocarunt æternâ in basi:
Patere honoris scirent ut cuncti viam;
Nec generi tribui sed virtuti gloriam.

These few facts are all that can be relied on with any degree of certainty, in reference to the birth, life, and death of Æsop. They were first brought to light, after a patient search and diligent perusal of ancient authors, by a Frenchman, M. Claude Gaspard Bachet de Mezeriac, who declined the honour of being tutor to Louis XIII. of France, from his desire to devote himself exclusively to literature. He published his Life of Æsop, Anno Domini 1632. The later investigations of a host of English and German scholars have added very little to the facts given by M. Mezeriac. The substantial truth of his statements has been confirmed by later criticism and inquiry. It remains to state, that prior to this publication of M. Mezeriac, the life of Æsop was from the pen of Maximus Planudes, a monk of Constantinople, who was sent on an embassy to Venice by the Byzantine Emperor Andronicus the elder, and who wrote in the early part of the fourteenth century. His life was prefixed to all the early editions of these fables, and was republished as late as 1727 by Archdeacon Croxall as the introduction to his edition of Æsop. This life by Planudes contains, however, so small an amount of truth, and is so full of absurd pictures of the grotesque deformity of Æsop, of wondrous apocryphal stories, of lying legends, and gross anachronisms, that it is now universally condemned as false, puerile, and unauthentic.[20] It is given up in the present day, by general consent, as unworthy of the slightest credit.
translated_paragraphs: 伊索的生平，和希腊最著名的诗人荷马的生平一样，笼罩在许多迷雾之中。吕底亚的首都萨尔迪斯、希腊岛屿萨摩斯、色雷斯的古殖民城梅森布里亚、弗里吉亚一省的首府科蒂埃翁，都争称自己是伊索的诞生地。这样的荣誉固然很难肯定地判给其中任何一地，不过关于他的出生、一生和去世，却有少数事迹是当时学者普遍接受为已知事实的。人们大抵同意，他生于公元前620年左右，生来是奴隶。他先后属于两个主人，都住在萨摩斯，一位名叫克桑托斯，一位名叫伊阿德蒙。后者为奖赏他的学识和机智，还给他自由。古希腊各共和国里，自由民所享有的特权之一，是可以积极参与公共事务。伊索与较后时代的哲学家斐多、梅尼普斯和爱比克泰德一样，从卑下的奴役身份走到了极有声望的地位。他既愿教人，也愿受教，因此走过许多国家，来到萨尔迪斯等城。萨尔迪斯正是那位著名吕底亚国王的都城，国王是当时学业和学者的重要赞助者。在克罗伊索斯的宫廷，伊索遇到了梭伦、泰勒斯及其他贤者。据说他参加这些哲学家的论谈，发言使国王如此满意，国王便用后来成为谚语的一句话赞许他：“μᾶλλον ὁ Φρύξ。”意思是“弗里吉亚人比谁说得都好”。

应克罗伊索斯的邀请，伊索定居萨尔迪斯，国王又派他办理多种棘手而须谨慎应付的国事。执行这些使命时，他遍访希腊的小共和国。有时他在科林斯，有时在雅典，设法讲几则明智的寓言，使两城居民能够接受各自的统治者佩里安德和庇西特拉图的治理。一次奉克罗伊索斯之命前往他邦的出使，成为他的死因。他带着大笔金子到德尔福，原是要分发给当地居民。那些人的贪婪却将他激怒，以至于他拒绝分钱，把金子送还了主人。德尔福人大为愤怒，指控他不敬神，罔顾他身为使者应受保护的身份，竟将他当作罪犯处死。这样残酷的死并非没有得到报应。德尔福的居民接二连三遭逢灾祸，直到他们公开为罪行作出补偿。“伊索的血”也成了一句人所熟知的谚语，见证恶行终将受罚的道理。这位大寓言家身后也并不缺少哀荣。雅典为他竖立塑像纪念他，作者是希腊最著名的雕塑家之一利西波斯。费德鲁斯以这样的诗句使这件事长留后世：

阿提卡人为伊索立下巍巍的像，
让一位奴隶站上不朽的基座。
要使众人知道，荣誉之路向人敞开；
光荣不归出身，而归于美德。

关于伊索的出生、生平及死亡，可以稍有把握地依靠的，就是上述几件事。最先为它们拂尘使其重见天日的是法国人克洛德·加斯帕尔·巴谢·德·梅泽里亚克。他耐心搜寻、细读古代作家的作品，为了专务文学，甚至谢绝担任法国国王路易十三的教师这一殊荣。他于公元1632年出版《伊索传》。此后众多英德学者的考察，对他给出的事实几乎没有什么补充。后来的批评与考证证实了他陈述的大体真实性。还应说明，在梅泽里亚克的著作以前，流传的《伊索传》出于君士坦丁堡修士马克西穆斯·普拉努德斯之手。拜占庭皇帝老安德罗尼库斯派他出使过威尼斯，他在十四世纪初写下这篇传记。一切早期寓言印本都把传记放在卷首。迟至1727年，克罗克索尔副主教还把它重印作他那版伊索的引言。然而这篇传记所含的真实成分如此之少，关于伊索形貌怪异丑陋的描画如此荒唐，充斥离奇缺据的故事、虚假的传说和严重的时代错置，以至如今普遍被评为虚妄、幼稚、不足凭信。〔20〕今天人们一致弃而不取，认为它丝毫不足采信。

source_paragraphs: A LION was awakened from sleep by a Mouse running over his face. Rising up angrily, he caught him and was about to kill him, when the Mouse piteously entreated, saying: “If you would only spare my life, I would be sure to repay your kindness.” The Lion laughed and let him go. It happened shortly after this that the Lion was caught by some hunters, who bound him by strong ropes to the ground. The Mouse, recognizing his roar, came and gnawed the rope with his teeth, and set him free, exclaiming:

“You ridiculed the idea of my ever being able to help you, not expecting to receive from me any repayment of your favour; now you know that it is possible for even a Mouse to confer benefits on a Lion.”
translated_paragraphs: 有一只老鼠从狮子脸上跑过，把熟睡的狮子惊醒了。狮子恼怒地起身，一爪将它按住，正要弄死它，老鼠可怜巴巴地哀求：“只要您肯饶我一条命，我一定会报答这份好心。”狮子笑了一声，放它走了。没过多久，几个猎人逮到狮子，用结实的绳子将它缚在地上。老鼠认出了它的吼声，赶来用牙齿把绳咬断，放了它，说道：
“上回我说能帮您，您还笑话我。您哪里料得到，这份恩情我也还得起？如今您知道了，一只老鼠也能帮上一头狮子。”

source_paragraphs: WOLF, meeting with a Lamb astray from the fold, resolved not to lay violent hands on him, but to find some plea to justify to the Lamb the Wolf’s right to eat him. He thus addressed him: “Sirrah, last year you grossly insulted me.” “Indeed,” bleated the Lamb in a mournful tone of voice, “I was not then born.” Then said the Wolf, “You feed in my pasture.” “No, good sir,” replied the Lamb, “I have not yet tasted grass.” Again said the Wolf, “You drink of my well.” “No,” exclaimed the Lamb, “I never yet drank water, for as yet my mother’s milk is both food and drink to me.” Upon which the Wolf seized him and ate him up, saying, “Well! I won’t remain supperless, even though you refute every one of my imputations.” The tyrant will always find a pretext for his tyranny.
translated_paragraphs: 狼遇见一只离群的小羊，打定主意，不忙动粗，先找条理由，好向小羊证明自己吃它吃得有理。“小子！”狼开口道，“去年你狠狠地侮辱过我。”小羊凄凄地咩了一声：“我那时还没出生呢。”狼又说：“你吃我的草场里的草。”“没有呀，先生，”小羊说，“我还没尝过青草。”狼又说：“你喝我井里的水！”小羊叫道：“没有！我从来没喝过水。到今天，我吃的喝的，都只是母亲的奶。”狼一把抓住小羊，把它吃了，还说：“好吧！哪怕你把我的每条指控都驳倒，我也不会让晚餐没了着落。”暴君要行暴，总找得到借口。

source_paragraphs: AN ASS having heard some Grasshoppers chirping, was highly enchanted; and, desiring to possess the same charms of melody, demanded what sort of food they lived on to give them such beautiful voices. They replied, “The dew.” The Ass resolved that he would live only upon dew, and in a short time died of hunger.
translated_paragraphs: 一头驴听见几只蚱蜢鸣唱，深深着迷，恨不得自己也有一样动听的调子。它连忙打听：“你们靠吃什么过活，才有这么好的嗓音？”蚱蜢们回答：“露水。”驴于是下定决心，此后只靠露水生活。没过多久，它就饿死了。

source_paragraphs: A WOLF who had a bone stuck in his throat hired a Crane, for a large sum, to put her head into his mouth and draw out the bone. When the Crane had extracted the bone and demanded the promised payment, the Wolf, grinning and grinding his teeth, exclaimed: “Why, you have surely already had a sufficient recompense, in having been permitted to draw out your head in safety from the mouth and jaws of a wolf.”
In serving the wicked, expect no reward, and be thankful if you escape injury for your pains.
translated_paragraphs: 狼的喉咙里卡了一根骨头。它许下重金，请鹤把头探进它嘴里，将骨头取出。鹤取出了骨头，来要说好的报酬。狼咧嘴一笑，磨着牙说：“咦！你能够把脑袋从一头狼的嘴里、从这两排牙齿中平平安安抽出去，还嫌这份报酬不够丰厚吗？”
替恶人办事，别指望报酬。出力之后还能全身而退，就该庆幸了。

source_paragraphs: A FATHER had a family of sons who were perpetually quarreling among themselves. When he failed to heal their disputes by his exhortations, he determined to give them a practical illustration of the evils of disunion; and for this purpose he one day told them to bring him a bundle of sticks. When they had done so, he placed the faggot into the hands of each of them in succession, and ordered them to break it in pieces. They tried with all their strength, and were not able to do it. He next opened the faggot, took the sticks separately, one by one, and again put them into his sons’ hands, upon which they broke them easily. He then addressed them in these words: “My sons, if you are of one mind, and unite to assist each other, you will be as this faggot, uninjured by all the attempts of your enemies; but if you are divided among yourselves, you will be broken as easily as these sticks.”
translated_paragraphs: 有个父亲，他那些儿子成年累月争吵不休。劝了又劝，既然解不开他们的纷争，他决定让他们亲眼看看兄弟不和的坏处。一天，他叫儿子们拿来一捆树枝。他接过来，把整捆树枝挨个儿交到他们手上，叫各人折断它。大家使足了力气，谁也没能成功。接下来，他解开绳子，将枝条一根一根分开，又递到儿子们手里。这次他们轻轻松松就折断了。父亲便对他们说：“我的孩子们，假如你们同心，肯团结起来互相帮助，就会像方才那一捆树枝，敌人怎么折腾也伤不到你们。可你们若从中分裂，就会像这些散枝一样容易折断。”

source_paragraphs: A BAT who fell upon the ground and was caught by a Weasel pleaded to be spared his life. The Weasel refused, saying that he was by nature the enemy of all birds. The Bat assured him that he was not a bird, but a mouse, and thus was set free. Shortly afterwards the Bat again fell to the ground and was caught by another Weasel, whom he likewise entreated not to eat him. The Weasel said that he had a special hostility to mice. The Bat assured him that he was not a mouse, but a bat, and thus a second time escaped.
It is wise to turn circumstances to good account.
translated_paragraphs: 一只蝙蝠掉到地上，给一只黄鼠狼捉住，便恳求它饶自己一命。黄鼠狼不肯，说自己天生就与一切鸟儿为敌。蝙蝠向它保证，自己不是鸟，是老鼠。这才得以脱身。没过多久，蝙蝠又落到地面，被另一只黄鼠狼捉住，同样央求对方别吃自己。黄鼠狼说，它最痛恨的恰恰是老鼠。蝙蝠向它保证，自己不是老鼠，是蝙蝠，于是第二次逃过一劫。
懂得因应处境，往往能转危为安。

source_paragraphs: A COCK, scratching for food for himself and his hens, found a precious stone and exclaimed: “If your owner had found thee, and not I, he would have taken thee up, and have set thee in thy first estate; but I have found thee for no purpose. I would rather have one barleycorn than all the jewels in the world.”
translated_paragraphs: 公鸡给自己和母鸡们刨食，刨到了一颗宝石。它叫道：“要是发现你的是你的主人，不是我，他准会把你捡起来，送你回到昔日尊贵的地方。可碰上我，这下你算是白给找见啦。一粒大麦，对我也好过全世界的珠宝。”

source_paragraphs: THE SWALLOW and the Crow had a contention about their plumage. The Crow put an end to the dispute by saying, “Your feathers are all very well in the spring, but mine protect me against the winter.”
Fair weather friends are not worth much.
translated_paragraphs: 燕子和乌鸦为谁的羽毛好起了争执。乌鸦一句话结束了争论：“春天里，你的羽毛确实漂亮。可我的这一身，到了冬天还能替我挡风寒。”
只在好天气里才肯作伴的朋友，值不了多少。

source_paragraphs: THE BEASTS of the field and forest had a Lion as their king. He was neither wrathful, cruel, nor tyrannical, but just and gentle as a king could be. During his reign he made a royal proclamation for a general assembly of all the birds and beasts, and drew up conditions for a universal league, in which the Wolf and the Lamb, the Panther and the Kid, the Tiger and the Stag, the Dog and the Hare, should live together in perfect peace and amity. The Hare said, “Oh, how I have longed to see this day, in which the weak shall take their place with impunity by the side of the strong.” And after the Hare said this, he ran for his life.
translated_paragraphs: 原野与森林里的走兽们有一位狮王。它不暴怒，不残酷，也不专横，是一位君王所能做得到的那样公正、温和。在位期间，它颁下诏书，召集一切飞禽走兽，又拟好条款，要大家缔结一项普遍的盟约。狼和小羊、豹和小山羊、虎和雄鹿、狗和野兔，全都该从此和平相处、彼此友爱。野兔说：“唉，这一天我惦记多久了！弱者终于能挨着强者站，什么坏处也不会有。”刚说完这番话，它就撒腿逃命去了。

source_paragraphs: A TRAVELER about to set out on a journey saw his Dog stand at the door stretching himself. He asked him sharply: “Why do you stand there gaping? Everything is ready but you, so come with me instantly.” The Dog, wagging his tail, replied: “O, master! I am quite ready; it is you for whom I am waiting.”
The loiterer often blames delay on his more active friend.
translated_paragraphs: 一个人就要出远门，看见他的狗在门口伸懒腰，便厉声问它：“你还站在那儿打什么呵欠？样样都齐了，就差你了。快跟我走！”
狗摇了摇尾巴：“主人，我早就准备好了呀。我等的是您。”
磨磨蹭蹭的人，倒常怪走得快的同伴耽搁了他。

source_paragraphs: THE ANTS were spending a fine winter’s day drying grain collected in the summertime. A Grasshopper, perishing with famine, passed by and earnestly begged for a little food. The Ants inquired of him, “Why did you not treasure up food during the summer?” He replied, “I had not leisure enough. I passed the days in singing.” They then said in derision: “If you were foolish enough to sing all the summer, you must dance supperless to bed in the winter.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个晴朗的冬日，蚂蚁们正把夏天收的谷粒摊开晾晒。一只蚱蜢快饿死了，路过此处，诚恳地乞求一点吃的。蚂蚁问它：“夏天你怎么没把粮食存起来？”它回答：“我抽不出空。那些天，我都在唱歌。”蚂蚁们便嘲笑道：“整个夏天你傻到只顾唱歌，那么冬天就只好饿着肚子，跳着舞上床去吧。”

source_paragraphs: A HARE one day ridiculed the short feet and slow pace of the Tortoise, who replied, laughing: “Though you be swift as the wind, I will beat you in a race.” The Hare, believing her assertion to be simply impossible, assented to the proposal; and they agreed that the Fox should choose the course and fix the goal. On the day appointed for the race the two started together. The Tortoise never for a moment stopped, but went on with a slow but steady pace straight to the end of the course. The Hare, lying down by the wayside, fell fast asleep. At last waking up, and moving as fast as he could, he saw the Tortoise had reached the goal, and was comfortably dozing after her fatigue.
Slow but steady wins the race.
translated_paragraphs: 有一天，野兔嘲笑乌龟脚短、走得慢。乌龟笑着答：“哪怕你快得像风，赛跑我也能赢你。”野兔认定它这话绝无可能，便答应比赛。他们商量好，让狐狸挑路线、定终点。比赛那天，两个一起上路。乌龟一刻也不休息，步子虽慢却很稳，一直朝终点走。野兔在路旁一躺，睡熟了。它总算醒来，能跑多快就跑多快，抬眼一看，乌龟早已到了终点，赶了这么久的路，正在安安稳稳地打盹儿呢。
走得慢却不肯停，照样能赢得比赛。

source_paragraphs: A CHARCOAL-BURNER carried on his trade in his own house. One day he met a friend, a Fuller, and entreated him to come and live with him, saying that they should be far better neighbors and that their housekeeping expenses would be lessened. The Fuller replied, “The arrangement is impossible as far as I am concerned, for whatever I should whiten, you would immediately blacken again with your charcoal.”
Like will draw like.
translated_paragraphs: 烧炭人就在自己家里烧炭。一天，他遇见一位给人漂布的朋友，热心地请朋友搬来同住：“我们做近邻多好！两个人合起来过日子，开销也小。”
漂布人说：“这主意我可办不到。我刚把布漂白，你的炭灰就又把它弄黑啦。”
相投的才容易聚在一起。

source_paragraphs: A BOY was hunting for locusts. He had caught a goodly number, when he saw a Scorpion, and mistaking him for a locust, reached out his hand to take him. The Scorpion, showing his sting, said: “If you had but touched me, my friend, you would have lost me, and all your locusts too!”
translated_paragraphs: 一个男孩在捉蝗虫，已经捉了不少。忽然他看见一只蝎子，还当也是蝗虫，伸手就去抓。蝎子把毒刺一亮，说：“朋友，你要是真的碰到了我，连我带你捉的那些蝗虫，可就一只都别想留住啦！”

source_paragraphs: A FISHERMAN skilled in music took his flute and his nets to the seashore. Standing on a projecting rock, he played several tunes in the hope that the fish, attracted by his melody, would of their own accord dance into his net, which he had placed below. At last, having long waited in vain, he laid aside his flute, and casting his net into the sea, made an excellent haul of fish. When he saw them leaping about in the net upon the rock he said: “O you most perverse creatures, when I piped you would not dance, but now that I have ceased you do so merrily.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个渔夫很会吹笛子。他把笛子和渔网一同带到海边，站上一块探出水面的石头，在石头底下张开网，接连吹了好几支曲子。他盼着鱼儿迷上笛声，自己跳着舞游进网里。
等啊等，一条鱼也没来。渔夫搁下笛子，把网往海里一撒，这一网倒捞起好多鱼。他把网拖上石头，看见鱼儿在网眼里蹦跳，便说：“你们这些爱跟人作对的小东西！我吹的时候，你们不肯跳。我不吹了，一个个反倒跳得这么起劲！”

source_paragraphs: A DOG, crossing a bridge over a stream with a piece of flesh in his mouth, saw his own shadow in the water and took it for that of another Dog, with a piece of meat double his own in size. He immediately let go of his own, and fiercely attacked the other Dog to get his larger piece from him. He thus lost both: that which he grasped at in the water, because it was a shadow; and his own, because the stream swept it away.
translated_paragraphs: 一条狗叼着一块肉过溪桥，看见自己在水里的倒影，以为是另一条狗，那狗嘴里叼着一块比它的大一倍的肉。它立刻松开自己的那块，凶猛地扑向另一条狗，要把那块大的夺过来。这样一来，两块都没了。水里那块它抓不到，因为那只是一道影子；自己的那块也没了，因为溪水已把肉冲走。

source_paragraphs: A CARTER was driving a wagon along a country lane, when the wheels sank down deep into a rut. The rustic driver, stupefied and aghast, stood looking at the wagon, and did nothing but utter loud cries to Hercules to come and help him. Hercules, it is said, appeared and thus addressed him: “Put your shoulders to the wheels, my man. Goad on your bullocks, and never more pray to me for help, until you have done your best to help yourself, or depend upon it you will henceforth pray in vain.”
Self-help is the best help.
translated_paragraphs: 一个车夫赶着货车行在乡间小路上。车轮深深陷进车辙里，庄稼汉慌得不知所措，呆望着车子，别的什么也不干，只大声呼唤大力神赫拉克勒斯快来相助。据说大力神真的出现了，对他说：“伙计，把你自己的肩膀顶在车轮上。赶着你那几头牛使劲拉。你还没尽全力帮自己，以后就别再求我帮忙。否则我可告诉你，往后的祷告也一定是白费。”
自助是最好的帮助。

source_paragraphs: A MOLE, a creature blind from birth, once said to his Mother: “I am sure than I can see, Mother!” In the desire to prove to him his mistake, his Mother placed before him a few grains of frankincense, and asked, “What is it?” The young Mole said, “It is a pebble.” His Mother exclaimed: “My son, I am afraid that you are not only blind, but that you have lost your sense of smell.”
translated_paragraphs: 鼹鼠在这个故事里生来就是个瞎子。有一回，小鼹鼠对母亲说：“妈妈，我敢肯定，我看得见！”母亲要让它明白自己错在哪里，就在它面前放了几颗乳香，问：“这是什么？”小鼹鼠答：“是一颗小石子。”母亲叹道：“孩子，只怕你不但眼睛看不见，连鼻子也不管用啦。”

sections.title_en: The Herdsman and the Lost Bull
source_paragraphs: A HERDSMAN tending his flock in a forest lost a Bull-calf from the fold. After a long and fruitless search, he made a vow that, if he could only discover the thief who had stolen the Calf, he would offer a lamb in sacrifice to Hermes, Pan, and the Guardian Deities of the forest. Not long afterwards, as he ascended a small hillock, he saw at its foot a Lion feeding on the Calf. Terrified at the sight, he lifted his eyes and his hands to heaven, and said: “Just now I vowed to offer a lamb to the Guardian Deities of the forest if I could only find out who had robbed me; but now that I have discovered the thief, I would willingly add a full-grown Bull to the Calf I have lost, if I may only secure my own escape from him in safety.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个牧人赶牲口进树林，圈中走失了一头小公牛。他找了很久，一无所得，便立誓说，只要能发现是谁偷了小牛，就拿一只羊羔献给赫尔墨斯神、潘神和护佑森林的神灵。不久以后，他登上一座小丘，看见丘脚有头狮子，正在吃他的小牛。这个景象吓坏了他。他举起两手，抬眼望天，说：“刚才我许下心愿，只要找到偷我牲口的是谁，就向森林的守护神献一只羊羔。如今我知道谁是贼了。要是我能平平安安从它口下逃出去，除了那头已经丢掉的小牛，我还心甘情愿再添上一头长大了的公牛。”

source_paragraphs: A YOUNG FAWN once said to his Mother, “You are larger than a dog, and swifter, and more used to running, and you have your horns as a defense; why, then, O Mother! do the hounds frighten you so?” She smiled, and said: “I know full well, my son, that all you say is true. I have the advantages you mention, but when I hear even the bark of a single dog I feel ready to faint, and fly away as fast as I can.”
No arguments will give courage to the coward.
translated_paragraphs: 小鹿有一次问母亲：“你比狗高大，比狗跑得快，也比狗更惯于奔跑，还有角可以防卫。妈妈，为什么猎犬会把你吓成那个样子？”母鹿微笑着说：“孩子，你说的句句属实，我完全明白。你说的那些长处，我也样样都有。可是，只要听到哪怕一条狗的叫声，我就觉得眼前发黑，要昏过去，只会拔腿飞逃。”
再有道理的话，也给不了胆怯者勇气。

sections.title_en: The Ass, the Fox, and the Lion
source_paragraphs: THE ASS and the Fox, having entered into partnership together for their mutual protection, went out into the forest to hunt. They had not proceeded far when they met a Lion. The Fox, seeing imminent danger, approached the Lion and promised to contrive for him the capture of the Ass if the Lion would pledge his word not to harm the Fox. Then, upon assuring the Ass that he would not be injured, the Fox led him to a deep pit and arranged that he should fall into it. The Lion, seeing that the Ass was secured, immediately clutched the Fox, and attacked the Ass at his leisure.
translated_paragraphs: 驴和狐狸结为伙伴，为的是相互保护。它们一起进林子打猎，没走多远，碰见了狮子。狐狸看出危险就在眼前，便走近狮子，答应设计让它捉住驴，只要狮子保证绝不伤害狐狸。随后狐狸向驴担保它不会受害，把它带到一个深坑旁，设法叫它掉了下去。狮子一看驴子已经插翅难逃，立刻伸爪抓住了狐狸，至于坑里的驴，留待方便的时候再去对付。

source_paragraphs: A NUMBER of Flies were attracted to a jar of honey which had been overturned in a housekeeper’s room, and placing their feet in it, ate greedily. Their feet, however, became so smeared with the honey that they could not use their wings, nor release themselves, and were suffocated. Just as they were expiring, they exclaimed, “O foolish creatures that we are, for the sake of a little pleasure we have destroyed ourselves.”
Pleasure bought with pains, hurts.
translated_paragraphs: 管家屋里翻倒了一罐蜂蜜，引来了许多苍蝇。它们把脚落在蜜里，贪婪地吃了起来。可是脚上沾的蜜太多，翅膀使不上劲，也挣脱不了，最后都窒息了。临死时，它们喊道：“我们这些蠢东西！就为了一点点快活，竟把自己毁了。”
拿苦痛换来的快乐，终究会伤人。

source_paragraphs: A CONTROVERSY prevailed among the beasts of the field as to which of the animals deserved the most credit for producing the greatest number of whelps at a birth. They rushed clamorously into the presence of the Lioness and demanded of her the settlement of the dispute. “And you,” they said, “how many sons have you at a birth?” The Lioness laughed at them, and said: “Why! I have only one; but that one is altogether a thoroughbred Lion.”
The value is in the worth, not in the number.
translated_paragraphs: 田野上的走兽争论不休：哪一种动物一胎生的小崽最多，就最该得称赞？它们吵吵嚷嚷拥到母狮面前，要她裁决这场争论。“那你呢，”它们问，“你一胎生几个孩子？”母狮笑它们：“我呀，只生一个。可那一个，从头到尾都是头纯种的狮子。”
衡量价值，看的是质地，不是数量。

source_paragraphs: ONE WINTER a Farmer found a Snake stiff and frozen with cold. He had compassion on it, and taking it up, placed it in his bosom. The Snake was quickly revived by the warmth, and resuming its natural instincts, bit its benefactor, inflicting on him a mortal wound. “Oh,” cried the Farmer with his last breath, “I am rightly served for pitying a scoundrel.”
The greatest kindness will not bind the ungrateful.
translated_paragraphs: 一个冬天，农夫看见一条蛇冻得僵直，动弹不得。他起了怜悯心，捡起蛇放进怀里。蛇受到温暖，很快醒了，立即恢复了本性，咬伤恩人，留下致命的伤口。“唉，”农夫用最后一口气说，“我可怜一个无赖，落得这下场也是活该。”
对不知感恩者，再深的好意也束不住他。

source_paragraphs: A MAN and a Lion traveled together through the forest. They soon began to boast of their respective superiority to each other in strength and prowess. As they were disputing, they passed a statue carved in stone, which represented “a Lion strangled by a Man.” The traveler pointed to it and said: “See there! How strong we are, and how we prevail over even the king of beasts.” The Lion replied: “This statue was made by one of you men. If we Lions knew how to erect statues, you would see the Man placed under the paw of the Lion.”
One story is good, till another is told.
translated_paragraphs: 一个人和一头狮子结伴穿过树林。他们不久就各自夸口，说自己的体力和本领胜过对方。争论中，他们经过一座石刻，刻的是“人扼死狮子”。那旅人一指雕像：“看哪！我们多强壮，连百兽之王，也被我们制服了。”狮子回答：“这座像是你们人类刻的。要是我们狮子也懂得怎么造像，你看见的，就会是人趴在狮子爪下。”
只听一面的说法，它总有它的道理，且等另一面也讲过再说。

source_paragraphs: THE POMEGRANATE and Apple-Tree disputed as to which was the most beautiful. When their strife was at its height, a Bramble from the neighboring hedge lifted up its voice, and said in a boastful tone: “Pray, my dear friends, in my presence at least cease from such vain disputings.”
translated_paragraphs: 石榴树和苹果树吵了起来，都说自己长得最美。正吵得不可开交，旁边树篱上一丛荆棘扬起嗓门，摆足了架子说：“亲爱的朋友们，至少当着我的面，请别争这些没意思的事吧。”

source_paragraphs: A FARMER placed nets on his newly-sown plowlands and caught a number of Cranes, which came to pick up his seed. With them he trapped a Stork that had fractured his leg in the net and was earnestly beseeching the Farmer to spare his life. “Pray save me, Master,” he said, “and let me go free this once. My broken limb should excite your pity. Besides, I am no Crane, I am a Stork, a bird of excellent character; and see how I love and slave for my father and mother. Look too, at my feathers—they are not the least like those of a Crane.” The Farmer laughed aloud and said, “It may be all as you say, I only know this: I have taken you with these robbers, the Cranes, and you must die in their company.”
Birds of a feather flock together.
translated_paragraphs: 刚播完种的田里，农夫布下几张网，捉住了不少前来啄种子的鹤。他也网到了一只鹳。鹳在网里折断了腿，恳求农夫放它一条生路。“主人，求您救救我吧，这次让我自己走。您看我腿都断了，也该可怜我。何况我不是鹤。我是鹳，品行很好，您看我是多么爱自己的父母，为他们拼命干活。再瞧我的羽毛，和鹤哪有一点相像？”农夫放声大笑：“也许你说的全是真的，可我只知道一件事。我是在这一伙偷东西的鹤里面捉到你的，那你就得跟它们死在一块儿。”
同类的鸟，往往结队同行。

source_paragraphs: A MOUNTAIN was once greatly agitated. Loud groans and noises were heard, and crowds of people came from all parts to see what was the matter. While they were assembled in anxious expectation of some terrible calamity, out came a Mouse.
Don’t make much ado about nothing.
translated_paragraphs: 有一回，一座大山震动得厉害，传来阵阵响亮的呻吟和嘈杂声。人们从各处涌来看出了什么事。大家聚成一团，忐忑地等着一场大灾难。末了，钻出一只老鼠。
没什么大事，就别闹得惊天动地。

source_paragraphs: A BEAR boasted very much of his philanthropy, saying that of all animals he was the most tender in his regard for man, for he had such respect for him that he would not even touch his dead body. A Fox hearing these words said with a smile to the Bear, “Oh! that you would eat the dead and not the living.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只熊大大夸耀自己对人类的爱心，说所有动物当中，就数它对人最温柔。它如此敬重人，连一具人的尸体都绝不会碰。狐狸听见这话，微笑着对熊说：“唉，真愿你去吃死人，别吃活人啦。”

source_paragraphs: A TORTOISE, lazily basking in the sun, complained to the sea-birds of her hard fate, that no one would teach her to fly. An Eagle, hovering near, heard her lamentation and demanded what reward she would give him if he would take her aloft and float her in the air. “I will give you,” she said, “all the riches of the Red Sea.” “I will teach you to fly then,” said the Eagle; and taking her up in his talons he carried her almost to the clouds suddenly he let her go, and she fell on a lofty mountain, dashing her shell to pieces. The Tortoise exclaimed in the moment of death: “I have deserved my present fate; for what had I to do with wings and clouds, who can with difficulty move about on the earth?”
If men had all they wished, they would be often ruined.
translated_paragraphs: 一只乌龟懒洋洋地晒着太阳，对海鸟们诉苦，说自己的命不好，没人肯教它飞。一只鹰正在近处盘旋，听见这番叹息，便问它：若我带你升到高空，让你浮在空气里，你肯给我什么报酬？“我会把红海的一切财富都给你。”乌龟答道。“那我就教你飞吧。”鹰一把用爪子抓起它，带到差不多要碰着云的地方，突然一松。乌龟落在高山上，把壳摔得粉碎。临终时它叫道：“我落到这个地步也是活该。我在地上挪动都这样难，偏要惦记翅膀和云彩做什么呢？”
人要是想什么就能得到什么，许多时候，愿望反会断送他。

source_paragraphs: A FOX one day fell into a deep well and could find no means of escape. A Goat, overcome with thirst, came to the same well, and seeing the Fox, inquired if the water was good. Concealing his sad plight under a merry guise, the Fox indulged in a lavish praise of the water, saying it was excellent beyond measure, and encouraging him to descend. The Goat, mindful only of his thirst, thoughtlessly jumped down, but just as he drank, the Fox informed him of the difficulty they were both in and suggested a scheme for their common escape. “If,” said he, “you will place your forefeet upon the wall and bend your head, I will run up your back and escape, and will help you out afterwards.” The Goat readily assented and the Fox leaped upon his back. Steadying himself with the Goat’s horns, he safely reached the mouth of the well and made off as fast as he could. When the Goat upbraided him for breaking his promise, he turned around and cried out, “You foolish old fellow! If you had as many brains in your head as you have hairs in your beard, you would never have gone down before you had inspected the way up, nor have exposed yourself to dangers from which you had no means of escape.”
Look before you leap.
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸掉进一口深井，怎么也逃不出来。一只快渴坏的山羊来到井边，见着狐狸，就问水好不好。狐狸藏起自己的苦相，装得开开心心，把井水夸得天上少有，还招呼山羊下来。山羊满心只想着解渴，不假思索就跳下去了。它刚喝上一口，狐狸这才告诉它，这井口谁也够不着，不过倒有个法子，能让它俩都出去。“你把前蹄搭在井壁，弯下脖子，我就能从你背上爬出去，随后再帮你上来。”山羊爽快地答应了。狐狸跳上它的背，攀着羊角站稳，平平安安到了井口，撒腿就跑。山羊责怪它不守信用，它转过身子叫道：“好个糊涂老伙计！你的心眼要是跟下巴上的胡子一样多，下来以前就会先看看怎么上去，哪会叫自己陷入没法脱身的险境？”
先看清，再跳。

source_paragraphs: A RAVEN saw a Swan and desired to secure for himself the same beautiful plumage. Supposing that the Swan’s splendid white color arose from his washing in the water in which he swam, the Raven left the altars in the neighborhood where he picked up his living, and took up residence in the lakes and pools. But cleansing his feathers as often as he would, he could not change their color, while through want of food he perished.
Change of habit cannot alter Nature.
translated_paragraphs: 渡鸦看见天鹅，想给自己也弄到那样漂亮的一身羽毛。它以为天鹅的漂亮白色是因为天鹅老在水里游，一遍遍洗出来的，就离开了自己平日拣食为生的祭坛一带，迁往湖泊和池塘。不论它怎样反复洗刷，羽毛仍没法变色，它反倒因缺少食物送了命。
换个生活习惯，换不掉天性。

source_paragraphs: A PIGEON, oppressed by excessive thirst, saw a goblet of water painted on a signboard. Not supposing it to be only a picture, she flew towards it with a loud whir and unwittingly dashed against the signboard, jarring herself terribly. Having broken her wings by the blow, she fell to the ground, and was caught by one of the bystanders.
Zeal should not outrun discretion.
translated_paragraphs: 一只鸽子渴得难受，看见招牌上画着一只盛水的高脚杯。它没想到那只是幅画，便扑棱棱响亮地一振翅，向水飞去，不知不觉间狠狠撞上了招牌，撞得浑身剧震。它的翅膀折断，跌落地面，给旁边的人捉住了。
热切的愿望不该跑在审慎的判断前头。

source_paragraphs: A DOG lay in a manger, and by his growling and snapping prevented the oxen from eating the hay which had been placed for them. “What a selfish Dog!” said one of them to his companions; “he cannot eat the hay himself, and yet refuses to allow those to eat who can.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只狗躺在食槽里，只要牛走近它们的干草，它就低声咆哮，龇牙去咬，拦着它们不让吃。有头牛对同伴说：“多么自私的狗啊！它自己吃不了干草，也偏不许我们吃。”

source_paragraphs: A HEAVY WAGON was being dragged along a country lane by a team of Oxen. The Axle-trees groaned and creaked terribly; whereupon the Oxen, turning round, thus addressed the wheels: “Hullo there! why do you make so much noise? We bear all the labor, and we, not you, ought to cry out.”
Those who suffer most cry out the least.
translated_paragraphs: 一队牛沿着乡间小路拖着沉甸甸的大车。车轴吱呀，吱呀，响得真厉害。
牛回头冲着车轮说：“喂，你们干吗闹得这样响？出力的全是我们。就算要叫苦，也该轮到我们呀！”
吃苦最多的，往往最少叫苦。

source_paragraphs: SOME CRANES made their feeding grounds on some plowlands newly sown with wheat. For a long time the Farmer, brandishing an empty sling, chased them away by the terror he inspired; but when the birds found that the sling was only swung in the air, they ceased to take any notice of it and would not move. The Farmer, on seeing this, charged his sling with stones, and killed a great number. The remaining birds at once forsook his fields, crying to each other, “It is time for us to be off to Liliput: for this man is no longer content to scare us, but begins to show us in earnest what he can do.”
If words suffice not, blows must follow.
translated_paragraphs: 几只鹤把新种上小麦的耕地当作了吃饭的地方。很长一段日子，农夫挥着空投石索，仗着声势把它们赶开。可鸟儿发觉，他不过是让那绳索在半空转转，便不再理会，赶也不肯走。农夫见状，把石子装进投石索，打死了许多鹤。剩下的立刻离开他的田，互相招呼：“该去利利普特了。这个人已经不满足于吓唬我们，他开始来真的，要让我们看一看他的本事啦。”
话若不管用，接下来就要动手了。

source_paragraphs: A LION, unable from old age and infirmities to provide himself with food by force, resolved to do so by artifice. He returned to his den, and lying down there, pretended to be sick, taking care that his sickness should be publicly known. The beasts expressed their sorrow, and came one by one to his den, where the Lion devoured them. After many of the beasts had thus disappeared, the Fox discovered the trick and presenting himself to the Lion, stood on the outside of the cave, at a respectful distance, and asked him how he was. “I am very middling,” replied the Lion, “but why do you stand without? Pray enter within to talk with me.” “No, thank you,” said the Fox. “I notice that there are many prints of feet entering your cave, but I see no trace of any returning.”
He is wise who is warned by the misfortunes of others.
translated_paragraphs: 狮子年老体衰，再也不能凭力气找食，便决定改用诡计。它回到洞穴躺下，假装病了，还小心地设法叫大伙儿都知道它生病的消息。众兽纷纷表示难过，挨个来洞里探望，都叫它给吃了。许多走兽陆续消失以后，狐狸识破了计谋。它前来看狮子，却恭恭敬敬地隔着一段距离，站在洞外，问它可好。“马马虎虎，”狮子答，“不过你干吗站在外面？请进来和我说话。”狐狸说：“谢谢，不用了。我看见好多走进洞里的脚印，却找不到一串走出来的。”
能从别人的不幸得到警醒，是明智的人。

sections.title_en: The Bear and the Two Travelers
source_paragraphs: TWO MEN were traveling together, when a Bear suddenly met them on their path. One of them climbed up quickly into a tree and concealed himself in the branches. The other, seeing that he must be attacked, fell flat on the ground, and when the Bear came up and felt him with his snout, and smelt him all over, he held his breath, and feigned the appearance of death as much as he could. The Bear soon left him, for it is said he will not touch a dead body. When he was quite gone, the other Traveler descended from the tree, and jocularly inquired of his friend what it was the Bear had whispered in his ear. “He gave me this advice,” his companion replied. “Never travel with a friend who deserts you at the approach of danger.”
Misfortune tests the sincerity of friends.
translated_paragraphs: 两个人结伴赶路，半路上突然出现一只熊。其中一人飞快爬上树，躲入枝叶之间。另一个眼看非挨袭击不可，一下趴倒在地。熊走到身边，拿鼻子碰他，又在身上嗅来嗅去，他便憋住呼吸，尽可能装得跟死了一样。据说熊不碰尸体，没多久它就丢下他走了。等它走远，树上的旅人爬下来，开玩笑地问朋友，刚才那熊挨在他耳边，悄悄说的是些什么。“它给我一个忠告，”同伴答道，“永远别跟那种危险一来就撇下你的朋友一起出门。”
患难考验朋友的真心。

sections.title_en: The Fox Who Had Lost His Tail
source_paragraphs: A FOX caught in a trap escaped, but in so doing lost his tail. Thereafter, feeling his life a burden from the shame and ridicule to which he was exposed, he schemed to convince all the other Foxes that being tailless was much more attractive, thus making up for his own deprivation. He assembled a good many Foxes and publicly advised them to cut off their tails, saying that they would not only look much better without them, but that they would get rid of the weight of the brush, which was a very great inconvenience. One of them interrupting him said, “If you had not yourself lost your tail, my friend, you would not thus counsel us.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只狐狸中了捕兽夹，好容易逃出来，却把尾巴丢了。从此怕丢脸又受人嘲笑，觉得活着实在累赘，便想出计策，要说服其余的狐狸，让大家都相信没有尾巴要好看得多，这样便能弥补它自己的损失。它召来一大群狐狸，公然劝大家都去把尾巴砍掉。它说少了尾巴不只会漂亮得多，还能甩掉那一大蓬毛的重量，省去好大的不便。一只狐狸打断它：“朋友，你若没弄丢自己的尾巴，可不会来劝我们这么干。”

source_paragraphs: A CAT caught a Cock, and pondered how he might find a reasonable excuse for eating him. He accused him of being a nuisance to men by crowing in the nighttime and not permitting them to sleep. The Cock defended himself by saying that he did this for the benefit of men, that they might rise in time for their labours. The Cat replied, “Although you abound in specious apologies, I shall not remain supperless;” and he made a meal of him.
translated_paragraphs: 猫逮住一只公鸡，琢磨怎么才找得到一个说得过去的借口，好把它吃掉。它指控公鸡夜里啼鸣，搅得人们没法睡觉，是个祸害。公鸡为自己辩护：“我这样做，是想给人们带来好处，好叫他们按时起床干活。”猫回答：“你尽管还找得出很多听来有理的辩词，我可不会因此少吃一顿晚饭。”它拿这只公鸡作了自己的一餐。

source_paragraphs: ONCE UPON A TIME a Wolf resolved to disguise his appearance in order to secure food more easily. Encased in the skin of a sheep, he pastured with the flock deceiving the shepherd by his costume. In the evening he was shut up by the shepherd in the fold; the gate was closed, and the entrance made thoroughly secure. But the shepherd, returning to the fold during the night to obtain meat for the next day, mistakenly caught up the Wolf instead of a sheep, and killed him instantly.
Harm seek, harm find.
translated_paragraphs: 从前，一只狼拿定主意，要换身打扮，让找吃的容易一些。它披上一张羊皮，和羊群一起在草地走动，穿这身装束，竟瞒过了牧羊人。到了晚上，牧羊人把它也关进羊圈，锁上门，把入口看守得妥妥当当。可那一夜，牧羊人回羊圈取肉，打算第二天吃。他把狼错当成羊捉了去，当场宰了。
存心害人，害到自己。

source_paragraphs: A GOATHERD had sought to bring back a stray goat to his flock. He whistled and sounded his horn in vain; the straggler paid no attention to the summons. At last the Goatherd threw a stone, and breaking its horn, begged the Goat not to tell his master. The Goat replied, “Why, you silly fellow, the horn will speak though I be silent.”
Do not attempt to hide things which cannot be hid.
translated_paragraphs: 牧羊人想把一只走散的山羊叫回羊群。他打口哨，又吹号角，全没有用，那只掉队的山羊根本不理他的召唤。末了，他扔出一块石头，不料打断了一只羊角，便央求山羊不要把事情告诉主人。山羊回答：“嘿，你这傻子，我就算一声不响，这断角也会开口呀。”
藏不住的事，就别指望把它遮盖过去。

source_paragraphs: A MAN who had traveled in foreign lands boasted very much, on returning to his own country, of the many wonderful and heroic feats he had performed in the different places he had visited. Among other things, he said that when he was at Rhodes he had leaped to such a distance that no man of his day could leap anywhere near him as to that, there were in Rhodes many persons who saw him do it and whom he could call as witnesses. One of the bystanders interrupted him, saying: “Now, my good man, if this be all true there is no need of witnesses. Suppose this to be Rhodes, and leap for us.”
translated_paragraphs: 有一个人，出过几趟远门。回到本国后，便大吹大擂，夸说自己到了这处那处，都干了许多惊人的英雄事迹。他说起其中特别得意的一件。当初在罗得岛，他一跃跳出那么远，当时天下谁来跳都望尘莫及。岛上好多人亲眼看见他这一跳，他随时可以请他们来作证。旁边有人打断他：“朋友，如果你说的都真，不用劳烦什么证人啦。你就把这里当作罗得岛，跳给我们瞧瞧。”

source_paragraphs: A LION demanded the daughter of a woodcutter in marriage. The Father, unwilling to grant, and yet afraid to refuse his request, hit upon this expedient to rid himself of his importunities. He expressed his willingness to accept the Lion as the suitor of his daughter on one condition: that he should allow him to extract his teeth, and cut off his claws, as his daughter was fearfully afraid of both. The Lion cheerfully assented to the proposal. But when the toothless, clawless Lion returned to repeat his request, the Woodman, no longer afraid, set upon him with his club, and drove him away into the forest.
translated_paragraphs: 狮子向一位樵夫求娶他的女儿。做父亲的不愿点头，却也不敢回绝它。为了摆脱这番纠缠，他想出个法子。他说情愿让狮子做女儿的追求者，只有一个条件：得让他拔去狮牙，剪掉狮爪，因为女儿对这两样东西都怕得厉害。狮子欢欢喜喜答应了。等到它无牙无爪，再去重提婚事，樵夫已经不必害怕，拾起木棍迎头便打，一直把它赶回了树林。

source_paragraphs: A MISER sold all that he had and bought a lump of gold, which he buried in a hole in the ground by the side of an old wall and went to look at daily. One of his workmen observed his frequent visits to the spot and decided to watch his movements. He soon discovered the secret of the hidden treasure, and digging down, came to the lump of gold, and stole it. The Miser, on his next visit, found the hole empty and began to tear his hair and to make loud lamentations. A neighbor, seeing him overcome with grief and learning the cause, said, “Pray do not grieve so; but go and take a stone, and place it in the hole, and fancy that the gold is still lying there. It will do you quite the same service; for when the gold was there, you had it not, as you did not make the slightest use of it.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个守财奴卖掉全部家产，换来一大块黄金。他在旧墙边挖了个洞，把金子埋下去，一天不落地去看。一个工人留意到他常往那地方跑，就决定观察他的动静。工人很快发现了藏宝的秘密，向下挖，挖出那块金子，把它偷走了。守财奴下回来，一看洞都空了，便撕扯着头发，放声痛哭。邻人见他悲伤得不能自已，问明事情始末，说：“求你别难过成这样。去取块石头，埋进洞里，想象黄金仍躺在那儿就是了。它俩替你做的事保准一模一样。想那黄金还在的时候，你一丁点儿都没有拿来用过，就等于根本没有拥有过它。”

sections.title_en: The Porker, the Sheep, and the Goat
source_paragraphs: A young Pig was shut up in a fold-yard with a Goat and a Sheep. On one occasion the shepherd laid hold of him, when he grunted, and squeaked, and resisted violently. The Sheep and the Goat complained of his distressing cries, and said, “He often handles us, and we do not cry out.” To this he replied, “Your handling and mine are very different things. He catches you only for your wool, or your milk, but he lays hold on me for my very life.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只小猪和一只山羊、一只绵羊，一起关在牲畜圈里。有一天，牧人一把逮住了小猪。小猪又哼又尖叫，拼命挣扎。绵羊和山羊嫌它叫得叫人难受，说：“他经常也这样抓我们，我们可不叫唤。”小猪答道：“捉你们和捉我，是两回事啊。他捉你们，不过要你们的毛，或是你们的奶。他来捉我，却是要我的命。”

source_paragraphs: A BOY put his hand into a pitcher full of filberts. He grasped as many as he could possibly hold, but when he tried to pull out his hand, he was prevented from doing so by the neck of the pitcher. Unwilling to lose his filberts, and yet unable to withdraw his hand, he burst into tears and bitterly lamented his disappointment. A bystander said to him, “Be satisfied with half the quantity, and you will readily draw out your hand.”
Do not attempt too much at once.
translated_paragraphs: 一个男孩把手伸进装满榛子的罐子，尽他一把攥得住的，满满抓了一大把。可要把手抽回来，才发现手卡在罐颈里，出不来了。榛子他舍不得放，手却也没法儿抽，只好哭了起来，为自己的失望伤心不已。旁边一个人告诉他：“知足些吧，只拿一半，你的手便能轻轻松松抽出来。”
别指望一回就得到太多。

sections.title_en: The Frogs Asking for a King
source_paragraphs: THE FROGS, grieved at having no established Ruler, sent ambassadors to Jupiter entreating for a King. Perceiving their simplicity, he cast down a huge log into the lake. The Frogs were terrified at the splash occasioned by its fall and hid themselves in the depths of the pool. But as soon as they realized that the huge log was motionless, they swam again to the top of the water, dismissed their fears, climbed up, and began squatting on it in contempt. After some time they began to think themselves ill-treated in the appointment of so inert a Ruler, and sent a second deputation to Jupiter to pray that he would set over them another sovereign. He then gave them an Eel to govern them. When the Frogs discovered his easy good nature, they sent yet a third time to Jupiter to beg him to choose for them still another King. Jupiter, displeased with all their complaints, sent a Heron, who preyed upon the Frogs day by day till there were none left to croak upon the lake.
translated_paragraphs: 青蛙们苦恼于自己没有一位正式的统治者，派了使者朝见朱庇特，求他赐一位国王。朱庇特看它们心思简单，将一根巨大的圆木丢进了湖中。木头落水，激起好大一阵水花，青蛙们吓得全躲到深水里。待它们察觉圆木根本一动不动，又游回水面，丢开了恐惧，甚至爬到它身上，轻蔑地蹲坐在上头。过了一些日子，它们觉得，给它们派来这么一位动都不动的统治者，分明是轻待它们。于是再次派出使团去求朱庇特另立一位君主。这回他给了它们一条鳗鱼当国王。青蛙们一发现它脾气温顺、好说话，第三次派人去求朱庇特再另选一个。朱庇特听够了它们的抱怨，很不高兴，便派去一只苍鹭。苍鹭一天又一天吃掉青蛙，直到湖里再也没有一只青蛙能呱呱叫。

source_paragraphs: A SNAKE, having made his hole close to the porch of a cottage, inflicted a mortal bite on the Cottager’s infant son. Grieving over his loss, the Father resolved to kill the Snake. The next day, when it came out of its hole for food, he took up his axe, but by swinging too hastily, missed its head and cut off only the end of its tail. After some time the Cottager, afraid that the Snake would bite him also, endeavored to make peace, and placed some bread and salt in the hole. The Snake, slightly hissing, said: “There can henceforth be no peace between us; for whenever I see you I shall remember the loss of my tail, and whenever you see me you will be thinking of the death of your son.”
No one truly forgets injuries in the presence of him who caused the injury.
translated_paragraphs: 有条蛇把窝安在一间村屋的门廊边，咬死了屋主尚在襁褓的儿子。父亲痛失孩子，决意杀了蛇。第二天，蛇出洞寻找食物，父亲抡起斧头，可动手太仓促，没砍中蛇头，只削掉一小截尾巴。过了一阵，屋主担心蛇也会咬他，想跟它讲和，往洞里放了点面包和盐。蛇细声嘶了一下，说：“你我往后再不能和平相处。我一见到你，就想起断掉的尾巴。你一见到我，就想起死去的儿子。”
看见伤害过自己的人，谁也难以真正忘记从前受过的伤。

sections.title_en: The Lion, the Mouse, and the Fox
source_paragraphs: A LION, fatigued by the heat of a summer’s day, fell fast asleep in his den. A Mouse ran over his mane and ears and woke him from his slumbers. He rose up and shook himself in great wrath, and searched every corner of his den to find the Mouse. A Fox seeing him said: “A fine Lion you are, to be frightened of a Mouse.” “’Tis not the Mouse I fear,” said the Lion; “I resent his familiarity and ill-breeding.”
Little liberties are great offenses.
translated_paragraphs: 一个炎热的夏日，狮子热得疲乏，正在洞穴里熟睡。一只老鼠爬过它的鬃毛和耳朵，把它闹醒了。狮子气呼呼站起来，一阵猛抖，随后找遍洞内每一个角落，要找那只老鼠。一只狐狸瞧见，笑它：“好一头威风的狮子，竟怕起老鼠来了。”狮子说：“我并不怕这只老鼠。我恼的是它太随便、不懂礼貌。”
小小的放肆，可能是大大的冒犯。

source_paragraphs: A GROOM used to spend whole days in currycombing and rubbing down his Horse, but at the same time stole his oats and sold them for his own profit. “Alas!” said the Horse, “if you really wish me to be in good condition, you should groom me less, and feed me more.”
translated_paragraphs: 一名马夫常常花上一整天工夫，给自己的马梳理鬃毛，擦拭身子。可他同时又偷走马的燕麦，卖掉给自己赚钱。“唉！”马说，“你要真希望我长得好，就少给我梳几下毛，多给我吃几口粮吧。”

source_paragraphs: A MULETEER set forth on a journey, driving before him an Ass and a Mule, both well laden. The Ass, as long as he traveled along the plain, carried his load with ease, but when he began to ascend the steep path of the mountain, felt his load to be more than he could bear. He entreated his companion to relieve him of a small portion, that he might carry home the rest; but the Mule paid no attention to the request. The Ass shortly afterwards fell down dead under his burden. Not knowing what else to do in so wild a region, the Muleteer placed upon the Mule the load carried by the Ass in addition to his own, and at the top of all placed the hide of the Ass, after he had skinned him. The Mule, groaning beneath his heavy burden, said to himself: “I am treated according to my deserts. If I had only been willing to assist the Ass a little in his need, I should not now be bearing, together with his burden, himself as well.”
translated_paragraphs: 赶骡人起程，前面赶着一头驴和一头骡子，两头背上都驮满了货。在平地上走，驴背着货物还觉得轻松。可是一开始攀那条陡峭山路，它便觉得分量重得超过了自己能承受的限度，就恳求同伴替它分担一小部分，让它能把剩下的驮回家。骡子对这请求理也不理。不久，驴就给背上的重担压倒，死了。身处荒僻的山野，赶骡人想不出别的办法，只得把驴背上的货物全部加在骡子自己的货上，最后还剥下驴皮，压在最上面。骡子在重担底下呻吟，心里说：“我这是活该。要是当初我肯在驴支撑不住时稍微搭把手，就不会现在连它身上的货，带它自己，都要由我来背了。”

source_paragraphs: A MAN had an Ass, and a Maltese Lapdog, a very great beauty. The Ass was left in a stable and had plenty of oats and hay to eat, just as any other Ass would. The Lapdog knew many tricks and was a great favourite with his master, who often fondled him and seldom went out to dine without bringing him home some tidbit to eat. The Ass, on the contrary, had much work to do in grinding the corn-mill and in carrying wood from the forest or burdens from the farm. He often lamented his own hard fate and contrasted it with the luxury and idleness of the Lapdog, till at last one day he broke his cords and halter, and galloped into his master’s house, kicking up his heels without measure, and frisking and fawning as well as he could. He next tried to jump about his master as he had seen the Lapdog do, but he broke the table and smashed all the dishes upon it to atoms. He then attempted to lick his master, and jumped upon his back. The servants, hearing the strange hubbub and perceiving the danger of their master, quickly relieved him, and drove out the Ass to his stable with kicks and clubs and cuffs. The Ass, as he returned to his stall beaten nearly to death, thus lamented: “I have brought it all on myself! Why could I not have been contented to labor with my companions, and not wish to be idle all the day like that useless little Lapdog!”
translated_paragraphs: 有个人养了一头驴，还养了一只马耳他小犬，模样漂亮极了。驴住在马厩里，有的是燕麦和干草可吃，跟寻常驴差不多。哈巴狗却会许多把戏，最得主人疼爱。主人常常抱着它爱抚，外出赴宴时，几乎没有一回忘了带点好吃的回来给它。驴却正相反，有一大堆活等着它，要拉磨碾谷，要从树林驮木头，从田场驮货物。它常将自己的辛苦命运同哈巴狗舒适闲散的日子作比较，止不住叹气。终于有一天，它挣断绳索和笼头，飞奔进主人家里，后蹄高高抬起，一味学着小狗欢蹦、撒娇。它还想像亲眼见过哈巴狗做的那样，在主人跟前跃来跃去，却碰坏了桌子，把桌上的餐盘全打得粉碎。此后它又想舔舔主人，一跃跳上了主人的背。仆人们听见奇怪的喧嚷，眼见主人身处险境，赶紧把他解救出来，拳头、脚踢和棍棒齐下，将驴赶回马厩。驴给打得奄奄一息，走回自己的小栏，一路哀叹：“这一切是我自己招来的！我怎么就不能安心跟同伴一起干活，偏偏羡慕那只没用的小哈巴狗，成天想游手好闲呢！”

source_paragraphs: THE OXEN once upon a time sought to destroy the Butchers, who practiced a trade destructive to their race. They assembled on a certain day to carry out their purpose, and sharpened their horns for the contest. But one of them who was exceedingly old (for many a field had he plowed) thus spoke: “These Butchers, it is true, slaughter us, but they do so with skillful hands, and with no unnecessary pain. If we get rid of them, we shall fall into the hands of unskillful operators, and thus suffer a double death: for you may be assured, that though all the Butchers should perish, yet will men never want beef.”
Do not be in a hurry to change one evil for another.
translated_paragraphs: 从前，牛群打算将屠夫们统统除掉，因为屠夫所干的行当就是屠杀它们的族类。它们定下一天会齐，准备一齐动手，还把牛角磨得尖尖的，要去交战。其中有一头极老的牛（它已经犁过不知多少块田），却开口说道：“这些屠夫确实宰杀我们，但他们手艺熟练，不会让我们白白多受苦。除掉他们，我们就会落到不懂行的人手里，那便要受双倍的死罪了。你们尽可放心，就算把现有的屠夫全除光，人们也不会肯从此没牛肉吃。”
别忙着用一种坏处去交换另一种坏处。

sections.title_en: The Shepherd’s Boy and the Wolf
source_paragraphs: A SHEPHERD-BOY, who watched a flock of sheep near a village, brought out the villagers three or four times by crying out, “Wolf!
