Wolf!” and when his neighbors came to help him, laughed at them for their pains. The Wolf, however, did truly come at last. The Shepherd-boy, now really alarmed, shouted in an agony of terror: “Pray, do come and help me; the Wolf is killing the sheep;” but no one paid any heed to his cries, nor rendered any assistance. The Wolf, having no cause of fear, at his leisure lacerated or destroyed the whole flock.
There is no believing a liar, even when he speaks the truth.
translated_paragraphs: 有个牧童，在村子附近看守一群羊。他先后三四次大叫“狼来啦！狼来啦！”，把村民们喊出来；等人家赶来相助，他又嘲笑邻居们白费了力气。终于，狼当真来啦。这回牧童确实吓坏了，在万分惊恐中叫喊：“求求你们，快来帮我，狼在咬我的羊！”可是，再也没人理会他的呼救，更没有人伸出援手。狼毫无畏惧，可以慢条斯理地下口，把整个羊群咬伤、咬死，摧残个尽。
说过许多谎话的人，哪怕说的是真话，也没人肯信。

source_paragraphs: SOME BOYS, playing near a pond, saw a number of Frogs in the water and began to pelt them with stones. They killed several of them, when one of the Frogs, lifting his head out of the water, cried out: “Pray stop, my boys: what is sport to you, is death to us.”
translated_paragraphs: 几个男孩在池塘旁边玩耍，看见水里有好些青蛙，就拿石头朝它们砸去。接连砸死几只以后，一只青蛙将头探出水面，大声说：“孩子们，请罢手吧！你们玩的是游戏，我们丢的可是性命。”

sections.title_en: The Salt Merchant and His Ass
source_paragraphs: A PEDDLER drove his Ass to the seashore to buy salt. His road home lay across a stream into which his Ass, making a false step, fell by accident and rose up again with his load considerably lighter, as the water melted the sack. The Peddler retraced his steps and refilled his panniers with a larger quantity of salt than before. When he came again to the stream, the Ass fell down on purpose in the same spot, and, regaining his feet with the weight of his load much diminished, brayed triumphantly as if he had obtained what he desired. The Peddler saw through his trick and drove him for the third time to the coast, where he bought a cargo of sponges instead of salt. The Ass, again playing the fool, fell down on purpose when he reached the stream, but the sponges became swollen with water, greatly increasing his load. And thus his trick recoiled on him, for he now carried on his back a double burden.
translated_paragraphs: 一名小贩赶着毛驴去海岸买盐，回家的路经过一条溪流。驴一脚踏空，不小心跌倒在水里。等它起身时，背上却轻了许多，因为溪水融去了袋里的盐。小贩沿原路返回，这回给两边驮篓装上比先前更多的盐。又来到同一条溪边，驴在老地方故意倒下去，再站起时，重担又轻了一大截。它得意地昂起头叫，仿佛已经心想事成。小贩识破了它的把戏，第三度赶它去海岸，这回买了一批海绵，不再买盐。驴又耍起小聪明，一到溪流就故意摔进去。可是海绵吸饱了水，涨得满满的，让它的担子大大加重。这把戏反落在自己头上，驴背着的分量，如今竟有先前的两倍。

source_paragraphs: A DOG used to run up quietly to the heels of everyone he met, and to bite them without notice. His master suspended a bell about his neck so that the Dog might give notice of his presence wherever he went. Thinking it a mark of distinction, the Dog grew proud of his bell and went tinkling it all over the marketplace. One day an old hound said to him: “Why do you make such an exhibition of yourself? That bell that you carry is not, believe me, any order of merit, but on the contrary a mark of disgrace, a public notice to all men to avoid you as an ill mannered dog.”
Notoriety is often mistaken for fame.
translated_paragraphs: 有只狗无论碰见谁，总要轻悄悄跑到人家脚后跟边上，冷不丁咬一口。主人便给它脖子上系了个铃铛，好让它走到哪儿，先给人一个提醒。狗误以为这是身份不凡的标志，对自己的铃铛十分得意，整天叮叮当当地在集市里招摇过市。一天，一条老猎犬对它说：“你又何必这样炫耀自己？相信我，你带的铃铛绝不是什么表功的勋章。恰恰相反，它是个丢面子的记号，公开告诉人们，你是条没规矩的狗，要躲着你才好。”
臭名远扬，时常被误认作声名显赫。

sections.title_en: The Goatherd and the Wild Goats
source_paragraphs: A GOATHERD, driving his flock from their pasture at eventide, found some Wild Goats mingled among them, and shut them up together with his own for the night. The next day it snowed very hard, so that he could not take the herd to their usual feeding places, but was obliged to keep them in the fold. He gave his own goats just sufficient food to keep them alive, but fed the strangers more abundantly in the hope of enticing them to stay with him and of making them his own. When the thaw set in, he led them all out to feed, and the Wild Goats scampered away as fast as they could to the mountains. The Goatherd scolded them for their ingratitude in leaving him, when during the storm he had taken more care of them than of his own herd. One of them, turning about, said to him: “That is the very reason why we are so cautious; for if you yesterday treated us better than the Goats you have had so long, it is plain also that if others came after us, you would in the same manner prefer them to ourselves.”
Old friends cannot with impunity be sacrificed for new ones.
translated_paragraphs: 傍晚，牧人赶着羊群离开草场，发现有几只野山羊混在其间，便把它们跟自己的山羊一起关在圈里过夜。第二天雪下得很大，他没法儿像平日那样把羊带去吃草，只能让它们留在圈里。他给自己的羊只分了勉强维持性命的一点口粮，却给新来的山羊丰盛的食物，想诱它们留下，成为自己的羊。等冰雪消融，他领所有山羊出去吃草时，野山羊使足了劲，一溜烟跑回山里。牧人骂它们忘恩负义，说风雪天里，自己照看它们比照看自家的山羊还要周到，它们怎么能一走了之。有一只野山羊转过头回答：“正是因为这个，我们才这样提防你。昨天，你待我们胜过待跟了你好些年的羊；那么明天，如果又有几只羊跟在我们后边来，你肯定也会照样看重新来的，看轻我们。”
为了结交新友而牺牲旧友，绝不会没有代价。

sections.title_zh: 男子和他的两位心上人
sections.title_en: The Man and His Two Sweethearts
source_paragraphs: A MIDDLE-AGED MAN, whose hair had begun to turn gray, courted two women at the same time. One of them was young, and the other well advanced in years. The elder woman, ashamed to be courted by a man younger than herself, made a point, whenever her admirer visited her, to pull out some portion of his black hairs. The younger, on the contrary, not wishing to become the wife of an old man, was equally zealous in removing every gray hair she could find. Thus it came to pass that between them both he very soon found that he had not a hair left on his head.
Those who seek to please everybody please nobody.
translated_paragraphs: 一个中年男子，头发刚开始花白，同时向两个女人求爱。一位年轻，另一位已经上了年纪。年长的女人因为追求她的人比她年轻，觉得有点丢脸。她养成习惯，每逢情郎上门，便要拔掉他几根黑发。年轻的那位呢，正相反，不肯嫁个老人，也怀着同样的热忱，把自己能找见的白头发一根根全拔了。结果，经她俩这样合力，不久这男子便发现，自己的头上一根头发也没剩下。
想讨好每一个人的人，到头来谁也讨好不了。

source_paragraphs: A SICK STAG lay down in a quiet corner of its pasture-ground. His companions came in great numbers to inquire after his health, and each one helped himself to a share of the food which had been placed for his use; so that he died, not from his sickness, but from the failure of the means of living.
Evil companions bring more hurt than profit.
translated_paragraphs: 一头雄鹿病了，躺在草场上一个僻静的角落里。伙伴们成群结队地来探病，每个都拿了点专为它备下的食物吃。结果雄鹿的病没要它的命，倒是那些吃的给分光了，它活活饿死了。
坏伙伴带来的损害比益处更多。

source_paragraphs: A BOY was stung by a Nettle. He ran home and told his Mother, saying, “Although it hurts me very much, I only touched it gently.” “That was just why it stung you,” said his Mother. “The next time you touch a Nettle, grasp it boldly, and it will be soft as silk to your hand, and not in the least hurt you.”
Whatever you do, do with all your might.
translated_paragraphs: 一个男孩被荨麻刺痛，跑回家告诉妈妈：“我只是轻轻碰了它一下，它却把我刺得这么疼！”妈妈回答：“它刺了你，恰恰是因为你这样碰它。下回你遇到荨麻，大胆把它一把抓住，它在你手里就会像丝绸一样柔软，半点儿也不会伤你。”
无论做什么，都应全力以赴。

source_paragraphs: AN ASTRONOMER used to go out at night to observe the stars. One evening, as he wandered through the suburbs with his whole attention fixed on the sky, he fell accidentally into a deep well. While he lamented and bewailed his sores and bruises, and cried loudly for help, a neighbor ran to the well, and learning what had happened said: “Hark ye, old fellow, why, in striving to pry into what is in heaven, do you not manage to see what is on earth?”
translated_paragraphs: 有位天文学家，惯在夜间出门观察星星。一天晚上，他在城外兜来转去，一心只盯着天空，一不小心掉进一口深井。他在井里为了自己身上的青肿伤痛连声哀叹，大声求救。邻人闻声赶到井旁，打听出了什么事，说道：“我说，老兄，你这么费心探究天上的事，怎么竟没能看清地上的事呢？”

source_paragraphs: “WHY SHOULD there always be this fear and slaughter between us?” said the Wolves to the Sheep. “Those evil-disposed Dogs have much to answer for. They always bark whenever we approach you and attack us before we have done any harm. If you would only dismiss them from your heels, there might soon be treaties of peace and reconciliation between us.” The Sheep, poor silly creatures, were easily beguiled and dismissed the Dogs, whereupon the Wolves destroyed the unguarded flock at their own pleasure.
translated_paragraphs: “你我之间为什么总得这样，又是恐惧，又是屠杀？”狼群对羊群说，“那些不怀好意的狗可要负好大责任。我们每次一靠近，它们就乱叫，明明我们还什么也没做，它们已经扑来攻击。只要你们把整天跟在身边的狗打发走，双方要达成和平、重归和好，也就是早晚的事。”可怜那些傻乎乎的绵羊，轻易就中了计，把狗都遣了去。于是，狼可以毫无顾忌，把失去保护的羊群随心所欲地吃尽。

source_paragraphs: A CAT, hearing that the Birds in a certain aviary were ailing dressed himself up as a physician, and, taking his cane and a bag of instruments becoming his profession, went to call on them. He knocked at the door and inquired of the inmates how they all did, saying that if they were ill, he would be happy to prescribe for them and cure them. They replied, “We are all very well, and shall continue so, if you will only be good enough to go away, and leave us as we are.”
translated_paragraphs: 猫听说某个鸟舍里的鸟儿有病，便将自己打扮成医生，拄着手杖，提起一袋跟这门行当十分相配的器械，出门去探望它们。它叩了门，问里面各位身体如何，说它们若是有病，它很高兴替它们开个方子，治好它们。鸟儿们回答：“我们身体都好得很。只要你肯行行好，走开去，让我们就这么待着，我们就会一直好下去。”

source_paragraphs: JUPITER DETERMINED, it is said, to create a sovereign over the birds, and made proclamation that on a certain day they should all present themselves before him, when he would himself choose the most beautiful among them to be king. The Jackdaw, knowing his own ugliness, searched through the woods and fields, and collected the feathers which had fallen from the wings of his companions, and stuck them in all parts of his body, hoping thereby to make himself the most beautiful of all. When the appointed day arrived, and the birds had assembled before Jupiter, the Jackdaw also made his appearance in his many feathered finery. But when Jupiter proposed to make him king because of the beauty of his plumage, the birds indignantly protested, and each plucked from him his own feathers, leaving the Jackdaw nothing but a Jackdaw.
translated_paragraphs: 据说，朱庇特决定在群鸟当中设一位君王，颁令它们在指定的日子全到他面前来，到时他将亲自挑选其中最美的一只来称王。寒鸦知道自己不怎么漂亮，便在林子、田野间四处搜寻，拾起同伴们翅膀上脱落的羽毛，朝自己身上到处插，盼着就此成为天下最美丽的鸟。到了约定那天，群鸟齐聚朱庇特面前，寒鸦也披着这身五彩羽衣亮了相。可当朱庇特因这身羽毛的美丽，提出让它当王的时候，鸟儿们愤怒地抗议，每一只都从它身上拔回自己的羽毛，寒鸦剩下的，也就只有它原本那副寒鸦模样。

source_paragraphs: A KID standing on the roof of a house, out of harm’s way, saw a Wolf passing by and immediately began to taunt and revile him. The Wolf, looking up, said, “Sirrah! I hear thee: yet it is not thou who mockest me, but the roof on which thou art standing.”
Time and place often give the advantage to the weak over the strong.
translated_paragraphs: 小山羊站在屋顶，知道自己不受伤害。恰好一只狼路过，它马上又嘲弄，又辱骂起对方来。狼抬起头，说：“小家伙，你说的话我都听到了。可嘲笑我的不是你，是你站着的那个屋顶。”
时间和地点合适，有时弱者也能在强者面前占得上风。

sections.title_en: The Old Woman and the Physician
source_paragraphs: AN OLD WOMAN having lost the use of her eyes, called in a Physician to heal them, and made this bargain with him in the presence of witnesses: that if he should cure her blindness, he should receive from her a sum of money; but if her infirmity remained, she should give him nothing. This agreement being made, the Physician, time after time, applied his salve to her eyes, and on every visit took something away, stealing all her property little by little. And when he had got all she had, he healed her and demanded the promised payment. The Old Woman, when she recovered her sight and saw none of her goods in her house, would give him nothing. The Physician insisted on his claim, and, as she still refused, summoned her before the Judge. The Old Woman, standing up in the Court, argued: “This man here speaks the truth in what he says; for I did promise to give him a sum of money if I should recover my sight: but if I continued blind, I was to give him nothing. Now he declares that I am healed. I on the contrary affirm that I am still blind; for when I lost the use of my eyes, I saw in my house various chattels and valuable goods: but now, though he swears I am cured of my blindness, I am not able to see a single thing in it.”
translated_paragraphs: 一位老妇人双眼失明，将医生请上门来医治，并当着见证人的面与他讲好，要是医生能恢复她的视力，就给他一笔钱；如果眼疾未好，一个钱也不给。订下约定后，医生一次次上门给她抹眼膏，每回离开还要顺手带走一样东西，渐渐将她的家产偷了个精光。等能拿的全拿走，他这才治好了她的眼睛，索要说好的酬劳。老妇人重见光明，却发现自己家当一样也不在屋里，便一文钱也不肯给。医生坚持要钱，两人争执不下，就将她告到法官面前。老妇人在法庭上站起来争辩：“这位先生所说的约定完全属实。我的确答应过，若是恢复视力，我就给他一笔钱；如果我还是瞎着，就什么也不用给。现在他声称我已治愈，我却能肯定自己仍然是个瞎子。因为我眼睛还好、刚要失去视力的时候，还能看见家里各式各样的家具和贵重物品；可现在呢，他发誓说我眼睛好了，我却连一样也瞧不见。”

source_paragraphs: AN OX drinking at a pool trod on a brood of young frogs and crushed one of them to death. The Mother coming up, and missing one of her sons, inquired of his brothers what had become of him. “He is dead, dear Mother; for just now a very huge beast with four great feet came to the pool and crushed him to death with his cloven heel.” The Frog, puffing herself out, inquired, “if the beast was as big as that in size.” “Cease, Mother, to puff yourself out,” said her son, “and do not be angry; for you would, I assure you, sooner burst than successfully imitate the hugeness of that monster.”
translated_paragraphs: 一头牛在池塘喝水，一蹄子踩进一窝小青蛙，压死了其中一只。青蛙妈妈过来，发现少了一个孩子，就向其余兄弟打听它到哪儿去了。“亲爱的妈妈，它死了。刚刚来了一头个子非常大的野兽，它有四只巨大的脚，用那分成两半的蹄子把它踩死了。”青蛙妈妈使劲鼓起肚皮，问那野兽是不是有这么大。儿子说：“妈妈，别再鼓了，也别生气。我可以向你保证，你就是把自己胀破了，也还远远赶不上那头怪物那么大呀。”

source_paragraphs: A FATHER, being on the point of death, wished to be sure that his sons would give the same attention to his farm as he himself had given it. He called them to his bedside and said, “My sons, there is a great treasure hid in one of my vineyards.” The sons, after his death, took their spades and mattocks and carefully dug over every portion of their land. They found no treasure, but the vines repaid their labor by an extraordinary and superabundant crop.
translated_paragraphs: 一位父亲自知不久于人世，想确保自己的几个儿子今后会像自己一样用心照料农田。他叫儿子们到床边，说：“孩子们，我有一块葡萄园里，藏着好大一宗财宝。”父亲死后，几个儿子拿起铁锹和镐头，把自家土地的每一处都仔细翻挖了一遍。财宝没有挖到，可是那年葡萄结了极盛大、极丰厚的一季果实，偿还了他们付出的力气。

source_paragraphs: A HEIFER saw an Ox hard at work harnessed to a plow, and tormented him with reflections on his unhappy fate in being compelled to labor. Shortly afterwards, at the harvest festival, the owner released the Ox from his yoke, but bound the Heifer with cords and led him away to the altar to be slain in honour of the occasion. The Ox saw what was being done, and said with a smile to the Heifer: “For this you were allowed to live in idleness, because you were presently to be sacrificed.”
translated_paragraphs: 一头小母牛看到一头耕牛给套在犁上辛苦工作，便对它被迫干活的不幸命运说三道四，故意惹它难受。过了不久，时逢庆祝丰收的节日，主人卸下耕牛的轭，却拿绳索捆住小母牛，把它牵往祭坛，要将它宰了用作节日的一份敬献。耕牛看到这一切，对小母牛微微一笑，说：“你先前能够一味享受清闲，正是为了这个。因为转眼就要拿你做祭品了。”

sections.title_en: The Fighting Cocks and the Eagle
source_paragraphs: TWO GAME COCKS were fiercely fighting for the mastery of the farmyard. One at last put the other to flight. The vanquished Cock skulked away and hid himself in a quiet corner, while the conqueror, flying up to a high wall, flapped his wings and crowed exultingly with all his might. An Eagle sailing through the air pounced upon him and carried him off in his talons. The vanquished Cock immediately came out of his corner, and ruled henceforth with undisputed mastery.
Pride goes before destruction.
translated_paragraphs: 两只斗鸡为了争当农家庭院的霸主，争斗得十分凶狠。最后，一只把另一只打得落荒而逃。败者灰溜溜地躲到一个僻静的角落。胜者呢，飞上高墙，扑扇双翅，使尽全力，洋洋得意地打起鸣来。一只正在空中翱翔的鹰当即扑下，伸出利爪将它攫走。刚才战败的那只公鸡便从角落里走出来，从此称王，再没有谁同它争。
骄傲走在毁灭的前面。

source_paragraphs: A CHARGER, feeling the infirmities of age, was sent to work in a mill instead of going out to battle. But when he was compelled to grind instead of serving in the wars, he bewailed his change of fortune and called to mind his former state, saying, “Ah! Miller, I had indeed to go campaigning before, but I was barbed from counter to tail, and a man went along to groom me; and now I cannot understand what ailed me to prefer the mill before the battle.” “Forbear,” said the Miller to him, “harping on what was of yore, for it is the common lot of mortals to sustain the ups and downs of fortune.”
translated_paragraphs: 一匹战马渐渐有了衰老的毛病，便不再上阵，给送进磨坊服役。可是当它真的从驰骋沙场变成了拉磨，便开始哀叹命运的变迁，想起往日的生活，说：“唉，磨坊主，从前我的确得随军出征，可我从胸前到尾后都披着护甲，还专门有个人随行替我刷毛。现在我实在不懂，当初我犯了什么傻，竟会以为拉磨好过打仗。”磨坊主回答：“得了，别再反复念叨当年怎么样。命运有升有降，凡是活在世上的，都少不了要经受。”

source_paragraphs: A MONKEY once danced in an assembly of the Beasts, and so pleased them all by his performance that they elected him their King. A Fox, envying him the honour, discovered a piece of meat lying in a trap, and leading the Monkey to the place where it was, said that she had found a store, but had not used it, she had kept it for him as treasure trove of his kingdom, and counseled him to lay hold of it. The Monkey approached carelessly and was caught in the trap; and on his accusing the Fox of purposely leading him into the snare, she replied, “O Monkey, and are you, with such a mind as yours, going to be King over the Beasts?”
translated_paragraphs: 一次百兽集会，猴子上场跳舞。大伙儿看了它的表演，个个喜爱，便选它来当国王。狐狸嫉妒这份荣耀，发现有块肉落在陷阱里，便领着猴子到了有肉的地方。它说自己发现一处宝藏，并没有动用，特意留给猴王，算是献出在它国土上找到的一份财物，还劝猴王亲自上前取走。猴子毫无戒心地走过去，当场被陷阱夹住。它责备狐狸是有意领它来受困。狐狸回答：“哦，猴子呀，就凭你这点头脑，还想做统治百兽的国王？”

source_paragraphs: A HORSE SOLDIER took the utmost pains with his charger. As long as the war lasted, he looked upon him as his fellow-helper in all emergencies and fed him carefully with hay and corn. But when the war was over, he only allowed him chaff to eat and made him carry heavy loads of wood, subjecting him to much slavish drudgery and ill-treatment. War was again proclaimed, however, and when the trumpet summoned him to his standard, the Soldier put on his charger its military trappings, and mounted, being clad in his heavy coat of mail. The Horse fell down straightway under the weight, no longer equal to the burden, and said to his master, “You must now go to the war on foot, for you have transformed me from a Horse into an Ass; and how can you expect that I can again turn in a moment from an Ass to a Horse?”
translated_paragraphs: 一位骑兵曾经尽心照料自己的战马。战争期间，每遇急难，他都把马看作并肩相助的伙伴，细致地拿干草和谷物喂养它。可一停战，他便只给马一些谷糠吃，让它背负沉重的木材，把大批劳役和种种虐待都加在它身上。不料烽火又起。军号召他归队，他穿上一身厚重的锁甲，给战马配好上阵的鞍具，跨上马背。马已经负担不起这样的重量，一下子就倒了。它对主人说：“您这回得走路去打仗了。您先把我从一匹战马变成了一头驴，如今怎么能指望我转眼之间，又从驴变回战马呢？”

source_paragraphs: THE MEMBERS of the Body rebelled against the Belly, and said, “Why should we be perpetually engaged in administering to your wants, while you do nothing but take your rest, and enjoy yourself in luxury and self-indulgence?” The Members carried out their resolve and refused their assistance to the Belly. The whole Body quickly became debilitated, and the hands, feet, mouth, and eyes, when too late, repented of their folly.
translated_paragraphs: 身体的各个部位造起肚子的反，说：“凭什么我们必须没完没了地满足你的需要，你却除了休息和放纵享乐，什么也不干？”它们照着决心行事，再也不肯向肚子提供帮助。整个身子很快便衰弱下去。手、脚、嘴和眼睛终于为自己的愚蠢后悔，却已太迟。

sections.title_en: The Widow and Her Little Maidens
source_paragraphs: A WIDOW who was fond of cleaning had two little maidens to wait on her. She was in the habit of waking them early in the morning, at cockcrow. The maidens, aggravated by such excessive labor, resolved to kill the cock who roused their mistress so early. When they had done this, they found that they had only prepared for themselves greater troubles, for their mistress, no longer hearing the hour from the cock, woke them up to their work in the middle of the night.
translated_paragraphs: 一个寡妇喜欢打扫清洁，家中有两个年轻小姑娘服侍她。她惯于清早听见鸡鸣，就把姑娘们叫醒。姑娘们为过于劳累的工作烦恼，打定主意，要把那只老是过早唤醒女主人的公鸡杀掉。可是做完这件事，她们才发现自己招来了更大的麻烦。因为女主人听不见鸡鸣报时，到了半夜，就把她们喊起来干活了。

source_paragraphs: A VINE was luxuriant in the time of vintage with leaves and grapes. A Goat, passing by, nibbled its young tendrils and its leaves. The Vine addressed him and said: “Why do you thus injure me without a cause, and crop my leaves? Is there no young grass left? But I shall not have to wait long for my just revenge; for if you now should crop my leaves, and cut me down to my root, I shall provide the wine to pour over you when you are led as a victim to the sacrifice.”
translated_paragraphs: 收葡萄的时候，有一株葡萄藤果实累累，叶子十分茂盛。一只山羊路过，啃起它的嫩卷须和叶片。葡萄藤开口说：“你为什么无缘无故伤害我，吃掉我的叶子？附近就没有一点儿嫩草了吗？不过我也用不着等太久，该有的公道便能讨还。今天就算你啃尽我的叶子，把我一直咬到根，等你被牵去当祭品的时候，在你身上浇下的那杯祭酒，仍将由我来供给。”

source_paragraphs: JUPITER ISSUED a proclamation to all the beasts of the forest and promised a royal reward to the one whose offspring should be deemed the handsomest. The Monkey came with the rest and presented, with all a mother’s tenderness, a flat-nosed, hairless, ill-featured young Monkey as a candidate for the promised reward. A general laugh saluted her on the presentation of her son. She resolutely said, “I know not whether Jupiter will allot the prize to my son, but this I do know, that he is at least in the eyes of me his mother, the dearest, handsomest, and most beautiful of all.”
translated_paragraphs: 朱庇特向森林里的所有走兽颁了一道布告，哪一家的后代评出来最漂亮，就赐给哪一家隆重的赏赐。猴妈妈跟着大家来，带来了自己那鼻子扁扁、没长毛、五官并不好看的小猴，怀着做母亲的全部温存，让它来争取那份赏赐。她把儿子介绍给大家，人群中却响起一阵哄笑。她毫不动摇，说：“朱庇特会不会把奖励给我儿子，我不知道。我只知道，至少在做母亲的我眼里，它是最可爱、最俊俏、最美的孩子。”

sections.title_en: The Hawk, the Kite, and the Pigeons
source_paragraphs: THE PIGEONS, terrified by the appearance of a Kite, called upon the Hawk to defend them. He at once consented. When they had admitted him into the cote, they found that he made more havoc and slew a larger number of them in one day than the Kite could pounce upon in a whole year.
Avoid a remedy that is worse than the disease.
translated_paragraphs: 鸽群被一只鸢的出现吓坏了，便去求苍鹰做自己的保护者。苍鹰马上答应。等它们将它请进鸽舍，才发现，它一天造成的损害、杀掉的鸽子，竟比那只鸢一年能够扑到的还要多。
须提防比疾病本身更坏的疗法。

sections.title_en: The Dolphins, the Whales, and the Sprat
source_paragraphs: THE DOLPHINS and Whales waged a fierce war with each other. When the battle was at its height, a Sprat lifted its head out of the waves and said that he would reconcile their differences if they would accept him as an umpire. One of the Dolphins replied, “We would far rather be destroyed in our battle with each other than admit any interference from you in our affairs.”
translated_paragraphs: 海豚和鲸鱼打起一场恶战。战况最激烈时，一条小鲱鱼从波浪间伸出脑袋，说如果双方愿意请它担任仲裁者，它可以调解两家的争端。一只海豚答道：“我们宁可在相互争斗中丧生，也不愿意让你介入我们的事。”

sections.title_en: The Swallow, the Serpent, and the Court of Justice
source_paragraphs: A SWALLOW, returning from abroad and especially fond of dwelling with men, built herself a nest in the wall of a Court of Justice and there hatched seven young birds. A Serpent gliding past the nest from its hole in the wall ate up the young unfledged nestlings. The Swallow, finding her nest empty, lamented greatly and exclaimed: “Woe to me a stranger! that in this place where all others’ rights are protected, I alone should suffer wrong.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只燕子从外乡飞回来，格外爱与人相处，便在一座法庭的墙上筑窝，并在里面孵出七只小鸟。一条大蛇从墙洞游出，经过燕窝，把还未长齐羽毛的雏鸟吃了个精光。燕子回来，发现窝里空荡荡的，悲痛地哀叫：“我这异乡客真不幸！在这保障其他人权利的地方，唯独我竟然蒙受了不公。”

source_paragraphs: A RIVER carried down in its stream two Pots, one made of earthenware and the other of brass. The Earthen Pot said to the Brass Pot, “Pray keep at a distance and do not come near me, for if you touch me ever so slightly, I shall be broken in pieces, and besides, I by no means wish to come near you.”
Equals make the best friends.
translated_paragraphs: 一条河的流水送下来两只罐子，一只是陶的，另一只是黄铜的。陶罐告诉铜罐：“劳驾，你离得远些，别靠近我。我自己也绝不打算靠近你。因为只消你轻轻碰我一下，我就会碎成好多片。”
彼此相当的人，最适合做朋友。

source_paragraphs: A SHEPHERD once found the whelp of a Wolf and brought it up, and after a while taught it to steal lambs from the neighboring flocks. The Wolf, having shown himself an apt pupil, said to the Shepherd, “Since you have taught me to steal, you must keep a sharp lookout, or you will lose some of your own flock.”
translated_paragraphs: 从前，一个牧羊人捡到一只狼崽，将它养大，又教它去附近的羊群里偷羊羔。狼显出十足的聪明，是个一学就会的好学生。它对牧羊人说：“既然你教会了我偷窃，你可得把自己的羊也看得牢牢的，要不，你的羊群迟早也要少上几只。”

source_paragraphs: A CRAB said to her son, “Why do you walk so one-sided, my child? It is far more becoming to go straight forward.” The young Crab replied: “Quite true, dear Mother; and if you will show me the straight way, I will promise to walk in it.” The Mother tried in vain, and submitted without remonstrance to the reproof of her child.
Example is more powerful than precept.
translated_paragraphs: 一只母蟹问儿子：“孩子，你为什么走路总歪向一边？笔直地往前走，样子可好看得多。”小螃蟹答：“亲爱的妈妈，说得很是。只要你肯走一条直线给我看，我答应，一定照你的样子走。”母蟹努力试了，却怎么也走不出来，只好接受孩子的反驳，一句也没再争辩。
做给人看的榜样，比说给人听的训话更有力量。

sections.title_en: The Father and His Two Daughters
source_paragraphs: A MAN had two daughters, the one married to a gardener, and the other to a tile-maker. After a time he went to the daughter who had married the gardener, and inquired how she was and how all things went with her. She said, “All things are prospering with me, and I have only one wish, that there may be a heavy fall of rain, in order that the plants may be well watered.” Not long after, he went to the daughter who had married the tilemaker, and likewise inquired of her how she fared; she replied, “I want for nothing, and have only one wish, that the dry weather may continue, and the sun shine hot and bright, so that the bricks might be dried.” He said to her, “If your sister wishes for rain, and you for dry weather, with which of the two am I to join my wishes?”
translated_paragraphs: 有个人有两个女儿，一个嫁给园丁，一个嫁给做砖瓦的匠人。过了一阵，他去探望嫁给园丁的女儿，问她好不好，事事是否顺利。她说：“我这边什么都很兴旺。只有一个愿望，希望能降一场大雨，把园里的植物浇个透。”不久，他又去看嫁给砖瓦匠的女儿，也问她日子过得如何。她回答：“我什么都不缺，只有一个心愿。希望干燥的天气一直持续，日头又热又亮，好把那些砖全晒干。”父亲对她说：“你姊妹盼雨，你盼晴，我究竟该跟着你们两个当中的哪一个许愿呢？”

source_paragraphs: A BOY stole a lesson-book from one of his schoolfellows and took it home to his Mother. She not only abstained from beating him, but encouraged him. He next time stole a cloak and brought it to her, and she again commended him. The Youth, advanced to adulthood, proceeded to steal things of still greater value. At last he was caught in the very act, and having his hands bound behind him, was led away to the place of public execution. His Mother followed in the crowd and violently beat her breast in sorrow, whereupon the young man said, “I wish to say something to my Mother in her ear.” She came close to him, and he quickly seized her ear with his teeth and bit it off. The Mother upbraided him as an unnatural child, whereon he replied, “Ah! if you had beaten me when I first stole and brought to you that lesson-book, I should not have come to this, nor have been thus led to a disgraceful death.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个男孩从同学那里偷了本课本，拿回家给母亲看。母亲不仅没有打他，反而鼓励了他。下一回，他又偷了一件披风带回去，母亲再次夸奖他。年轻人渐渐长大，转而偷取价值更高的财物。最后，他在行窃时当场被捉，双手反绑，被押往公开行刑的地方。他母亲走在人群中紧随其后，因悲痛而拼命捶打胸口。这时年轻人说：“我有句话想贴着母亲的耳朵说。”她走近，他却忽地用牙咬住她的耳朵，一口咬了下来。母亲责骂他是个忤逆的孩子。他回答：“唉！第一次我偷了那本课本带给你的时候，你若肯打我一顿，我就不会弄到这般田地，也不会这样被押去死得不光彩了。”

source_paragraphs: AN OLD MAN was employed in cutting wood in the forest, and, in carrying the faggots to the city for sale one day, became very wearied with his long journey. He sat down by the wayside, and throwing down his load, besought “Death” to come. “Death” immediately appeared in answer to his summons and asked for what reason he had called him. The Old Man hurriedly replied, “That, lifting up the load, you may place it again upon my shoulders.”
translated_paragraphs: 有位老人在森林里砍柴为生。一天，他背着成捆的木柴进城去卖，路程太长，走得疲惫极了。他在路边坐下，丢下负担，求死神赶紧前来。死神闻召立刻现身，问他唤自己来，所为何事。老人急忙答道：“想请你将这捆柴提起来，重新放到我的肩膀上。”

source_paragraphs: A FIR-TREE said boastingly to the Bramble, “You are useful for nothing at all; while I am everywhere used for roofs and houses.” The Bramble answered: “You poor creature, if you would only call to mind the axes and saws which are about to hew you down, you would have reason to wish that you had grown up a Bramble, not a Fir-Tree.”
Better poverty without care, than riches with.
translated_paragraphs: 冷杉树向荆棘夸口：“你一点儿用处也没有。瞧我，到处都有人用我做屋顶、盖房子。”荆棘回答：“你这可怜的家伙。你要是稍微想一想那些即将劈砍你的斧子和锯子，就有理由宁愿自己当初长成一丛荆棘，而不是一棵冷杉啦。”
清贫而少忧，胜过富有而多虑。

source_paragraphs: THE PURCHASER of a black servant was persuaded that the color of his skin arose from dirt contracted through the neglect of his former masters. On bringing him home he resorted to every means of cleaning, and subjected the man to incessant scrubbings. The servant caught a severe cold, but he never changed his color or complexion.
What’s bred in the bone will stick to the flesh.
translated_paragraphs: 有个人买来一名黑人仆人，认定他的肤色是脏污造成的，只怪从前的主人没有好好替他打理。把人带回家以后，他想尽了一切清洗的办法，没完没了地给人擦洗。那名仆人却因此患上重感冒，肤色和面容一点也没有改变。
骨子里生就的东西，长在身上便不会脱落。

sections.title_en: The Mouse, the Frog, and the Hawk
source_paragraphs: A MOUSE who always lived on the land, by an unlucky chance formed an intimate acquaintance with a Frog, who lived for the most part in the water. The Frog, one day intent on mischief, bound the foot of the Mouse tightly to his own. Thus joined together, the Frog first of all led his friend the Mouse to the meadow where they were accustomed to find their food. After this, he gradually led him towards the pool in which he lived, until reaching the very brink, he suddenly jumped in, dragging the Mouse with him. The Frog enjoyed the water amazingly, and swam croaking about, as if he had done a good deed. The unhappy Mouse was soon suffocated by the water, and his dead body floated about on the surface, tied to the foot of the Frog. A Hawk observed it, and, pouncing upon it with his talons, carried it aloft. The Frog, being still fastened to the leg of the Mouse, was also carried off a prisoner, and was eaten by the Hawk.
Harm hatch, harm catch.
translated_paragraphs: 一只从小住在陆地上的老鼠，偏偏不走运，跟一只大半日子待在水里的青蛙成了亲密朋友。一天，青蛙存心使坏，把老鼠的一只脚牢牢绑到自己的脚上。这样系在一处，青蛙先带着它的朋友走到它们惯常觅食的草地。之后它渐渐领着老鼠走向自己住的水塘，一到水边，突然一跳，连老鼠也拖进了水。青蛙玩水玩得快活无比，一边到处游，一边呱呱叫，好像自己做了件好事。倒霉的老鼠很快就淹死了，尸体浮在水面上，身子仍旧拴在青蛙腿边。鹰瞅见了，合爪一扑，掠着老鼠飞上高空。青蛙还绑在老鼠脚上，就这样也成了俘虏，最后叫鹰吞了。
算计着去害人，到头来害了自己。

source_paragraphs: A FISHERMAN, engaged in his calling, made a very successful cast and captured a great haul of fish. He managed by a skillful handling of his net to retain all the large fish and to draw them to the shore; but he could not prevent the smaller fish from falling back through the meshes of the net into the sea.
translated_paragraphs: 一名渔夫正在劳作，撒下非常成功的一网，一下网住了好大一批鱼。他操网的本领娴熟，将大鱼全留下来，拖到了岸边，却终究没能阻挡那些小鱼从网眼中掉落，重新回到海里。

source_paragraphs: A WOLF, sorely wounded and bitten by dogs, lay sick and maimed in his lair. Being in want of food, he called to a Sheep who was passing, and asked him to fetch some water from a stream flowing close beside him. “For,” he said, “if you will bring me drink, I will find means to provide myself with meat.” “Yes,” said the Sheep, “if I should bring you the draught, you would doubtless make me provide the meat also.”
Hypocritical speeches are easily seen through.
translated_paragraphs: 一只狼受了重伤，还被一群狗咬过，病恹恹地瘫倒在自己的窝里。正缺东西吃，它唤住一只过路的绵羊，求它到近旁流过的一条小溪去，取些水来。“因为，”狼说，“你要是能替我弄来喝的，我就有办法给自己张罗吃的肉。”绵羊说：“可不是嘛，我一把水给你送到，你准会叫我连肉也一并供上。”
假惺惺的话，常常容易被人看穿。

sections.title_en: The Old Woman and the Wine-Jar
source_paragraphs: AN OLD WOMAN found an empty jar which had lately been full of prime old wine and which still retained the fragrant smell of its former contents. She greedily placed it several times to her nose, and drawing it backwards and forwards said, “O most delicious! How nice must the Wine itself have been, when it leaves behind in the very vessel which contained it so sweet a perfume!”
The memory of a good deed lives.
translated_paragraphs: 一位老妇人找到一只空坛。这坛子不久前还盛过上好的陈年佳酿，仍有先前那美酒的香气。她贪恋地把坛子一回又一回凑到鼻子跟前，拿远些，又拉近些，说：“哦，多么美妙！连盛过酒的空器皿上，都能留下这么芬芳的香气，那酒本身该有多么好啊！”
一件好事留下的记忆，长久不散。

sections.title_en: The Man Bitten by a Dog
source_paragraphs: A MAN who had been bitten by a Dog went about in quest of someone who might heal him. A friend, meeting him and learning what he wanted, said, “If you would be cured, take a piece of bread, and dip it in the blood from your wound, and go and give it to the Dog that bit you.” The Man who had been bitten laughed at this advice and said, “Why? If I should do so, it would be as if I should beg every Dog in the town to bite me.”
Benefits bestowed upon the evil-disposed increase their means of injuring you.
translated_paragraphs: 一个人被狗咬伤，四处寻找谁能治他的伤。一个朋友遇到了他，得知他要找什么，就说：“你若想治好，拿块面包来，蘸一蘸你自己伤口里的血，再去送给咬伤你的那条狗。”那人听了这劝告反倒笑了，说：“为什么要这样？要是我真照着做，岂不跟央求镇上每一条狗都来咬我差不多！”
给存心作恶的家伙好处，只会让他有更多本事继续害你。

source_paragraphs: A HUNTSMAN, returning with his dogs from the field, fell in by chance with a Fisherman who was bringing home a basket well laden with fish. The Huntsman wished to have the fish, and their owner experienced an equal longing for the contents of the game-bag. They quickly agreed to exchange the produce of their day’s sport. Each was so well pleased with his bargain that they made for some time the same exchange day after day. Finally a neighbor said to them, “If you go on in this way, you will soon destroy by frequent use the pleasure of your exchange, and each will again wish to retain the fruits of his own sport.”
Abstain and enjoy.
translated_paragraphs: 一名猎人带着猎犬从田野归来，碰巧遇上个渔夫，正提着满满一篮鱼回家。猎人想得到这些鱼，鱼的主人同样眼馋猎物袋里的东西。两人很快议定，交换双方当天的收获。彼此都对这笔交易十分满意，以至于之后好些日子，天天照样交换。最后，邻人劝他们说：“你们老这样下去，换得太频繁，很快就会消磨光交换原有的乐趣，到时谁都又想把自己打到的东西留给自己了。”
尝得有节制，才能一直有滋味。

source_paragraphs: A CROW having stolen a bit of meat, perched in a tree and held it in her beak. A Fox, seeing this, longed to possess the meat himself, and by a wily stratagem succeeded. “How handsome is the Crow,” he exclaimed, “in the beauty of her shape and in the fairness of her complexion! Oh, if her voice were only equal to her beauty, she would deservedly be considered the Queen of Birds!” This he said deceitfully; but the Crow, anxious to refute the reflection cast upon her voice, set up a loud caw and dropped the flesh. The Fox quickly picked it up, and thus addressed the Crow: “My good Crow, your voice is right enough, but your wit is wanting.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只乌鸦偷来一块肉，飞到树上落脚，嘴里衔着那块肉。狐狸望见，很想将肉据为己有，便施了个巧计，果然成功。它赞叹道：“瞧这位乌鸦，多俊哪！身形多美，面容多漂亮！哦，如果她的嗓音也配得上她这副美貌，人家尊她为鸟中女王，便再恰当不过啦！”狐狸这样说是为骗她。乌鸦却一心想反驳这句对她嗓音的疑虑，张嘴“哇”地大叫一声，肉从嘴里掉了下来。狐狸迅速衔起肉，再向乌鸦说道：“我的好乌鸦，你的嗓子完全没问题，欠缺的却是脑子。”

source_paragraphs: A CERTAIN poor widow had one solitary Sheep. At shearing time, wishing to take his fleece and to avoid expense, she sheared him herself, but used the shears so unskillfully that with the fleece she sheared the flesh. The Sheep, writhing with pain, said, “Why do you hurt me so, Mistress? What weight can my blood add to the wool? If you want my flesh, there is the butcher, who will kill me in an instant; but if you want my fleece and wool, there is the shearer, who will shear and not hurt me.”
The least outlay is not always the greatest gain.
translated_paragraphs: 有一位贫穷的寡妇，所有的羊就只孤零零的一头。到了剪羊毛的时候，她想取下羊毛，又想省一笔费用，便亲自动起手来。可是她对剪子实在太不熟练，剪毛时连羊身上的肉也剪下了。羊痛得扭着身子，说：“女主人，你何必这样弄疼我？我的血又能给羊毛增加多少分量？你若是想要我的肉，有个屠夫，转眼就能把我杀掉；可你若想要的是我身上的毛，那里也有剪羊毛的师傅，他会剪，却不会叫我受伤。”
花费最少，不见得收获最多。

source_paragraphs: AN ASS climbed up to the roof of a building, and frisking about there, broke in the tiling. The owner went up after him and quickly drove him down, beating him severely with a thick wooden cudgel. The Ass said, “Why, I saw the Monkey do this very thing yesterday, and you all laughed heartily, as if it afforded you very great amusement.”
translated_paragraphs: 一头驴爬上房顶，在上面又蹦又跳，踩塌了一片屋瓦。房主追到上面，抡起粗木棒狠揍它，没几下就把它赶了下去。驴问：“咦，我昨天还看见猴子干的就是这件事。你们当时个个开怀大笑，好像这给你们添了多大的乐子呢！”

source_paragraphs: A STAG, roundly chased by the hounds and blinded by fear to the danger he was running into, took shelter in a farmyard and hid himself in a shed among the oxen. An Ox gave him this kindly warning: “O unhappy creature! why should you thus, of your own accord, incur destruction and trust yourself in the house of your enemy?” The Stag replied: “Only allow me, friend, to stay where I am, and I will undertake to find some favourable opportunity of effecting my escape.” At the approach of the evening the herdsman came to feed his cattle, but did not see the Stag; and even the farm-bailiff with several laborers passed through the shed and failed to notice him. The Stag, congratulating himself on his safety, began to express his sincere thanks to the Oxen who had kindly helped him in the hour of need. One of them again answered him: “We indeed wish you well, but the danger is not over. There is one other yet to pass through the shed, who has as it were a hundred eyes, and until he has come and gone, your life is still in peril.” At that moment the master himself entered, and having had to complain that his oxen had not been properly fed, he went up to their racks and cried out: “Why is there such a scarcity of fodder? There is not half enough straw for them to lie on. Those lazy fellows have not even swept the cobwebs away.” While he thus examined everything in turn, he spied the tips of the antlers of the Stag peeping out of the straw. Then summoning his laborers, he ordered that the Stag should be seized and killed.
translated_paragraphs: 一头雄鹿给猎犬紧紧追赶，吓昏了头，没认出自己将要闯进的危险，跑进一处农家院子避难，在牛棚的牛群中藏起身。一头牛好心提醒它：“哦，可怜的家伙，你怎么会主动找死，相信自己在敌人的家里能平安无事呢？”鹿回答：“好朋友，只要肯让我留在此地，我一定设法等个合适的机会，自己逃出去。”傍晚将近，牧人过来喂牛，没有发现鹿。甚至庄稼管事带着几名工人从棚中走过，也没有看见它。雄鹿庆幸自己安全了，开始由衷感谢在它危急时好心帮忙的群牛。有一头牛又答道：“我们当然愿你平安。只是危险还没过去。还有一位要从这棚里经过，他仿佛长着一百只眼睛。他没来过又走开以前，你的性命就依然危在旦夕。”话音未落，主人已经亲自进来。他本来就对牛群没被喂好颇有怨言，一走到草料架前就喊：“饲料为什么这么少？用来给它们铺床的草，连应有的一半都不够。这些懒家伙，连蜘蛛网都没有扫！”就这样一处处查看时，他在稻草里发现了探出的鹿角尖，便将工人们唤来，下令把雄鹿捉住杀掉。

source_paragraphs: A MAN had two dogs: a Hound, trained to assist him in his sports, and a Housedog, taught to watch the house. When he returned home after a good day’s sport, he always gave the Housedog a large share of his spoil. The Hound, feeling much aggrieved at this, reproached his companion, saying, “It is very hard to have all this labor, while you, who do not assist in the chase, luxuriate on the fruits of my exertions.” The Housedog replied, “Do not blame me, my friend, but find fault with the master, who has not taught me to labor, but to depend for subsistence on the labor of others.”
Children are not to be blamed for the faults of their parents.
translated_paragraphs: 有人养了两条狗。一条是猎犬，经过训练，能在打猎时帮忙；另一条是看门狗，学的是守好屋子。每逢猎人满载而归，他总把猎物中挺大的一份拨给看门狗。猎犬深感委屈，向它的伙伴责备道：“这样太不公平。所有辛苦的活儿都是我干的，你毫不出力参加追猎，却舒舒服服享用我的成果。”看门狗回答：“朋友，不要责备我，你得去找主人评理。是他没教我怎样劳作，只教我靠着别人的辛劳养活自己。”
父母的过错，不该怪罪到孩子头上。

sections.title_en: The Wild Ass and the Lion
source_paragraphs: A WILD ASS and a Lion entered into an alliance so that they might capture the beasts of the forest with greater ease. The Lion agreed to assist the Wild Ass with his strength, while the Wild Ass gave the Lion the benefit of his greater speed. When they had taken as many beasts as their necessities required, the Lion undertook to distribute the prey, and for this purpose divided it into three shares. “I will take the first share,” he said, “because I am King: and the second share, as a partner with you in the chase: and the third share (believe me) will be a source of great evil to you, unless you willingly resign it to me, and set off as fast as you can.”
Might makes right.
translated_paragraphs: 野驴和狮子缔结同盟，想把捕捉林中走兽的活干得容易些。狮子答应用自己的力量帮助野驴，野驴则用自己更快的脚力帮助狮子。等猎取的野兽足够所需，狮子主动负责分猎物，将它们分作了三份。“第一份归我，”它说，“因为我是国王。第二份也归我，因为切切实实，我是你一同打猎的伙伴。至于第三份，相信我吧，除非你自愿让给我，并用最快的脚步赶紧离去，不然它将给你招来极大的灾祸。”
仗势凌人者，拿强权当道理。

source_paragraphs: A LION roaming by the seashore saw a Dolphin lift up its head out of the waves, and suggested that they contract an alliance, saying that of all the animals they ought to be the best friends, since the one was the king of beasts on the earth, and the other was the sovereign ruler of all the inhabitants of the ocean. The Dolphin gladly consented to this request. Not long afterwards the Lion had a combat with a wild bull, and called on the Dolphin to help him. The Dolphin, though quite willing to give him assistance, was unable to do so, as he could not by any means reach the land. The Lion abused him as a traitor. The Dolphin replied, “Nay, my friend, blame not me, but Nature, which, while giving me the sovereignty of the sea, has quite denied me the power of living upon the land.”
translated_paragraphs: 狮子沿着海滨漫步，望见一只海豚在波涛中抬起头来，便提议组成同盟。它说，全天下的动物当中，它们两个最该结成好朋友。因为一个是陆上百兽的国王，另一个是海洋一切居民的最高君主。海豚很高兴答应了它的提议。不久，狮子跟一头野公牛搏斗，高声召唤海豚助阵。海豚虽然十分愿意前来帮忙，却无论如何也没办法踏上陆地。狮子大骂它是叛徒。海豚答：“不，朋友，不要怪我。你要怪，就怪大自然吧。它给了我统治大海的权力，却全然不给我在陆地上生活的本领。”

source_paragraphs: AN EAGLE sat on a lofty rock, watching the movements of a Hare whom he sought to make his prey. An archer, who saw the Eagle from a place of concealment, took an accurate aim and wounded him mortally. The Eagle gave one look at the arrow that had entered his heart and saw in that single glance that its feathers had been furnished by himself. “It is a double grief to me,” he exclaimed, “that I should perish by an arrow feathered from my own wings.”
translated_paragraphs: 鹰停在一块高岩上，观察一只野兔的动静，准备捕它为食。一个弓箭手藏在隐蔽处望见了它，瞄得很准，给了它致命的一箭。鹰朝射穿心口的箭望过去，只一眼便认出，尾部的箭羽取自它自己。“我这有双重的悲伤啊，”它喊道，“我死在这样一支箭下，镶在箭上的，偏偏是我自己翅膀上长过的羽毛。”

source_paragraphs: A KITE, sick unto death, said to his mother: “O Mother! do not mourn, but at once invoke the gods that my life may be prolonged.” She replied, “Alas! my son, which of the gods do you think will pity you? Is there one whom you have not outraged by filching from their very altars a part of the sacrifice offered up to them?”
We must make friends in prosperity if we would have their help in adversity.
translated_paragraphs: 一只鸢重病将死，对母亲说：“哦，妈妈！先别悲伤，请赶紧去祈求诸神，让我再多活些时日。”它母亲回答：“唉，我的孩子！你想，哪一位神会怜悯你呢？有哪一位神没有受过你的冒犯？人们献给他们的祭品，你连在祭坛上都要去偷来一份。”
顺境中先得与人为善，逆境时才指望得上别人的帮助。

source_paragraphs: ON A SUMMER DAY, when the great heat induced a general thirst among the beasts, a Lion and a Boar came at the same moment to a small well to drink. They fiercely disputed which of them should drink first, and were soon engaged in the agonies of a mortal combat. When they stopped suddenly to catch their breath for a fiercer renewal of the fight, they saw some Vultures waiting in the distance to feast on the one that should fall first. They at once made up their quarrel, saying, “It is better for us to make friends, than to become the food of Crows or Vultures.”
translated_paragraphs: 盛夏的一天，酷热让走兽们个个干渴。一头狮子和一头野猪同时来到一口小井边饮水，为了谁该先喝，狠狠地吵了起来，很快便陷入一场你死我活的搏斗。它们停下喘口气，正准备再次更加凶猛地动手，忽然望见远处有几只秃鹫在等，打算拿最先倒下的那一个美餐一顿。它们当即和解，彼此说道：“我们两个做朋友，总比进了乌鸦或秃鹫的肚子强。”

source_paragraphs: THE MICE summoned a council to decide how they might best devise means of warning themselves of the approach of their great enemy the Cat. Among the many plans suggested, the one that found most favour was the proposal to tie a bell to the neck of the Cat, so that the Mice, being warned by the sound of the tinkling, might run away and hide themselves in their holes at his approach. But when the Mice further debated who among them should thus “bell the Cat,” there was no one found to do it.
translated_paragraphs: 老鼠们召集议事会，商量怎样想出个最好的办法，让它们在天敌猫靠近之前就收到警报。在大家提出的许多计谋当中，最得众心的是这个建议：往猫的脖子上系个铃铛。这样，猫一靠近，鼠群听到叮当声，便可四散逃跑，躲回洞中。可是当它们进一步讨论，该由哪一位实际去“给猫挂铃铛”时，却找不到一个肯动手的。

source_paragraphs: A DOE blind in one eye was accustomed to graze as near to the edge of the cliff as she possibly could, in the hope of securing her greater safety. She turned her sound eye towards the land that she might get the earliest tidings of the approach of hunter or hound, and her injured eye towards the sea, from whence she entertained no anticipation of danger. Some boatmen sailing by saw her, and taking a successful aim, mortally wounded her. Yielding up her last breath, she gasped forth this lament: “O wretched creature that I am! to take such precaution against the land, and after all to find this seashore, to which I had come for safety, so much more perilous.”
translated_paragraphs: 一头瞎了一只眼睛的母鹿，惯于尽量挨近悬崖边吃草，指望这样能更加安全。它把完好的那只眼睛朝向陆地，好让自己第一时间发觉猎人或猎犬来临；受伤的眼睛则朝海，因为它完全不曾设想危险会从那一侧临近。可是几个乘船经过的人看见了它，瞄个正着，将它击成致命的重伤。在咽下最后一口气时，它喘息着哀叹：“我这个苦命的家伙！陆上防得如此周到。可到头来，偏偏是我为了安全才投奔的海边，竟然危险得多！”

source_paragraphs: THE WEASELS and the Mice waged a perpetual war with each other, in which much blood was shed. The Weasels were always the victors. The Mice thought that the cause of their frequent defeats was that they had no leaders set apart from the general army to command them, and that they were exposed to dangers from lack of discipline. They therefore chose as leaders Mice that were most renowned for their family descent, strength, and counsel, as well as those most noted for their courage in the fight, so that they might be better marshaled in battle array and formed into troops, regiments, and battalions. When all this was done, and the army disciplined, and the herald Mouse had duly proclaimed war by challenging the Weasels, the newly chosen generals bound their heads with straws, that they might be more conspicuous to all their troops. Scarcely had the battle begun, when a great rout overwhelmed the Mice, who scampered off as fast as they could to their holes. The generals, not being able to get in on account of the ornaments on their heads, were all captured and eaten by the Weasels.
The more honour the more danger.
translated_paragraphs: 黄鼠狼和老鼠常年交战，流了许多的血。胜者总是黄鼠狼。老鼠们认为，屡战屡败的原因是没有从普通军队中选出专门的首领统一指挥，又因缺少纪律而易受伤害。于是它们选出家世、气力和智谋最享盛名的几只，又选出战斗时最以勇气著称的一批来担任将领。如此便能更好地排兵布阵，分编成队、成团、成营。一切安排妥当，军队也受过训练，担任传令官的老鼠照规矩向黄鼠狼下书挑战，正式宣战。新任将军们为了让手下的人更容易认出自己，拿些稻草绑在头上当标志。战斗刚开始没多久，鼠军就已全线溃败，老鼠们四散疾窜，以最快的速度朝自家洞穴逃命。唯独将军们，顶着脑袋上的装饰，钻不进洞去，全被黄鼠狼抓住吃掉了。
荣誉越大，危险也越大。

source_paragraphs: A SHEPHERD, keeping watch over his sheep near the shore, saw the Sea very calm and smooth, and longed to make a voyage with a view to commerce. He sold all his flock, invested it in a cargo of dates, and set sail. But a very great tempest came on, and the ship being in danger of sinking, he threw all his merchandise overboard, and barely escaped with his life in the empty ship. Not long afterwards when someone passed by and observed the unruffled calm of the Sea, he interrupted him and said, “It is again in want of dates, and therefore looks quiet.”
translated_paragraphs: 一名牧羊人在海岸边看守羊群，见海面如此平整安静，就很想出海作一趟买卖。他卖掉整群羊，把钱投进一船椰枣，随即扬帆启程。可是一场极为猛烈的暴风雨来临。船有沉没的危险，他只好把所有货物抛进海里，自己坐在空船里，也堪堪才保住性命。不久之后，有人路过，望着又已恢复平静、一丝波澜也没有的大海，说了句赞叹的话。牧羊人打断他，说：“它又想吃椰枣了，所以才装得这样安静。”

sections.title_en: The Ass, the Cock, and the Lion
source_paragraphs: AN ASS and a Cock were in a straw-yard together when a Lion, desperate from hunger, approached the spot. He was about to spring upon the Ass, when the Cock (to the sound of whose voice the Lion, it is said, has a singular aversion) crowed loudly, and the Lion fled away as fast as he could. The Ass, observing his trepidation at the mere crowing of a Cock summoned courage to attack him, and galloped after him for that purpose. He had run no long distance, when the Lion, turning about, seized him and tore him to pieces.
False confidence often leads into danger.
translated_paragraphs: 一头驴同一只公鸡在堆放稻草的院子里待着，正好有头饿得走投无路的狮子来到附近。狮子眼看便要扑向驴，公鸡却响亮地叫了起来。传说狮子尤其厌恶公鸡的啼声，因此，它撒开腿以最快的速度跑了。驴一瞧，原来狮子连公鸡叫都怕成这样，便鼓起勇气想去袭击狮子，为此一路疾驰追在后头。还没跑出多远，狮子突然掉头，一把捉住驴，将它撕成了碎片。
没有根据的自信，往往会把人送进危险之中。

source_paragraphs: THE RIVERS joined together to complain to the Sea, saying, “Why is it that when we flow into your tides so potable and sweet, you work in us such a change, and make us salty and unfit to drink?” The Sea, perceiving that they intended to throw the blame on him, said, “Pray cease to flow into me, and then you will not be made briny.”
translated_paragraphs: 江河联合起来向大海抱怨：“我们水质清甜，本来都能饮用。为什么一汇入你的潮水，你便要把我们改变得如此彻底，叫我们又咸又涩，再不能喝？”大海发觉它们有意将过错推到自己身上，于是说：“那就拜托你们，不要再往我这里流来。这样自然不会咸了。”

sections.title_en: The Wild Boar and the Fox
source_paragraphs: A WILD BOAR stood under a tree and rubbed his tusks against the trunk. A Fox passing by asked him why he thus sharpened his teeth when there was no danger threatening from either huntsman or hound. He replied, “I do it advisedly; for it would never do to have to sharpen my weapons just at the time I ought to be using them.”
To be well prepared for war is the best guarantee of peace.
translated_paragraphs: 一头野猪站在树下，对着树干来回磨自己的獠牙。路过的狐狸问它，眼前既没有猎人，也没有猎犬，有什么危险需要它这样磨利牙齿呢？野猪答道：“我正是经过考虑才这样做。等到了该动用武器的时候才来磨，那个工夫怎么来得及？”
为交战做好充分准备，是守住和平最有力的保证。

source_paragraphs: A FARMER’S daughter was carrying her Pail of milk from the field to the farmhouse, when she fell a-musing. “The money for which this milk will be sold, will buy at least three hundred eggs. The eggs, allowing for all mishaps, will produce two hundred and fifty chickens. The chickens will become ready for the market when poultry will fetch the highest price, so that by the end of the year I shall have money enough from my share to buy a new gown. In this dress I will go to the Christmas parties, where all the young fellows will propose to me, but I will toss my head and refuse them every one.” At this moment she tossed her head in unison with her thoughts, when down fell the milk pail to the ground, and all her imaginary schemes perished in a moment.
translated_paragraphs: 一个农家的姑娘从田里往农舍搬一桶牛奶，一路上出了神。“这牛奶卖掉的钱，至少能买三百个鸡蛋。把各种可能的损耗都算上，鸡蛋能孵出两百五十只小鸡。这些小鸡长到可以上市时，刚好赶上家禽最卖得起价的季节。这样，到年底我就能用自己分到的那份钱买条新裙子。穿上这条裙子，我要去参加圣诞聚会，所有的年轻小伙都会来向我求婚，到时候我一扬头，把他们个个回绝。”她想到这儿，脑袋便跟着神气地一扬，牛奶桶当啷跌落地面。她想象中的种种打算，全在这一瞬间消失干净。

source_paragraphs: A BEE from Mount Hymettus, the queen of the hive, ascended to Olympus to present Jupiter some honey fresh from her combs. Jupiter, delighted with the offering of honey, promised to give whatever she should ask. She therefore besought him, saying, “Give me, I pray thee, a sting, that if any mortal shall approach to take my honey, I may kill him.” Jupiter was much displeased, for he loved the race of man, but could not refuse the request because of his promise. He thus answered the Bee: “You shall have your request, but it will be at the peril of your own life. For if you use your sting, it shall remain in the wound you make, and then you will die from the loss of it.”
Evil wishes, like chickens, come home to roost.
translated_paragraphs: 来自希梅托斯山的一只蜜蜂，是蜂房里的女王，登上奥林匹斯山，将新从蜂巢取出的蜜献给朱庇特。朱庇特很喜欢这个供品，答应无论她请求什么，都将赐给她。于是她恳求道：“请您赐我一枚毒刺，好让我在有凡人靠近来取我的蜂蜜时，能够杀死他。”朱庇特因热爱人类，很不喜欢这个要求，却又不能违背自己先前许下的承诺，于是答道：“你会得到你所要的，但要冒着丢失自己性命的风险。如果你使用这枚刺，它将留在你刺出的伤口里。而你，便要因失去它而死。”
怀着恶意许下的愿望，像走出门的鸡一样，终究要回到自己的窝里。

source_paragraphs: A WOLF, meeting a big well-fed Mastiff with a wooden collar about his neck asked him who it was that fed him so well and yet compelled him to drag that heavy log about wherever he went. “The master,” he replied. Then said the Wolf: “May no friend of mine ever be in such a plight; for the weight of this chain is enough to spoil the appetite.”
translated_paragraphs: 狼遇见一头高大的獒犬，养得肥肥壮壮，脖子上却套着一副木枷。狼问，是谁给它吃得这样好，却又逼迫它无论走到哪儿，都得拖着那块沉重的木头？“主人啊。”獒犬回答。狼说：“但愿我没有一个朋友会落入这般境地。单是这副镣铐的分量，就够叫人没了胃口。”

source_paragraphs: A GREAT CITY was besieged, and its inhabitants were called together to consider the best means of protecting it from the enemy. A Bricklayer earnestly recommended bricks as affording the best material for an effective resistance. A Carpenter, with equal enthusiasm, proposed timber as a preferable method of defense. Upon which a Currier stood up and said, “Sirs, I differ from you altogether: there is no material for resistance equal to a covering of hides; and nothing so good as leather.”
Every man for himself.
translated_paragraphs: 一座大城遭到围困，居民们集合起来，商议抵御敌人的最好办法。一个泥瓦匠极其诚恳地推荐使用砖头，说这是进行有效抵抗最合适的材料。一位木匠也同样热心，说拿木材来防守才胜一筹。接着，加工皮革的匠人站了起来，说：“各位先生，我跟诸位的意见完全不同。要抵挡进攻，没有什么材料比得上一层兽皮。世上就没有比皮革更好的东西啦。”
各人都为自己的行当打算。

source_paragraphs: AN ASS once carried through the streets of a city a famous wooden Image, to be placed in one of its Temples. As he passed along, the crowd made lowly prostration before the Image. The Ass, thinking that they bowed their heads in token of respect for himself, bristled up with pride, gave himself airs, and refused to move another step. The driver, seeing him thus stop, laid his whip lustily about his shoulders and said, “O you perverse dull-head! it is not yet come to this, that men pay worship to an Ass.”
They are not wise who give to themselves the credit due to others.
translated_paragraphs: 从前，一头驴背着一尊出名的木雕神像，穿过城中街道，要把它安放到神庙里。沿途民众在神像前低首拜倒。驴误以为人们低头是表示对它自己的敬意，便神气活现、摆足架势，不肯再迈一步。赶驴人见它停住，抡起鞭子在它肩背上着实抽了几下，骂道：“哦，你这不知好歹的笨脑袋！还没到人类会跪下来叩拜一头驴的那天呢。”
把原应属于别人的敬意记到自己头上，可算不上有智慧。

source_paragraphs: A CERTAIN MAN, detained by a storm in his country house, first of all killed his sheep, and then his goats, for the maintenance of his household. The storm still continuing, he was obliged to slaughter his yoke oxen for food. On seeing this, his Dogs took counsel together, and said, “It is time for us to be off, for if the master spare not his oxen, who work for his gain, how can we expect him to spare us?”
He is not to be trusted as a friend who mistreats his own family.
translated_paragraphs: 有个人给暴风雨困在乡下的房子里。为了给一家人弄到吃的，他先杀了绵羊，又杀了山羊。风雨还不停歇，他只好把那几头一同套着轭拉犁的牛也杀来充饥。几条狗见状，聚在一块儿商议：“咱们可该逃啦。那些替主人干活、叫他获利的牛，他都不肯放过，我们凭什么指望他会放过我们呢？”
一个人连自己的家人都苛待，就不值得托为朋友。

source_paragraphs: A HOUND, who in the days of his youth and strength had never yielded to any beast of the forest, encountered in his old age a boar in the chase. He seized him boldly by the ear, but could not retain his hold because of the decay of his teeth, so that the boar escaped. His master, quickly coming up, was very much disappointed, and fiercely abused the dog. The Hound looked up and said, “It was not my fault master: my spirit was as good as ever, but I could not help my infirmities. I rather deserve to be praised for what I have been, than to be blamed for what I am.”
translated_paragraphs: 有条猎犬，年轻力壮的时候，在树林中遇上任何野兽从不退让。到了老年，一次围猎碰见一头野猪，它勇敢地从耳朵上将野猪咬住，却因牙齿已经衰败，没能一直咬牢，野猪因此逃走。主人飞快赶上，失望万分，狠狠责骂了猎犬。猎犬抬头说：“主人，那并不是我的过错。我拿出的勇气和从前一样，可我没法左右身体的衰弱。想想我从前做过的事吧，那是值得夸奖的。我今天老了，怎么倒要因此挨骂呢？”

sections.title_en: The Two Travelers and the Axe
source_paragraphs: TWO MEN were journeying together. One of them picked up an axe that lay upon the path, and said, “I have found an axe.” “Nay, my friend,” replied the other, “do not say ‘I,’ but ‘We’ have found an axe.” They had not gone far before they saw the owner of the axe pursuing them, and he who had picked up the axe said, “We are undone.” “Nay,” replied the other, “keep to your first mode of speech, my friend; what you thought right then, think right now. Say ‘I,’ not ‘We’ are undone.”
He who shares the danger ought to share the prize.
translated_paragraphs: 两个人结伴出远门。一个人在路上拾得一把斧子，说：“我找到一把斧子。”“朋友，这话不对，”另一个答道，“别说‘我’，该说是‘我们’找到一把斧子。”两人没走多远，就见那把斧子的主人追了过来。捡斧子的人说：“我们可完蛋了！”“这话也不对，”另一个回答，“朋友，还是照你开头那套说法吧。开头你怎么认为合适，现在还怎么来。该说‘我’完蛋了，不是‘我们’完蛋了。”
该分担危险的人，也理应共享收获。

source_paragraphs: A LION, worn out with years and powerless from disease, lay on the ground at the point of death. A Boar rushed upon him, and avenged with a stroke of his tusks a long-remembered injury. Shortly afterwards the Bull with his horns gored him as if he were an enemy. When the Ass saw that the huge beast could be assailed with impunity, he let drive at his forehead with his heels. The expiring Lion said, “I have reluctantly brooked the insults of the brave, but to be compelled to endure such treatment from thee, a disgrace to Nature, is indeed to die a double death.”
translated_paragraphs: 一头狮子年迈力衰，又被疾病折磨得浑身没劲，躺在地上就要死了。野猪冲上去，拿獠牙狠狠扎了它一下，报那一桩记了好久的旧仇。不多久，公牛也用角去抵它，仿佛对待仇敌。驴一看，原来欺负这庞然大物也不必受罚，便用后蹄猛踢狮子的额头。奄奄一息的狮子说：“那些勇士的侮辱，我也只是勉强咽下。还要被迫忍受你这给万物丢脸的东西这般对我，可真是死上两回了。”

source_paragraphs: A WOLF, passing by, saw some Shepherds in a hut eating a haunch of mutton for their dinner. Approaching them, he said, “What a clamor you would raise if I were to do as you are doing!”
translated_paragraphs: 一只狼路过一间小棚屋，见几个牧羊人正在里面拿一条羊后腿当正餐。它走近，对他们说：“要是我干你们眼下正干的事，你们得喊出多大的动静呀！”

source_paragraphs: SOME TRAVELERS, journeying along the seashore, climbed to the summit of a tall cliff, and looking over the sea, saw in the distance what they thought was a large ship. They waited in the hope of seeing it enter the harbor, but as the object on which they looked was driven nearer to shore by the wind, they found that it could at the most be a small boat, and not a ship. When however it reached the beach, they discovered that it was only a large faggot of sticks, and one of them said to his companions, “We have waited for no purpose, for after all there is nothing to see but a load of wood.”
Our mere anticipations of life outrun its realities.
translated_paragraphs: 几位旅人沿海滨赶路，爬上了一块高高的峭壁顶端。向海上张望时，他们见远方有一样东西，以为是一艘大船。大家留下来等，想看看大船驶进港口的情景。随着风把那样东西吹得越来越靠近海岸，他们发觉，那充其量不过一只小艇，哪是什么大船。可等它到达海滩，他们才发现，原来只是一大捆树枝。其中一位便对同伴说：“我们白等啦。说来说去，能看的不过是一担木柴。”
还没亲见时所抱的期待，常跑到了实情的前头。

source_paragraphs: A TRAVELER hired an Ass to convey him to a distant place. The day being intensely hot, and the sun shining in its strength, the Traveler stopped to rest, and sought shelter from the heat under the Shadow of the Ass. As this afforded only protection for one, and as the Traveler and the owner of the Ass both claimed it, a violent dispute arose between them as to which of them had the right to the Shadow. The owner maintained that he had let the Ass only, and not his Shadow. The Traveler asserted that he had, with the hire of the Ass, hired his Shadow also. The quarrel proceeded from words to blows, and while the men fought, the Ass galloped off.
In quarreling about the shadow we often lose the substance.
translated_paragraphs: 一个旅人租了一头驴，骑它去一处遥远的地方。那天酷热，太阳用尽力气照下来，旅人便停下休息，要借驴的影子遮一遮烈日。可是这片阴凉只够一个人容身，而旅人和赶驴主人两位都要占，于是为了谁有权使用驴影，闹起了一场激烈的争执。主人坚持说，租出去的只有驴，并不包括它的影子。旅人则声称，自己既然租下驴，便也把驴影一并租下。双方从斗口闹到动手。他俩打得正起劲，驴却撒开腿跑远了。
为影子争吵，常把实在的东西弄丢。

source_paragraphs: AN ASS, belonging to an herb-seller who gave him too little food and too much work made a petition to Jupiter to be released from his present service and provided with another master. Jupiter, after warning him that he would repent his request, caused him to be sold to a tile-maker. Shortly afterwards, finding that he had heavier loads to carry and harder work in the brick-field, he petitioned for another change of master. Jupiter, telling him that it would be the last time that he could grant his request, ordained that he be sold to a tanner. The Ass found that he had fallen into worse hands, and noting his master’s occupation, said, groaning: “It would have been better for me to have been either starved by the one, or to have been overworked by the other of my former masters, than to have been bought by my present owner, who will even after I am dead tan my hide, and make me useful to him.”
translated_paragraphs: 一头驴属于一个贩卖香草的商人。主人给它的饲料太少，交下来的活又太多，于是驴向朱庇特祈求，准它从眼前的差事上脱身，替它另找一位主人。朱庇特先警告它，说这个要求提出来，以后是会后悔的，然后使它给卖到砖瓦匠那里。不久，驴发现在砖场上背的货更沉，活也更苦，就又求一次换主人。朱庇特告诉它，这将是他最后一次满足它的要求，便安排它被卖给一个鞣皮匠。驴这才发现自己落入了更糟糕的人手里。看看新主人的行当，它呻吟道：“唉，比起来，哪怕我给先前第一位主人饿着，或是在第二位手底下累坏，都胜过给现在这位买下。因为这个人连我死了都要鞣我的皮，让我继续为他所用。”

source_paragraphs: MERCURY once determined to learn in what esteem he was held among mortals. For this purpose he assumed the character of a man and visited in this disguise a Sculptor’s studio having looked at various statues, he demanded the price of two figures of Jupiter and Juno. When the sum at which they were valued was named, he pointed to a figure of himself, saying to the Sculptor, “You will certainly want much more for this, as it is the statue of the Messenger of the Gods, and author of all your gain.” The Sculptor replied, “Well, if you will buy these, I’ll fling you that into the bargain.”
translated_paragraphs: 墨丘利有一回打定主意，想亲自了解凡人对他究竟有几分敬重。为了这件事，他化成普通人的模样，乔装去了一位雕刻家的作坊。他看过几尊塑像，便问朱庇特和朱诺两尊像各值多少钱。听完价钱，他指着一尊自己的像，对雕刻家说：“这尊你一定开价更高得多。因为这是众神的使者，又是给你们带来一切收益的神呀。”雕刻家答：“嗯，你若肯将这两尊买下，那尊我就添进去，白送给你。”

source_paragraphs: A FOX, running before the hounds, came across a Woodcutter felling an oak and begged him to show him a safe hiding-place. The Woodcutter advised him to take shelter in his own hut, so the Fox crept in and hid himself in a corner. The huntsman soon came up with his hounds and inquired of the Woodcutter if he had seen the Fox. He declared that he had not seen him, and yet pointed, all the time he was speaking, to the hut where the Fox lay hidden. The huntsman took no notice of the signs, but believing his word, hastened forward in the chase. As soon as they were well away, the Fox departed without taking any notice of the Woodcutter: whereon he called to him and reproached him, saying, “You ungrateful fellow, you owe your life to me, and yet you leave me without a word of thanks.” The Fox replied, “Indeed, I should have thanked you fervently if your deeds had been as good as your words, and if your hands had not been traitors to your speech.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只狐狸让猎犬紧追，逃命时碰见一个樵夫正伐橡树，便求他指个藏身的安全去处。樵夫叫它去自己棚屋里躲一躲。狐狸悄悄钻进去，藏在角落。不多时，猎人领着狗追至，向樵夫打听有没有见过狐狸。他嘴上说自己没见，手却边说边指着狐狸藏身的棚屋。猎人没有留心这些暗示，信了他的话，匆匆往前追。人狗一走远，狐狸便出了棚屋，没搭理樵夫，径直离去。樵夫在后面叫住它，责备道：“你这不知感恩的家伙，欠我一条命，竟连个谢字也不说就走？”狐狸回答：“当真，如果你的所作所为跟你说的话同样好，如果你的双手没出卖你的嘴，我会诚心诚意向你道谢的。”

source_paragraphs: A VERY LARGE OAK was uprooted by the wind and thrown across a stream. It fell among some Reeds, which it thus addressed: “I wonder how you, who are so light and weak, are not entirely crushed by these strong winds.” They replied, “You fight and contend with the wind, and consequently you are destroyed; while we on the contrary bend before the least breath of air, and therefore remain unbroken, and escape.”
Stoop to conquer.
translated_paragraphs: 一棵极大的橡树被风连根拔起，横着倒向一条溪流。它落入一片芦苇中间，向芦苇们说：“我真不明白，你们这么轻、这么弱，竟没有给这样的大风全压碎。”它们回答：“你跟风较劲，要奋力同它相争，结果给毁掉了。我们恰恰相反，微风只须轻轻一吹，便会随风弯腰。因此我们既没折断，又能逃过灾祸。”
肯低下身来，有时才能取胜。

source_paragraphs: A LION entered a farmyard. The Farmer, wishing to catch him, shut the gate. When the Lion found that he could not escape, he flew upon the sheep and killed them, and then attacked the oxen. The Farmer, beginning to be alarmed for his own safety, opened the gate and released the Lion. On his departure the Farmer grievously lamented the destruction of his sheep and oxen, but his wife, who had been a spectator to all that took place, said, “On my word, you are rightly served, for how could you for a moment think of shutting up a Lion along with you in your farmyard when you know that you shake in your shoes if you only hear his roar at a distance?”
translated_paragraphs: 狮子闯进一个农家院落。农夫要捉它，便关上了大门。狮子见自己逃不出去，一下子扑向绵羊，咬死了它们，又去袭击耕牛。农夫这会儿开始担忧自己的安危，赶紧开门，放走狮子。狮子离开以后，农夫为羊和牛的死伤悲悲切切地哀叹。他妻子旁观了事情的始末，便说：“依我看，你是自作自受。你明明知道，光在远处听见狮吼，就能吓得两腿发抖，怎么竟会哪怕一瞬间想过把自己和狮子一起锁在这院子里呢？”

source_paragraphs: A WOLF, having stolen a lamb from a fold, was carrying him off to his lair. A Lion met him in the path, and seizing the lamb, took it from him. Standing at a safe distance, the Wolf exclaimed, “You have unrighteously taken that which was mine from me!” To which the Lion jeeringly replied, “It was righteously yours, eh? The gift of a friend?”
translated_paragraphs: 狼从羊圈偷到一只小羊，正叼着往自己的窝里走。路上碰见狮子，狮子一把攫住小羊，从狼那里抢了过去。狼站得远远的，确保安全才喊：“你竟然从我这里硬抢本属我的东西，太不公道了！”狮子嘲笑着回道：“真是公公平平就属于你的，对吧？朋友送你的礼物？”

sections.title_en: The Birdcatcher, the Partridge, and the Cock
source_paragraphs: A BIRDCATCHER was about to sit down to a dinner of herbs when a friend unexpectedly came in. The bird-trap was quite empty, as he had caught nothing, and he had to kill a pied Partridge, which he had tamed for a decoy. The bird entreated earnestly for his life: “What would you do without me when next you spread your nets? Who would chirp you to sleep, or call for you the covey of answering birds?” The Birdcatcher spared his life, and determined to pick out a fine young Cock just attaining to his comb. But the Cock expostulated in piteous tones from his perch: “If you kill me, who will announce to you the appearance of the dawn? Who will wake you to your daily tasks or tell you when it is time to visit the bird-trap in the morning?” He replied, “What you say is true. You are a capital bird at telling the time of day. But my friend and I must have our dinners.”
Necessity knows no law.
translated_paragraphs: 捕鸟人正要坐下来吃一顿野菜饭，一位朋友不期而至。他当天什么都没捕到，鸟笼空空，只好去杀一只花羽鹧鸪。那是只养驯了给他引鸟的鹧鸪。它恳切地向他求饶：“下一回你撒网，没有我怎么办？谁啼叫着哄你入睡，又有谁能替你招来成群应答的同伴？”捕鸟人便饶了它一命，决定另挑一只才长出鸡冠、模样很好的小公鸡。公鸡在栖架上也凄声分辩：“要是你杀了我，谁来报告黎明到来？谁能叫醒你去做一天的活，又或者告诉你，早晨该什么时候去察看鸟笼？”捕鸟人答：“你说得不错。要报时，你真是个好手。可是我和我的朋友总得吃饭呀。”
情势紧迫的时候，规矩也顾不得了。

source_paragraphs: AN ANT went to the bank of a river to quench its thirst, and being carried away by the rush of the stream, was on the point of drowning. A Dove sitting on a tree overhanging the water plucked a leaf and let it fall into the stream close to her. The Ant climbed onto it and floated in safety to the bank. Shortly afterwards a birdcatcher came and stood under the tree, and laid his lime-twigs for the Dove, which sat in the branches. The Ant, perceiving his design, stung him in the foot. In pain the birdcatcher threw down the twigs, and the noise made the Dove take wing.
translated_paragraphs: 一只蚂蚁到河岸边解渴，却被急流卷走，眼看要淹死。临水伸出的树枝上坐着一只鸽子。它摘下一片树叶，丢进紧靠蚂蚁的水里。蚂蚁爬了上去，平安漂回岸边。不久，一个捕鸟人过来，站在树底，把涂了黏胶的树枝布置好，要拿来捉那只栖在枝头的鸽子。蚂蚁看穿他的打算，在他脚上蜇了一口。捕鸟人痛得扔下了枝条，响声惊动鸽子，它振翅飞走了。

source_paragraphs: THE HARES, oppressed by their own exceeding timidity and weary of the perpetual alarm to which they were exposed, with one accord determined to put an end to themselves and their troubles by jumping from a lofty precipice into a deep lake below. As they scampered off in large numbers to carry out their resolve, the Frogs lying on the banks of the lake heard the noise of their feet and rushed helter-skelter to the deep water for safety. On seeing the rapid disappearance of the Frogs, one of the Hares cried out to his companions: “Stay, my friends, do not do as you intended; for you now see that there are creatures who are still more timid than ourselves.”
translated_paragraphs: 野兔们为自己过分胆小苦恼透了，也受够了成天担惊受怕的日子。它们一致决定要从高耸的崖顶，跳到下面的深湖中，让生命和烦恼一同终结。它们成群结队奔去实行这个决定时，卧在湖岸上的青蛙听到脚步响，乱作一团，争先恐后地跳进深水里躲避。眼看青蛙转瞬逃得无影无踪，一只野兔朝同伴喊：“且慢，朋友们！可别照原先打算的去做。现在你们看清了，世上还有比我们更胆小的生灵呢。”

source_paragraphs: A MONKEY perched upon a lofty tree saw some Fishermen casting their nets into a river, and narrowly watched their proceedings. The Fishermen after a while gave up fishing, and on going home to dinner left their nets upon the bank. The Monkey, who is the most imitative of animals, descended from the treetop and endeavored to do as they had done. Having handled the net, he threw it into the river, but became tangled in the meshes and drowned. With his last breath he said to himself, “I am rightly served; for what business had I who had never handled a net to try and catch fish?”
translated_paragraphs: 一只猴子高踞树梢，看见几个渔夫朝河中撒网，便仔仔细细观察他们的一举一动。过了一会儿，渔夫们收手不打鱼了。他们回家吃饭，把网留在岸边。猴子是动物中最擅长模仿的，它从树顶下来，想照他们的样子做一回。它抓起网，扔进河里，自己却被网眼缠住，沉下去淹死了。咽下最后一口气以前，它对自己说：“我这是活该。我这样一个从来没摸过网的，干吗要来学人家打鱼？”

source_paragraphs: A CERTAIN rich man bought in the market a Goose and a Swan. He fed the one for his table and kept the other for the sake of its song. When the time came for killing the Goose, the cook went to get him at night, when it was dark, and he was not able to distinguish one bird from the other. By mistake he caught the Swan instead of the Goose. The Swan, threatened with death, burst forth into song and thus made himself known by his voice, and preserved his life by his melody.
translated_paragraphs: 一个富人从市场买回一只鹅和一只天鹅。喂养一个是为了上餐桌，留着另一个则为了听它唱歌。该杀鹅了，厨子趁黑夜去捉。天暗，他实在分不出两只鸟，将天鹅错当成鹅抓在手里。天鹅面临死亡，不由得放声歌唱。这么一来，它的叫声表明了它是谁，它靠自己的歌喉保住了一条命。

source_paragraphs: A DOE hard pressed by hunters sought refuge in a cave belonging to a Lion. The Lion concealed himself on seeing her approach, but when she was safe within the cave, sprang upon her and tore her to pieces. “Woe is me,” exclaimed the Doe, “who have escaped from man, only to throw myself into the mouth of a wild beast?”
In avoiding one evil, care must be taken not to fall into another.
translated_paragraphs: 母鹿被猎人追得走投无路，跑到一个山洞里躲避，却进了狮子的家。狮子一看她走来，先藏起身。等鹿觉得自己已经进洞，脱离危险，它猛扑上去，把她撕成了碎片。“我真苦啊！”母鹿叫道，“竟逃脱了人手，只为亲自投进一头野兽的嘴里！”
为躲避一种灾祸，也须当心别落进另一种灾祸中。

sections.title_en: The Fisherman and the Little Fish
source_paragraphs: A FISHERMAN who lived on the produce of his nets, one day caught a single small Fish as the result of his day’s labor. The Fish, panting convulsively, thus entreated for his life: “O Sir, what good can I be to you, and how little am I worth? I am not yet come to my full size. Pray spare my life, and put me back into the sea. I shall soon become a large fish fit for the tables of the rich, and then you can catch me again, and make a handsome profit of me.” The Fisherman replied, “I should indeed be a very simple fellow if, for the chance of a greater uncertain profit, I were to forego my present certain gain.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个渔夫靠渔网的收获维生。一天，他辛劳一整日，只有一条小小的鱼进网。小鱼抽搐着喘气，向他求饶：“先生，我对你能有什么用呢？我才值多么一点钱呀？我还没长成。求你饶我性命，把我放回海里吧。用不多久，我就能长成一条配得上富人餐桌的大鱼。到时你再捉我，就能大赚一笔。”渔夫回答：“要是我为了将来也许能多挣、也许不能多挣的一桩买卖，把眼下已经到手的东西丢掉，我可真是个傻瓜了。”

source_paragraphs: A HUNTER, not very bold, was searching for the tracks of a Lion. He asked a man felling oaks in the forest if he had seen any marks of his footsteps or knew where his lair was. “I will,” said the man, “at once show you the Lion himself.” The Hunter, turning very pale and chattering with his teeth from fear, replied, “No, thank you. I did not ask that; it is his track only I am in search of, not the Lion himself.”
The hero is brave in deeds as well as words.
translated_paragraphs: 一个胆子不怎么大的猎人在查找狮子的踪迹。他问一个正在林中伐橡树的人，有没有看见过狮子的脚印，又或者知道它的巢穴在哪里。“我这就带你去看那头狮子。”那人说。猎人脸色惨白，吓得牙齿直打战，答：“不，谢谢。我问的不是这个。我只是在找它的脚印，不是找狮子本身。”
真正的英雄，嘴上勇敢，行动也勇敢。

source_paragraphs: A VERY HUNGRY FOX, seeing some bread and meat left by shepherds in the hollow of an oak, crept into the hole and made a hearty meal. When he finished, he was so full that he was not able to get out, and began to groan and lament his fate. Another Fox passing by heard his cries, and coming up, inquired the cause of his complaining. On learning what had happened, he said to him, “Ah, you will have to remain there, my friend, until you become such as you were when you crept in, and then you will easily get out.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只狐狸饿坏了，看见牧羊人把一些面包和肉留在橡树洞里，便钻进去饱餐了一顿。等它吃完，肚子撑得太饱，已经出不来，只得呻吟，哀叹自己的命运。另一只狐狸经过，听见哀叫，走过去问它为什么抱怨。听明白发生了什么，它便说：“唉，我的朋友，你得留在这儿，直等到肚子瘪回钻进来时的模样，再想出去就容易啦。”

source_paragraphs: TWO FROGS dwelt in the same pool. When the pool dried up under the summer’s heat, they left it and set out together for another home. As they went along they chanced to pass a deep well, amply supplied with water, and when they saw it, one of the Frogs said to the other, “Let us descend and make our abode in this well: it will furnish us with shelter and food.” The other replied with greater caution, “But suppose the water should fail us. How can we get out again from so great a depth?”
Do nothing without a regard to the consequences.
translated_paragraphs: 两只青蛙住在同一口池塘。到了暑热时节，池水给晒干了，两只青蛙便结伴离开，另寻新家。途中碰巧经过一口深井，井里水源充足。一只青蛙看了一眼，说：“咱们干脆下去，就住在这井里吧。它可以给咱们吃的，还可以庇护咱们。”另一只更为谨慎，回答：“可是，万一井水也干了呢？这么深的地方，咱们怎样才能再出来？”
做任何事，都该顾及后果。

source_paragraphs: A LAMP, soaked with too much oil and flaring brightly, boasted that it gave more light than the sun. Then a sudden puff of wind arose, and the Lamp was immediately extinguished. Its owner lit it again, and said: “Boast no more, but henceforth be content to give thy light in silence. Know that not even the stars need to be relit.”
translated_paragraphs: 一盏灯吃了太多油，蹿起明亮的火焰，便夸口说自己放出的光比太阳还多。这时一阵风突然吹来，灯立刻灭了。主人重新点燃它，说：“别再夸口了。从今往后，就安心默默地放你的光。你要明白，别说太阳，就是星星，也用不着人重新点亮。”

source_paragraphs: AN ARAB Camel-driver, after completing the loading of his Camel, asked him which he would like best, to go up hill or down. The poor beast replied, not without a touch of reason: “Why do you ask me? Is it that the level way through the desert is closed?”
translated_paragraphs: 一个阿拉伯赶驼人把货物全装上骆驼的背，问它更喜欢上坡还是下坡。可怜的牲口回答，口气倒并非全无道理：“你问我这干什么？难道穿过沙漠的那条平路已经封了吗？”

sections.title_en: The Miller, His Son, and Their Ass
source_paragraphs: A MILLER and his son were driving their Ass to a neighboring fair to sell him. They had not gone far when they met with a troop of women collected round a well, talking and laughing. “Look there,” cried one of them, “did you ever see such fellows, to be trudging along the road on foot when they might ride?” The old man hearing this, quickly made his son mount the Ass, and continued to walk along merrily by his side. Presently they came up to a group of old men in earnest debate. “There,” said one of them, “it proves what I was a-saying. What respect is shown to old age in these days? Do you see that idle lad riding while his old father has to walk? Get down, you young scapegrace, and let the old man rest his weary limbs.” Upon this the old man made his son dismount, and got up himself. In this manner they had not proceeded far when they met a company of women and children: “Why, you lazy old fellow,” cried several tongues at once, “how can you ride upon the beast, while that poor little lad there can hardly keep pace by the side of you?” The good-natured Miller immediately took up his son behind him. They had now almost reached the town. “Pray, honest friend,” said a citizen, “is that Ass your own?” “Yes,” replied the old man. “O, one would not have thought so,” said the other, “by the way you load him. Why, you two fellows are better able to carry the poor beast than he you.” “Anything to please you,” said the old man; “we can but try.” So, alighting with his son, they tied the legs of the Ass together and with the help of a pole endeavored to carry him on their shoulders over a bridge near the entrance to the town. This entertaining sight brought the people in crowds to laugh at it, till the Ass, not liking the noise nor the strange handling that he was subject to, broke the cords that bound him and, tumbling off the pole, fell into the river. Upon this, the old man, vexed and ashamed, made the best of his way home again, convinced that by endeavoring to please everybody he had pleased nobody, and lost his Ass in the bargain.
translated_paragraphs: 磨坊主和儿子赶着驴去邻近的集市，打算把它卖掉。没走多远，看见一群女人围坐在井边，有说有笑。其中一个嚷道：“你们瞧！明明有驴可骑，却还拖着腿在路上走，有谁见过这样的家伙？”老头听见，忙叫儿子骑上驴背，自己高高兴兴跟在旁边走。没多久，他们来到一伙正在认真争辩的老者跟前。“你瞧，”其中一个说，“这就印证了我刚才的话。如今年轻人对老年人还有什么尊敬可言？那个闲小子骑在驴上，他老爹却得走路，你们看见没有？下来，小无赖，让老人家那双疲乏的腿歇歇！”老头便叫儿子下来，自己骑了上去。这样还没走多远，就遇见一群女人和孩子。好几张嘴同时喊道：“嘿，你这懒老头！那可怜的小娃娃几乎追不上你，你怎么好意思骑在牲口背上呢？”好脾气的磨坊主立即把儿子拉上来坐在身后。集镇已经快到了。一位镇民问：“请问，老实朋友，这驴是你自家的？”“是呀。”老头答。“噢，照你给它加负担的样子，可真叫人想不到呀，”那人说，“你们俩去抬这头可怜的牲口，也比叫它驮你们更有力气啊。”“怎么样都成，只要你满意，”老人说，“我们不妨试试。”于是他和儿子下了驴，绑住驴的腿，穿过一根长杆，抬在肩上，想过镇口附近的那座桥。这么有趣的景象，引来大群看热闹的人，人人放声发笑。驴既不喜欢喧闹，又不喜欢别人这样奇奇怪怪地摆布它，便挣断绳索，从木杆上翻落，掉进了河里。这下，老人又恼又羞，只好尽快往家赶。他终于信服，自己力求叫所有人满意，结果谁也没有叫满意，反倒赔上了那头驴。

source_paragraphs: A CERTAIN HOUSE was overrun with Mice. A Cat, discovering this, made her way into it and began to catch and eat them one by one. Fearing for their lives, the Mice kept themselves close in their holes. The Cat was no longer able to get at them and perceived that she must tempt them forth by some device. For this purpose she jumped upon a peg, and suspending herself from it, pretended to be dead. One of the Mice, peeping stealthily out, saw her and said, “Ah, my good madam, even though you should turn into a meal-bag, we will not come near you.”
translated_paragraphs: 一所房子里老鼠成了灾。一只猫发现后钻进屋，把老鼠一只一只捉来吃。老鼠担心丢了性命，都紧紧躲在洞里。猫再也够不着它们，知道非想个诡计，把它们诱出来不可。于是猫跳上一根木钉，把自己吊在上头，装作已经死了。一只老鼠悄悄探头，看见了她，说：“啊，好太太，哪怕您当真变成一只面粉袋子，我们也不会靠近您。”

source_paragraphs: A BULL was bitten by a Mouse and, angered by the wound, tried to capture him. But the Mouse reached his hole in safety. Though the Bull dug into the walls with his horns, he tired before he could rout out the Mouse, and crouching down, went to sleep outside the hole. The Mouse peeped out, crept furtively up his flank, and again biting him, retreated to his hole. The Bull rising up, and not knowing what to do, was sadly perplexed. At which the Mouse said, “The great do not always prevail. There are times when the small and lowly are the strongest to do mischief.”
translated_paragraphs: 老鼠咬了公牛一口。公牛为这伤口发怒，想捉住它，可老鼠平安回到洞里。公牛用角猛刨墙壁，没等把老鼠从藏身处赶出来，自己先累坏了，就趴在洞外睡着了。老鼠探头一看，悄悄爬上它的身侧，又一口咬下去，再逃回洞中。公牛站起身来，不知道该拿它怎么办，正发愁。老鼠说：“大个子并不总能取胜。有些时候，要说使个坏的本领，矮小卑微的家伙反而最强。”

source_paragraphs: A RICH MAN gave a great feast, to which he invited many friends and acquaintances. His Dog availed himself of the occasion to invite a stranger Dog, a friend of his, saying, “My master gives a feast, and there is always much food remaining; come and sup with me tonight.” The Dog thus invited went at the hour appointed, and seeing the preparations for so grand an entertainment, said in the joy of his heart, “How glad I am that I came! I do not often get such a chance as this. I will take care and eat enough to last me both today and tomorrow.” While he was congratulating himself and wagging his tail to convey his pleasure to his friend, the Cook saw him moving about among his dishes and, seizing him by his fore and hind paws, bundled him without ceremony out of the window. He fell with force upon the ground and limped away, howling dreadfully. His yelling soon attracted other street dogs, who came up to him and inquired how he had enjoyed his supper. He replied, “Why, to tell you the truth, I drank so much wine that I remember nothing. I do not know how I got out of the house.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个富人举行盛宴，邀请了许多亲友熟人。他的狗趁这机会，也邀请了一位外来的狗朋友，说：“我家主人摆了宴席，总有好多吃食剩下来。你今晚来同我吃晚饭吧。”被邀请的狗按时到达，看见这场盛宴张罗得如此丰盛，心中欢喜地想：“我真高兴自己来了！这样的机会我可不常有。我得留心吃足，吃下一顿，够我今天和明天两天用。”它一边暗自庆幸，一边向朋友摇尾巴表示快乐。厨子看见它在一道道菜之间穿来穿去，一把揪住它的前后腿，不客气地从窗户扔了出去。它重重跌到地上，惨叫着一瘸一拐地走了。嚎叫声很快引来街上别的狗。它们上前打听，这顿晚餐它吃得是否尽兴。那狗答：“嗯，说句实话，我喝的酒太多，什么都不记得。我连自己怎么出的那座房子也不知道啦。”

source_paragraphs: SOME THIEVES broke into a house and found nothing but a Cock, whom they stole, and got off as fast as they could. Upon arriving at home they prepared to kill the Cock, who thus pleaded for his life: “Pray spare me; I am very serviceable to men. I wake them up in the night to their work.” “That is the very reason why we must the more kill you,” they replied; “for when you wake your neighbors, you entirely put an end to our business.”
The safeguards of virtue are hateful to those with evil intentions.
translated_paragraphs: 几个小偷闯入一所房子，除了公鸡，什么也没找见，只好把它偷走，尽快脱身。到家后，他们正要杀掉公鸡，它这样恳求活命：“求你们饶我！我对人非常有用。我会在夜里便把人们叫醒，好让他们起来干活。”“正是为这个，我们更加非杀你不可，”小偷们答，“因为你一叫醒四邻，我们的生意就全给毁了。”
守护美德的东西，心怀恶意的人见了就恨。

source_paragraphs: A PRINCE had some Monkeys trained to dance. Being naturally great mimics of men’s actions, they showed themselves most apt pupils, and when arrayed in their rich clothes and masks, they danced as well as any of the courtiers. The spectacle was often repeated with great applause, till on one occasion a courtier, bent on mischief, took from his pocket a handful of nuts and threw them upon the stage. The Monkeys at the sight of the nuts forgot their dancing and became (as indeed they were) Monkeys instead of actors. Pulling off their masks and tearing their robes, they fought with one another for the nuts. The dancing spectacle thus came to an end amidst the laughter and ridicule of the audience.
translated_paragraphs: 一位王子训练了几只猴子学跳舞。猴子天生便擅长模仿人类的动作，表现得十分聪明。一穿上华贵的衣裳，戴上面具，它们就能跟随便哪位宫廷大臣舞得一样好。这节目屡屡上演，赢得满堂喝彩。直到有一次，一个存心作弄它们的朝臣从兜里摸出一把坚果，扔到了台上。猴子一见坚果，立即忘了跳舞。从演员变回猴子——它们本来就是猴子。它们扯掉面具，撕破衣袍，为争那些坚果彼此大打出手。这场舞蹈表演，就在观众的笑声和嘲弄声里收了场。

source_paragraphs: A FARMER, who bore a grudge against a Fox for robbing his poultry yard, caught him at last, and being determined to take an ample revenge, tied some rope well soaked in oil to his tail, and set it on fire. The Fox by a strange fatality rushed to the fields of the Farmer who had captured him. It was the time of the wheat harvest; but the Farmer reaped nothing that year and returned home grieving sorely.
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸偷了农夫家禽院里的东西，农夫一直怀着怨恨。最后他终于逮住狐狸，决心狠狠报复，便将一截用油浸透的绳索系在它尾巴上，再点上火。偏偏造化弄人，狐狸竟朝抓住它的农夫家的田野里冲去。那正是小麦该收割的时候。这一年，农夫颗粒无收，怀着深深的伤痛回了家。

source_paragraphs: A TRAVELER wearied from a long journey lay down, overcome with fatigue, on the very brink of a deep well. Just as he was about to fall into the water, Dame Fortune, it is said, appeared to him and waking him from his slumber thus addressed him: “Good Sir, pray wake up: for if you fall into the well, the blame will be thrown on me, and I shall get an ill name among mortals; for I find that men are sure to impute their calamities to me, however much by their own folly they have really brought them on themselves.”
Everyone is more or less master of his own fate.
translated_paragraphs: 一位旅人长途跋涉，疲惫不堪，在一口深井的边沿倒下睡着了。眼看他就要跌进水里，据说命运女神此时出现在他面前，将他从睡梦中叫醒，说：“好先生，请醒醒！要是你掉进井里，这罪名就要扣到我头上，我在人世间就要落个坏名声。因为我发现，不论人们的灾祸多大程度上是他们自己愚蠢招来的，他们总要归罪给我。”
人或多或少总是自己命运的主人。

source_paragraphs: A SEAGULL having bolted down too large a fish, burst its deep gullet-bag and lay down on the shore to die. A Kite saw him and exclaimed: “You richly deserve your fate; for a bird of the air has no business to seek its food from the sea.”
Every man should be content to mind his own business.
translated_paragraphs: 一只海鸥急忙吞下一条过大的鱼，把自己深深的喉囊撑破了，只能躺在岸边等死。一只鸢瞧见它，说：“你落到这个下场，实在应该。你一只空中的鸟儿，本就不该到海里去找食物。”
人人都该安心照管自己的事务。

sections.title_en: The Lion, the Bear, and the Fox
source_paragraphs: A LION and a Bear seized a Kid at the same moment, and fought fiercely for its possession. When they had fearfully lacerated each other and were faint from the long combat, they lay down exhausted with fatigue. A Fox, who had gone round them at a distance several times, saw them both stretched on the ground with the Kid lying untouched in the middle. He ran in between them, and seizing the Kid scampered off as fast as he could.
