The Lion and the Bear saw him, but not being able to get up, said, “Woe be to us, that we should have fought and belabored ourselves only to serve the turn of a Fox.”
It sometimes happens that one man has all the toil, and another all the profit.
translated_paragraphs: 狮子和熊同时抓到一只小山羊，为了争它，大打出手。双方彼此抓得遍体鳞伤，久战之后眼前发花，都力竭倒地。一只狐狸已经远远绕着它们转过几圈。现在它看见两个都躺在地上，小山羊在正中央，谁也没动，便从两者中间蹿进去，叼起山羊，拼命逃远了。狮子和熊眼睁睁看着，却站不起来，只得说：“苦了我们呀，争斗半天，打残了自己，竟只是替一只狐狸效了劳！”
有时，一个人吃尽了所有苦，另一个人却拿走了全部好处。

sections.title_en: The Philosopher, the Ants, and Mercury
source_paragraphs: A PHILOSOPHER witnessed from the shore the shipwreck of a vessel, of which the crew and passengers were all drowned. He inveighed against the injustice of Providence, which would for the sake of one criminal perchance sailing in the ship allow so many innocent persons to perish. As he was indulging in these reflections, he found himself surrounded by a whole army of Ants, near whose nest he was standing. One of them climbed up and stung him, and he immediately trampled them all to death with his foot. Mercury presented himself, and striking the Philosopher with his wand, said, “And are you indeed to make yourself a judge of the dealings of Providence, who hast thyself in a similar manner treated these poor Ants?”
translated_paragraphs: 一位哲学家站在岸上，眼看一艘船遇难，船员与乘客尽数溺亡。他痛斥天意不公，只因船上也许坐着一个罪犯，竟让那么多无辜的人陪葬。他满心作此感慨时，发现自己周围来了一大队蚂蚁，原来站的地方就在蚁巢旁边。其中一只爬上来，蜇了他一下，他立即抬脚，把整队蚂蚁全部踩死。墨丘利出现在他跟前，用手杖击了他一下，说：“你方才正是用同样的办法，对待这些可怜的蚂蚁。这样的人，竟要坐下来评断上天如何行事吗？”

source_paragraphs: A PEASANT found an Eagle captured in a trap, and much admiring the bird, set him free. The Eagle did not prove ungrateful to his deliverer, for seeing the Peasant sitting under a wall which was not safe, he flew toward him and with his talons snatched a bundle from his head. When the Peasant rose in pursuit, the Eagle let the bundle fall again. Taking it up, the man returned to the same place, to find that the wall under which he had been sitting had fallen to pieces; and he marveled at the service rendered him by the Eagle.
translated_paragraphs: 一个农民发现鹰落进了捕具，很欣赏这只鸟，便将它放走。鹰也没有对救命的人忘恩负义。有一回，它看见农民坐在一堵不大牢靠的墙下，便飞过去，用利爪夺走他顶在头上的包袱。等农民起身追赶，鹰又把包袱丢下。农民拾了包袱回到原处，才发现刚才自己倚着坐的墙已经坍塌，碎成了一地。他不禁为鹰回报他的这番好意而惊叹。

source_paragraphs: THE FOX and the Leopard disputed which was the more beautiful of the two. The Leopard exhibited one by one the various spots which decorated his skin. But the Fox, interrupting him, said, “And how much more beautiful than you am I, who am decorated, not in body, but in mind.”
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸和豹子争谁更美。豹子把身上的斑纹一道一道指给狐狸看。狐狸打断它说：“那我可比你美多了。你的好看全在皮毛上，我的好看可在脑子里。”

source_paragraphs: A LION came across a Hare, who was fast asleep. He was just in the act of seizing her, when a fine young Hart trotted by, and he left the Hare to follow him. The Hare, scared by the noise, awoke and scudded away. The Lion was unable after a long chase to catch the Hart, and returned to feed upon the Hare. On finding that the Hare also had run off, he said, “I am rightly served, for having let go of the food that I had in my hand for the chance of obtaining more.”
translated_paragraphs: 狮子碰见一只熟睡的野兔。它正要伸爪去捉，一头俊俏的年轻雄鹿小步跑过。它便丢下兔子，转身去追鹿。野兔为那响动惊醒，拔腿逃走了。狮子追了好久，也没逮住雄鹿，只好回来吃兔子。发现兔子竟也溜了，它说：“我这是活该。本来食物已经拿在手里，却为了一点也许能多得的指望，把它放走了。”

sections.title_en: The Image of Mercury and the Carpenter
source_paragraphs: A VERY POOR MAN, a Carpenter by trade, had a wooden image of Mercury, before which he made offerings day by day, and begged the idol to make him rich, but in spite of his entreaties he became poorer and poorer. At last, being very angry, he took his image down from its pedestal and dashed it against the wall. When its head was knocked off, out came a stream of gold, which the Carpenter quickly picked up and said, “Well, I think thou art altogether contradictory and unreasonable; for when I paid you honour, I reaped no benefits: but now that I maltreat you I am loaded with an abundance of riches.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个很穷的人，以做木匠为生。他有一尊木刻的墨丘利神像，日日在像前献上供品，恳求神灵让他发大财。尽管苦苦哀求，他却越来越穷。终于，他气坏了，把神像从座上取下，狠命往墙上一摔。像的脑袋一磕掉，金子竟流水似的从里面涌出来。木匠赶紧捡起，说：“嘿，我看你真是前后竟这样矛盾，一点儿道理也不讲！我尊敬你时，得不着半点好处。如今我虐待你，却有这么多金银财宝往我身上堆。”

sections.title_en: The Lion, the Fox, and the Ass
source_paragraphs: THE LION, the Fox and the Ass entered into an agreement to assist each other in the chase. Having secured a large booty, the Lion on their return from the forest asked the Ass to allot his due portion to each of the three partners in the treaty. The Ass carefully divided the spoil into three equal shares and modestly requested the two others to make the first choice. The Lion, bursting out into a great rage, devoured the Ass. Then he requested the Fox to do him the favour to make a division. The Fox accumulated all that they had killed into one large heap and left to himself the smallest possible morsel. The Lion said, “Who has taught you, my very excellent fellow, the art of division? You are perfect to a fraction.” He replied, “I learned it from the Ass, by witnessing his fate.”
Happy is the man who learns from the misfortunes of others.
translated_paragraphs: 狮子、狐狸和驴订了约定，要一起打猎，彼此照应。它们猎获颇丰，从森林归来时，狮子请驴给订约的三个伙伴分一分，各拿应得的一份。驴仔仔细细分作三份，份份相等，谦恭地请另两位先挑。狮子勃然大怒，把驴吃了。随后，它请狐狸行个好，为它重新分一回。狐狸将所有猎物都堆成高高的一大堆，只给自己留了最小最小的一口。狮子说：“我优秀的朋友，是谁教会你分东西的艺术？连个零头也分得没有偏差。”狐狸答：“我是从驴身上学来的，刚才亲眼看见了它的下场。”
能够从别人的不幸中学到教训，是一种幸福。

source_paragraphs: A BULL, escaping from a Lion, hid in a cave which some shepherds had recently occupied. As soon as he entered, a He-Goat left in the cave sharply attacked him with his horns. The Bull quietly addressed him: “Butt away as much as you will. I have no fear of you, but of the Lion. Let that monster go away and I will soon let you know what is the respective strength of a Goat and a Bull.”
It shows an evil disposition to take advantage of a friend in distress.
translated_paragraphs: 一头公牛躲避狮子，藏进不久前牧羊人还住过的山洞。它刚进洞，留在洞里的一头公山羊就拿角狠狠顶它。公牛平静地说：“你爱顶多少下，就顶多少下吧。我怕的是狮子，不是你。等那猛兽走了，我很快就让你知道，我们俩一个是山羊，一个是公牛，各有多大力气。”
趁朋友落难时占他的便宜，显出的是恶劣的品性。

source_paragraphs: A BALD KNIGHT, who wore a wig, went out to hunt. A sudden puff of wind blew off his hat and wig, at which a loud laugh rang forth from his companions. He pulled up his horse, and with great glee joined in the joke by saying, “What a marvel it is that hairs which are not mine should fly from me, when they have forsaken even the man on whose head they grew.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个骑士秃了头，戴着假发出门打猎。一阵风突然把他的帽子和假发一齐吹掉，同行的伙伴随即哄堂大笑。他勒住马，也高高兴兴凑进来开玩笑：“真稀奇呀，不是我的头发竟然也从我这里逃跑了。仔细想想，头发连最早长出它们的那位先生都撇下啦！”

source_paragraphs: THE OAKS presented a complaint to Jupiter, saying, “We bear for no purpose the burden of life, as of all the trees that grow we are the most continually in peril of the axe.” Jupiter made answer: “You have only to thank yourselves for the misfortunes to which you are exposed: for if you did not make such excellent pillars and posts, and prove yourselves so serviceable to the carpenters and the farmers, the axe would not so frequently be laid to your roots.”
translated_paragraphs: 橡树们向朱庇特诉苦，说：“我们受着活命的苦，却图个什么呀？所有生长着的树当中，数我们最常面临斧头的危险。”朱庇特回答：“你们遭遇这种不幸，只该归咎于自己。若不是你们做柱子、做立桩都这么出色，又对木匠和农夫如此有用，斧头哪里会这么频繁地砍向你们的根？”

source_paragraphs: THE MONKEY, it is said, has two young ones at each birth. The Mother fondles one and nurtures it with the greatest affection and care, but hates and neglects the other. It happened once that the young one which was caressed and loved was smothered by the too great affection of the Mother, while the despised one was nurtured and reared in spite of the neglect to which it was exposed.
The best intentions will not always ensure success.
translated_paragraphs: 据说，猴子每胎会生两个孩子。猴妈妈爱抚其中一个，以最深的疼爱和最细心的照料抚养它，却嫌弃另一个，任它自生自灭。有一回，备受爱抚的孩子因为妈妈抱得太紧，给活活闷死了。反倒是遭她鄙弃的那个，尽管被冷落，终究活了下来，好好长大了。
本意再好，也未必总能得到一个好结果。

source_paragraphs: A HOUND started a Hare from his lair, but after a long run, gave up the chase. A goat-herd seeing him stop, mocked him, saying “The little one is the best runner of the two.” The Hound replied, “You do not see the difference between us: I was only running for a dinner, but he for his life.”
translated_paragraphs: 猎犬从窝里惊起一只野兔，追了很长一段，终于不再追了。一个牧羊人见它停下，嘲笑说：“你们两个，还是那个小家伙最会跑。”猎犬答：“你没瞧见，我俩有什么不同。我跑只为一顿饭，它跑却是为了一条命。”

source_paragraphs: A SHEPHERD penning his sheep in the fold for the night was about to shut up a wolf with them, when his Dog perceiving the wolf said, “Master, how can you expect the sheep to be safe if you admit a wolf into the fold?”
translated_paragraphs: 牧羊人赶羊进圈过夜，眼看要把一头狼也关进去。他的狗认出了狼，说：“主人，你既把狼放进了羊圈，又怎么能指望羊群平安无事？”

source_paragraphs: THE WOODCUTTER cut down a Mountain Oak and split it in pieces, making wedges of its own branches for dividing the trunk. The Oak said with a sigh, “I do not care about the blows of the axe aimed at my roots, but I do grieve at being torn in pieces by these wedges made from my own branches.”
Misfortunes springing from ourselves are the hardest to bear.
translated_paragraphs: 伐木人砍倒一棵山橡树，要把它劈成一块块木料，便用树本身的枝条削了楔子，用来劈开树干。橡树叹口气说：“斧子对着我的树根砍，我倒不放在心上。可让这些出自我自己枝条的楔子把我生生撕开，实在叫我痛心。”
起因出在自身的不幸，最为难以忍受。

source_paragraphs: A WASP seated himself upon the head of a Snake and, striking him unceasingly with his stings, wounded him to death. The Snake, being in great torment and not knowing how to rid himself of his enemy, saw a wagon heavily laden with wood, and went and purposely placed his head under the wheels, saying, “At least my enemy and I shall perish together.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只黄蜂伏在蛇头上，接连不断地蜇它，把蛇伤得眼看要死。蛇饱受剧痛，不知怎样才甩得掉这敌人。恰好看见一辆满载木柴的重车过来，它便爬过去，故意把脑袋伸到车轮底下，说：“至少，我可同仇敌一起死去。”

source_paragraphs: A PEACOCK spreading its gorgeous tail mocked a Crane that passed by, ridiculing the ashen hue of its plumage and saying, “I am robed, like a king, in gold and purple and all the colors of the rainbow; while you have not a bit of color on your wings.” “True,” replied the Crane; “but I soar to the heights of heaven and lift up my voice to the stars, while you walk below, like a cock, among the birds of the dunghill.”
Fine feathers don’t make fine birds.
translated_paragraphs: 孔雀展开绚丽的尾屏，嘲笑从旁经过的鹤，拿它一身灰白的羽色取乐：“我像个国王，披着黄金和紫衣，彩虹上的颜色一样不缺。你那双翅膀，却一点儿颜色也没有。”鹤回答：“没错。不过我能飞上天穹，放开嗓子，对着星星高歌。你只能留在底下，像只公鸡，在粪堆上的禽鸟中间踱步。”
漂亮的羽毛，未必造就出色的鸟。

sections.title_en: The Hen and the Golden Eggs
source_paragraphs: A COTTAGER and his wife had a Hen that laid a golden egg every day. They supposed that the Hen must contain a great lump of gold in its inside, and in order to get the gold they killed it. Having done so, they found to their surprise that the Hen differed in no respect from their other hens. The foolish pair, thus hoping to become rich all at once, deprived themselves of the gain of which they were assured day by day.
translated_paragraphs: 住在茅舍里的一对夫妇养了只母鸡，每天给他们生一枚金蛋。两人猜想，鸡肚子里一定藏着一大块金子。为了得到它，他们把鸡杀了。做完才惊讶地发现，它和其他母鸡并没有丝毫不同。这对糊涂夫妇指望一下子变富，结果连一天一枚、本来稳稳到手的收益也断送了。

source_paragraphs: AN ASS, carrying a load of wood, passed through a pond. As he was crossing through the water he lost his footing, stumbled and fell, and not being able to rise on account of his load, groaned heavily. Some Frogs frequenting the pool heard his lamentation, and said, “What would you do if you had to live here always as we do, when you make such a fuss about a mere fall into the water?”
Men often bear little grievances with less courage than they do large misfortunes.
translated_paragraphs: 一头驴驮着柴，涉水穿过池塘。它在水里一脚踩滑，绊倒了。背上的货沉，站不起来，它便一声声哀叹。常住池里的几只青蛙听到，说：“你不过跌到水里一次，就闹得这样厉害。要是和我们一样，成天都得住在这里，你又该怎么办？”
人们忍受小委屈时的勇气，往往还比不上他们遭遇大不幸时的勇气。

source_paragraphs: A CROW was jealous of the Raven, because he was considered a bird of good omen and always attracted the attention of men, who noted by his flight the good or evil course of future events. Seeing some travelers approaching, the Crow flew up into a tree, and perching herself on one of the branches, cawed as loudly as she could. The travelers turned towards the sound and wondered what it foreboded, when one of them said to his companion, “Let us proceed on our journey, my friend, for it is only the caw of a crow, and her cry, you know, is no omen.”
Those who assume a character which does not belong to them, only make themselves ridiculous.
translated_paragraphs: 乌鸦嫉妒渡鸦，因为人们把渡鸦看成带来预兆的鸟，时时留心它，凭它的飞行判断未来事情的吉凶。看见几个旅人走近，乌鸦飞上一棵树，落在枝头，尽可能大声地叫。旅人循声转身，纳闷这会是什么预兆。一个人对同伴说：“朋友，赶路吧。那不过是只寻常乌鸦在叫。你知道，它的叫声并不预告什么。”
硬要扮演不属于自己的角色，只会叫自己显得可笑。

source_paragraphs: A MAN came into a forest and asked the Trees to provide him a handle for his axe. The Trees consented to his request and gave him a young ash-tree. No sooner had the man fitted a new handle to his axe from it, than he began to use it and quickly felled with his strokes the noblest giants of the forest. An old oak, lamenting when too late the destruction of his companions, said to a neighboring cedar, “The first step has lost us all. If we had not given up the rights of the ash, we might yet have retained our own privileges and have stood for ages.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个人走进森林，向树木们要一根斧柄。树木答应了他的要求，给他一棵年轻的白蜡树。他刚用它做好新柄，往斧子上一安，就用起来，一斧接一斧，很快便砍倒林中最挺拔高贵的巨树。眼见同伴被毁，老橡树伤心得太迟，向近旁的雪松说：“头一步便断送了咱们大家。当初要是不拿白蜡树的权利来送人，自己的权利或许也还保得住，咱们原可以长久长久地站在这里。”

source_paragraphs: THE WOLVES thus addressed the Sheepdogs: “Why should you, who are like us in so many things, not be entirely of one mind with us, and live with us as brothers should? We differ from you in one point only. We live in freedom, but you bow down to and slave for men, who in return for your services flog you with whips and put collars on your necks. They make you also guard their sheep, and while they eat the mutton throw only the bones to you. If you will be persuaded by us, you will give us the sheep, and we will enjoy them in common, till we all are surfeited.” The Dogs listened favourably to these proposals, and, entering the den of the Wolves, they were set upon and torn to pieces.
translated_paragraphs: 狼群对牧羊犬说：“你们同我们这么多地方都相像，为什么不索性同我们一条心，像兄弟该做的那样住在一起？咱们只差一件事。我们自由自在，你们却向人们低头，替他们做苦役。他们又拿什么酬谢你们？鞭子抽你们，拿项圈套住你们的脖子，还叫你们替他们看羊。他们自己吃羊肉，只把骨头扔给你们。听我们的劝吧，把羊交给我们，咱们就能一道享受，吃得个个都撑得饱饱的。”狗儿们觉得这番提议很诱人，便进了狼窝。群狼随即扑上去，把它们撕成了碎片。

sections.title_zh: 公牛、母狮和猎野猪的人
sections.title_en: The Bull, the Lioness, and the Wild-Boar Hunter
source_paragraphs: A BULL finding a lion’s cub asleep gored him to death with his horns. The Lioness came up, and bitterly lamented the death of her whelp. A wild-boar Hunter, seeing her distress, stood at a distance and said to her, “Think how many men there are who have reason to lament the loss of their children, whose deaths have been caused by you.”
translated_paragraphs: 公牛撞见一只睡着的狮崽，拿双角把它顶死了。母狮赶来，面对死去的幼崽，悲恸地哀哭。一名猎野猪的人看见她伤心的模样，远远站着对她说：“你想想吧，有多少人也曾有理由哀悼他们的孩子，而那些孩子的死，正是你造成的。”

source_paragraphs: A VERY SKILLFUL BOWMAN went to the mountains in search of game, but all the beasts of the forest fled at his approach. The Lion alone challenged him to combat. The Bowman immediately shot out an arrow and said to the Lion: “I send thee my messenger, that from him thou mayest learn what I myself shall be when I assail thee.” The wounded Lion rushed away in great fear, and when a Fox who had seen it all happen told him to be of good courage and not to back off at the first attack he replied: “You counsel me in vain; for if he sends so fearful a messenger, how shall I abide the attack of the man himself?”
Be on guard against men who can strike from a distance.
translated_paragraphs: 一位技艺高超的弓箭手上山寻猎。森林里的野兽见他走近，都纷纷逃遁。只有狮子挺身来同他交战。弓箭手立即放出一支箭，说：“我先派我的信使前来，你可从他身上领教，等我亲自攻过来会是什么样子。”狮子中了箭，吓得转身奔逃。一只狐狸目睹经过，劝它拿出勇气，别让对方头一下进攻就打退。狮子答：“你劝我也没有用。他派来的信使已经如此可怕，若是他亲自出手，我如何受得住？”
须防备那些能从远处伤人的人。

source_paragraphs: WHEN MAN first saw the Camel, he was so frightened at his vast size that he ran away. After a time, perceiving the meekness and gentleness of the beast’s temper, he summoned courage enough to approach him. Soon afterwards, observing that he was an animal altogether deficient in spirit, he assumed such boldness as to put a bridle in his mouth, and to let a child drive him.
Use serves to overcome dread.
translated_paragraphs: 人第一次见到骆驼，它那庞大的个头把他吓得转身就逃。过些时候，人看出这牲口秉性柔和温驯，便鼓起勇气，敢于近前。再往后一些，见这动物一点儿反抗的劲头也没有，他的胆子大到给它嘴里装上嚼子，交给一个孩子去驱赶。
习以为常，便能克服畏惧。

source_paragraphs: A CRAB, forsaking the seashore, chose a neighboring green meadow as its feeding ground. A Fox came across him, and being very hungry ate him up. Just as he was on the point of being eaten, the Crab said, “I well deserve my fate, for what business had I on the land, when by my nature and habits I am only adapted for the sea?”
Contentment with our lot is an element of happiness.
translated_paragraphs: 一只螃蟹离开海岸，选了近旁绿油油的草地作为觅食的去处。狐狸碰巧遇见，正饿得厉害，就把它吃了。眼看要给吞下，螃蟹说：“我实在该落得这个下场。我的天性和习惯，只适合海里生活，我到陆地上来干什么？”
对自己的处境知足，是幸福的一个要素。

sections.title_en: The Ass and the Old Shepherd
source_paragraphs: A SHEPHERD, watching his Ass feeding in a meadow, was alarmed all of a sudden by the cries of the enemy. He appealed to the Ass to fly with him, lest they should both be captured, but the animal lazily replied, “Why should I, pray? Do you think it likely the conqueror will place on me two sets of panniers?” “No,” rejoined the Shepherd. “Then,” said the Ass, “as long as I carry the panniers, what matters it to me whom I serve?”
In a change of government the poor change nothing beyond the name of their master.
translated_paragraphs: 一位老牧羊人看着自己的驴在草地上啃草，猛然被敌人的喊杀声惊动。他催驴跟自己快逃，以免两个都被俘虏。驴却懒洋洋地回答：“请问，我为什么得逃？你看，打胜仗的人会让我驮两副驮筐吗？”“那倒不会。”牧羊人回答。“既然不管怎样，我仍是驮这一副筐，为谁出力又有什么分别呢？”驴说。
政权换了，穷人的生活往往只换了主人的姓名。

source_paragraphs: A FOX swimming across a rapid river was carried by the force of the current into a very deep ravine, where he lay for a long time very much bruised, sick, and unable to move. A swarm of hungry blood-sucking flies settled upon him. A Hedgehog, passing by, saw his anguish and inquired if he should drive away the flies that were tormenting him. “By no means,” replied the Fox; “pray do not molest them.” “How is this?” said the Hedgehog; “do you not want to be rid of them?” “No,” returned the Fox, “for these flies which you see are full of blood, and sting me but little, and if you rid me of these which are already satiated, others more hungry will come in their place, and will drink up all the blood I have left.”
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸游过一条急流，被水势卷入一道很深的山沟。它周身碰伤，躺了好久，病恹恹的动弹不得。一群饥饿的吸血飞虫落在它身上。刺猬经过，瞧见它如此痛苦，就问要不要自己帮它赶走那些折磨它的虫子。“千万不要，”狐狸回答，“求你别去打搅它们。”“这是怎么说？”刺猬问，“你不想摆脱这些虫子吗？”“不想，”狐狸答，“你瞧见的这一群，肚里都吸饱了血，已经不大蜇我了。要是你把这群饱足的赶走，新来替换的只会更饿，它们会把我还剩的血统统吸干。”

source_paragraphs: A WOMAN possessed a Hen that gave her an egg every day. She often pondered how she might obtain two eggs daily instead of one, and at last, to gain her purpose, determined to give the Hen a double allowance of barley. From that day the Hen became fat and sleek, and never once laid another egg.
translated_paragraphs: 一个女人养着一只母鸡，每天给她生一枚蛋。她常常盘算，怎样才能每天得到两个，而不只一个呢？最后，她为了达成心愿，决定给母鸡喂双份的大麦。从那天起，母鸡长得肥肥胖胖，羽毛溜光，却再也没有下过哪怕一枚蛋。

source_paragraphs: TEE KITES of olden times, as well as the Swans, had the privilege of song. But having heard the neigh of the horse, they were so enchanted with the sound, that they tried to imitate it; and, in trying to neigh, they forgot how to sing.
The desire for imaginary benefits often involves the loss of present blessings.
translated_paragraphs: 在古时候，和天鹅一样，鸢本来也蒙赐一副歌喉。但它们听见马儿嘶鸣，竟给那种声音迷住，一心模仿。试着学马嘶的工夫，它们把怎么唱歌给忘了。
一心追逐想象中的好处，常会丢掉眼前原本享有的福分。

source_paragraphs: A HOUND having started a Hare on the hillside pursued her for some distance, at one time biting her with his teeth as if he would take her life, and at another fawning upon her, as if in play with another dog. The Hare said to him, “I wish you would act sincerely by me, and show yourself in your true colors. If you are a friend, why do you bite me so hard? If an enemy, why do you fawn on me?”
No one can be a friend if you know not whether to trust or distrust him.
translated_paragraphs: 一只猎犬在山坡上惊起一只野兔，追出老远。它一会儿张嘴狠咬，仿佛定要夺走兔子的性命，一会儿又摇尾讨好，像是跟另一条狗玩耍。野兔说：“我盼你能以诚相待，叫我看看你的真面目。若是朋友，为什么咬我这么重？若是敌人，为什么又向我摇尾示好？”
一个人叫你摸不准究竟该信他还是防着他，便做不得朋友。

source_paragraphs: THE HARES waged war with the Eagles, and called upon the Foxes to help them. They replied, “We would willingly have helped you, if we had not known who you were, and with whom you were fighting.”
Count the cost before you commit yourselves.
translated_paragraphs: 野兔们向鹰群开战，号召狐狸们前来助阵。狐狸回答：“要不是我们知道你们是谁、你们要和谁交战，我们本来很乐意伸出援手。”
答应出手以前，先算清代价。

source_paragraphs: A BULL was striving with all his might to squeeze himself through a narrow passage which led to his stall. A young Calf came up, and offered to go before and show him the way by which he could manage to pass. “Save yourself the trouble,” said the Bull; “I knew that way long before you were born.”
translated_paragraphs: 公牛使尽力气，正要挤过一条通往自己畜栏的狭窄通道。小牛过来，主动提出在前头带路，指点它怎样才能通过。“省省你这份好心吧。”公牛说，“早在你没出生以前，我已经认得这条路。”

sections.title_en: The Stag, the Wolf, and the Sheep
source_paragraphs: A STAG asked a Sheep to lend him a measure of wheat, and said that the Wolf would be his surety. The Sheep, fearing some fraud was intended, excused herself, saying, “The Wolf is accustomed to seize what he wants and to run off; and you, too, can quickly outstrip me in your rapid flight. How then shall I be able to find you, when the day of payment comes?”
Two blacks do not make one white.
translated_paragraphs: 雄鹿向绵羊借一斗小麦，说狼愿为它作担保。绵羊怕这其中有什么骗局，推辞说：“狼想要什么，就抢了走。你呢，跑起来又是这么快，眨眼便能把我甩在后头。等到了还款的日子，我又去什么地方找你们？”
两样黑的凑在一起，也变不成一样白的。

sections.title_en: The Eagle, the Cat, and the Wild Sow
source_paragraphs: AN EAGLE made her nest at the top of a lofty oak; a Cat, having found a convenient hole, moved into the middle of the trunk; and a Wild Sow, with her young, took shelter in a hollow at its foot. The Cat cunningly resolved to destroy this chance-made colony. To carry out her design, she climbed to the nest of the Eagle, and said, “Destruction is preparing for you, and for me too, unfortunately. The Wild Sow, whom you see daily digging up the earth, wishes to uproot the oak, so she may on its fall seize our families as food for her young.” Having thus frightened the Eagle out of her senses, she crept down to the cave of the Sow, and said, “Your children are in great danger; for as soon as you go out with your litter to find food, the Eagle is prepared to pounce upon one of your little pigs.” Having instilled these fears into the Sow, she went and pretended to hide herself in the hollow of the tree. When night came she went forth with silent foot and obtained food for herself and her kittens, but feigning to be afraid, she kept a lookout all through the day. Meanwhile, the Eagle, full of fear of the Sow, sat still on the branches, and the Sow, terrified by the Eagle, did not dare to go out from her cave. And thus they both, along with their families, perished from hunger, and afforded ample provision for the Cat and her kittens.
translated_paragraphs: 一只鹰把巢筑在高高的橡树顶。一只猫找到个合适的洞，搬到树干半腰。母野猪则带着一窝小猪，住到树根底下的空洞里。那猫心机深沉，拿定主意要毁掉这个偶然聚起来的小邻里。为了施行诡计，她爬到鹰巢跟前，说：“灾祸正在等你，也在等着倒霉的我。你天天都瞧见那母野猪刨土，她是想把橡树连根刨倒。等到树一倒，你我两家的孩子就会给她抓去喂猪崽！”这样把鹰吓得魂不附体之后，她溜到母野猪的洞口，说：“你的孩子们有大危险呀！你一带这窝小猪出洞找食，鹰就准备扑下来捉走一只。”把恐惧也灌进母野猪心里，猫便回自己的树洞里假装躲藏。到了夜晚，她轻手轻脚出门，给自己和小猫弄来食物，白天则一直装出害怕的模样，警觉地东张西望。这工夫，鹰因为畏惧母野猪，端坐树头，不肯离开；母野猪怕了鹰，也不敢走出树洞。就这样，两家带着孩子活活饿死，倒给猫和她的孩子们留下了丰盛的食物。

source_paragraphs: AT ONE TIME a very large and strong Wolf was born among the wolves, who exceeded all his fellow-wolves in strength, size, and swiftness, so that they unanimously decided to call him “Lion.” The Wolf, with a lack of sense proportioned to his enormous size, thought that they gave him this name in earnest, and, leaving his own race, consorted exclusively with the lions. An old sly Fox, seeing this, said, “May I never make myself so ridiculous as you do in your pride and self-conceit; for even though you have the size of a lion among wolves, in a herd of lions you are definitely a wolf.”
translated_paragraphs: 有一回，狼群中生出一只格外高大健壮的狼。论力气，论个头，论脚力，它都胜过所有的伙伴，于是众狼一致决定，称它作“狮子”。它的头脑有多不灵光，恰同它的身量有多高大相称。它以为大家是认认真真送给它这个名字，便离开同类，专去同狮群交往。狡猾的老狐狸见了，说：“但愿我不要像你这样骄傲自负，叫自己丢人。你就是在狼群里有狮子一样的个头，到了一群狮子当中，你也明明白白只是一头狼。”

source_paragraphs: A MULE, frolicsome from lack of work and from too much corn, galloped about in a very extravagant manner, and said to himself: “My father surely was a high-mettled racer, and I am his own child in speed and spirit.” On the next day, being driven a long journey, and feeling very wearied, he exclaimed in a disconsolate tone: “I must have made a mistake; my father, after all, could have been only an ass.”
translated_paragraphs: 一头骡子不用干活，又吃了太多谷子，闹着玩儿，神气十足地四处撒欢狂奔。它对自己说：“我父亲想必是一匹烈性好赛马。我这脚力，我这精神，肯定是它的亲骨肉。”第二天，它给人赶着走了一趟长路，累得够呛，便沮丧地叹道：“我准是搞错了。到底，我的爸爸多半只可能是一头驴。”

source_paragraphs: A WIZARD, sitting in the marketplace, was telling the fortunes of the passers-by when a person ran up in great haste, and announced to him that the doors of his house had been broken open and that all his goods were being stolen. He sighed heavily and hastened away as fast as he could run. A neighbor saw him running and said, “Oh! you fellow there! you say you can foretell the fortunes of others; how is it you did not foresee your own?”
translated_paragraphs: 一个巫师坐在集市上，正给过路者卜算吉凶，忽然有人急急忙忙跑来，告诉他说，他家的门已经被人撬开，财物正被洗劫一空。他深深叹口气，急着飞跑回家。一个邻居看到他拔足狂奔，便说：“喂，那边那位！你不是能预知别人的运数吗，怎么倒没预见你自己的呢？”

source_paragraphs: TWO FROGS were neighbors. One inhabited a deep pond, far removed from public view; the other lived in a gully containing little water, and traversed by a country road. The Frog that lived in the pond warned his friend to change his residence and entreated him to come and live with him, saying that he would enjoy greater safety from danger and more abundant food. The other refused, saying that he felt it so very hard to leave a place to which he had become accustomed. A few days afterwards a heavy wagon passed through the gully and crushed him to death under its wheels.
A willful man will have his way to his own hurt.
translated_paragraphs: 两只青蛙是邻居。一只住在远离行人视线的深池里，另一只住在一条水量很少的沟里，正有条乡间大路横穿过去。深池里的青蛙劝朋友另择住处，恳请它搬来同住，说这样既能更稳妥地避开危险，又有更充足的食物。对方拒绝了，说自己实在很难离开一个已经住惯的地方。几天以后，一辆沉重的大车从沟里经过，轮子把它碾死了。
一意孤行的人即便如了意，到头来受损的还是他自己。

source_paragraphs: A SERPENT and an Eagle were struggling with each other in deadly conflict. The Serpent had the advantage, and was about to strangle the bird. A countryman saw them, and running up, loosed the coil of the Serpent and let the Eagle go free. The Serpent, irritated at the escape of his prey, injected his poison into the drinking horn of the countryman. The rustic, ignorant of his danger, was about to drink, when the Eagle struck his hand with his wing, and, seizing the drinking horn in his talons, carried it aloft.
translated_paragraphs: 一条蛇和一只鹰正在进行殊死搏斗。蛇占了上风，眼看要把鹰绞死。一名乡下人看见，跑来解开蛇盘着的身子，把鹰给放走了。蛇气愤猎物逃脱，把毒液注进乡下人的饮水角杯里。乡下人丝毫不知危险，举杯正要喝，鹰用翅膀击了他的手，用利爪抓住那只角杯，带上高空去了。

source_paragraphs: A CROW perishing with thirst saw a pitcher, and hoping to find water, flew to it with delight. When he reached it, he discovered to his grief that it contained so little water that he could not possibly get at it. He tried everything he could think of to reach the water, but all his efforts were in vain. At last he collected as many stones as he could carry and dropped them one by one with his beak into the pitcher, until he brought the water within his reach and thus saved his life.
Necessity is the mother of invention.
translated_paragraphs: 一只乌鸦渴得要命，看见一个水罐，满心盼它里面有水，高兴地飞过去。到了那里，却伤心地发现，里面的水少得它无论怎样都够不到。为了喝到水，它把想得到的办法全都试了一遍，所有努力却全白费。最后，它竭尽所能搜集来许多石子，用嘴叼起，一颗接一颗扔进罐子，直到水升到它够得着的地方。它就这样保住了性命。
需要是发明之母。

source_paragraphs: A THIEF hired a room in a tavern and stayed a while in the hope of stealing something which should enable him to pay his reckoning. When he had waited some days in vain, he saw the Innkeeper dressed in a new and handsome coat and sitting before his door. The Thief sat down beside him and talked with him. As the conversation began to flag, the Thief yawned terribly and at the same time howled like a wolf. The Innkeeper said, “Why do you howl so fearfully?” “I will tell you,” said the Thief, “but first let me ask you to hold my clothes, or I shall tear them to pieces. I know not, sir, when I got this habit of yawning, nor whether these attacks of howling were inflicted on me as a judgment for my crimes, or for any other cause; but this I do know, that when I yawn for the third time, I actually turn into a wolf and attack men.” With this speech he commenced a second fit of yawning and again howled like a wolf, as he had at first. The Innkeeper, hearing his tale and believing what he said, became greatly alarmed and, rising from his seat, attempted to run away. The Thief laid hold of his coat and entreated him to stop, saying, “Pray wait, sir, and hold my clothes, or I shall tear them to pieces in my fury, when I turn into a wolf.” At the same moment he yawned the third time and set up a terrible howl. The Innkeeper, frightened lest he should be attacked, left his new coat in the Thief’s hand and ran as fast as he could into the inn for safety. The Thief made off with the coat and did not return again to the inn.
Every tale is not to be believed.
translated_paragraphs: 一个小偷在客栈租下一间房，住了一阵，希望能偷到什么，够他付清房钱。守了几天，一无所得，他见客栈老板穿着一件漂亮的新外套，坐在门前。小偷走过来坐在旁边，跟他闲谈。等到谈兴渐淡，小偷打了一个吓人的呵欠，同时像狼一样嚎叫起来。老板问：“你怎么叫得这么吓人？”“我会告诉你，”小偷答，“不过先请你替我拿着衣裳，否则我会把它们撕成碎片。先生，我不知道自己什么时候染上了这种打呵欠的习惯。也不知道这一次次忍不住的嚎叫，是对我以前罪行的惩戒，还是另有什么缘故。不过有一点我能确定：每次等我打到第三个呵欠，就会真的变成一头狼，扑上去伤人。”讲完，小偷便打起第二阵呵欠，和起初一样，重新学起狼嚎。老板听信了这番话，十分害怕，从座位上起身，正想逃，小偷却揪住他的外套，恳求他留下，说：“请等等，先生，替我拿着衣裳。要不，我变成狼发起疯，会把它们撕成粉碎的！”话音未落，他已打出第三个呵欠，喉间响起一声凄厉的嗥叫。老板唯恐遭到扑袭，把自己的新外套丢在小偷手里，用最快的脚步逃进客栈躲避。小偷带上外套溜掉，再也没有回过那间客栈。
故事并非个个都可信。

source_paragraphs: A HART, hard pressed in the chase, hid himself beneath the large leaves of a Vine. The huntsmen, in their haste, overshot the place of his concealment. Supposing all danger to have passed, the Hart began to nibble the tendrils of the Vine. One of the huntsmen, attracted by the rustling of the leaves, looked back, and seeing the Hart, shot an arrow from his bow and struck it. The Hart, at the point of death, groaned: “I am rightly served, for I should not have maltreated the Vine that saved me.”
translated_paragraphs: 雄鹿给猎人逼得紧，钻到葡萄藤宽大的叶子底下藏起来。猎人一心赶路，竟一下超过了它藏身的地方。雄鹿以为危险全过去了，便开始啃食葡萄藤的卷须。叶子沙沙作响，引得一名猎人回头，看见了雄鹿。他拉弓射箭，一箭正中。雄鹿临死呻吟道：“我这是活该。我原不该损伤那株救过我的葡萄藤。”

source_paragraphs: A GNAT came and said to a Lion, “I do not in the least fear you, nor are you stronger than I am. For in what does your strength consist? You can scratch with your claws and bite with your teeth an a woman in her quarrels. I repeat that I am altogether more powerful than you; and if you doubt it, let us fight and see who will conquer.” The Gnat, having sounded his horn, fastened himself upon the Lion and stung him on the nostrils and the parts of the face devoid of hair. While trying to crush him, the Lion tore himself with his claws, until he punished himself severely. The Gnat thus prevailed over the Lion, and, buzzing about in a song of triumph, flew away. But shortly afterwards he became entangled in the meshes of a cobweb and was eaten by a spider. He greatly lamented his fate, saying, “Woe is me! that I, who can wage war successfully with the hugest beasts, should perish myself from this spider, the most inconsiderable of insects!”
translated_paragraphs: 一只小蚊子飞到狮子面前，说：“我一点也不怕你，你也并不比我强。说到底，你的本领是什么？拿爪子抓、拿牙齿咬，就像吵架的妇人。我再说一遍，我比你强得多。要是不信，咱们打一场，看谁能赢。”蚊子吹响它的号角，落到狮子身上，在鼻孔上和脸上没有毛的地方不停地蜇。狮子想把它拍死，却用利爪一次次撕破自己的皮肉，反而把自己伤得很重。蚊子就这样赢了狮子，嗡嗡哼唱着凯歌飞走。不一会儿，它被蜘蛛网的细眼缠住，让蜘蛛吃了。它大声哀叹自己的命运，说：“我真倒霉呀！对上最硕大的野兽，我也能交战取胜，却死在蜘蛛这种最微不足道的小虫手里！”

source_paragraphs: A FAMISHED FOX saw some clusters of ripe black grapes hanging from a trellised vine. She resorted to all her tricks to get at them, but wearied herself in vain, for she could not reach them. At last she turned away, hiding her disappointment and saying: “The Grapes are sour, and not ripe as I thought.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只饿极了的狐狸看见藤架上挂着一串串熟透的黑葡萄。它把全部本领都使出来，想够着那些果实，结果累了自己一场，却依然够不到。最后它转身离开，掩饰着失望说：“这些葡萄是酸的，不像我刚才以为的那样，根本没有熟。”

source_paragraphs: A WALNUT TREE standing by the roadside bore an abundant crop of fruit. For the sake of the nuts, the passers-by broke its branches with stones and sticks. The Walnut-Tree piteously exclaimed, “O wretched me! that those whom I cheer with my fruit should repay me with these painful requitals!”
translated_paragraphs: 一棵长在路边的胡桃树，结出了丰盛的果实。路人为了得到胡桃，又拿石头砸，又拿棍子敲，竟把它的枝条生生打断。胡桃树可怜地喊道：“我真苦啊！我拿果子叫人欢喜，享用了它们的人却拿这样的剧痛来回报我！”

source_paragraphs: A KID, returning without protection from the pasture, was pursued by a Wolf. Seeing he could not escape, he turned round, and said: “I know, friend Wolf, that I must be your prey, but before I die I would ask of you one favour you will play me a tune to which I may dance.” The Wolf complied, and while he was piping and the Kid was dancing, some hounds hearing the sound ran up and began chasing the Wolf. Turning to the Kid, he said, “It is just what I deserve; for I, who am only a butcher, should not have turned piper to please you.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只小山羊没有同伴护送，独自从牧场回来，后面有狼追赶。眼看已经逃不了，它转过身说：“狼朋友，我知道自己一定会成为你的猎物。不过临死以前，想请你帮个忙，吹上一支曲子，让我和着曲子跳个舞吧。”狼答应了。等它吹笛、小羊跳舞的时候，一群猎犬听见声音跑过来，开始追狼。狼转头朝小羊说：“我这是活该！我分明只是个屠夫，就不应该为了取悦你，转行做吹笛的人。”

source_paragraphs: A SAILOR, bound on a long voyage, took with him a Monkey to amuse him while on shipboard. As he sailed off the coast of Greece, a violent tempest arose in which the ship was wrecked and he, his Monkey, and all the crew were obliged to swim for their lives. A Dolphin saw the Monkey contending with the waves, and supposing him to be a man (whom he is always said to befriend), came and placed himself under him, to convey him on his back in safety to the shore. When the Dolphin arrived with his burden in sight of land not far from Athens, he asked the Monkey if he were an Athenian. The latter replied that he was, and that he was descended from one of the most noble families in that city. The Dolphin then inquired if he knew the Piræus (the famous harbor of Athens). Supposing that a man was meant, the Monkey answered that he knew him very well and that he was an intimate friend. The Dolphin, indignant at these falsehoods, dipped the Monkey under the water and drowned him.
translated_paragraphs: 一名水手即将远航，带上一只猴子，好在船上解闷。船驶到希腊近海，忽遇猛烈风暴，船只失事。水手、猴子和所有船员不得不下海游水逃命。海豚瞧见猴子在波涛中挣扎，以为那是个人（人们总说，海豚一向是人类的朋友），便游过去潜到它身下，要把它驮到岸上脱离险境。等海豚背着乘客来到离雅典不远、已经能看见陆地的地方，便问猴子可是雅典人。猴子说是，还说自己出身于那座城里最显贵的家族之一。海豚于是问它认不认识比雷埃夫斯，那是雅典著名的港口。猴子以为这是人名，便答：“我对他熟得很，我们是亲密的朋友。”海豚为这一串谎话愤怒，把猴子往水下一沉，淹死了它。

source_paragraphs: AT ONE TIME the Horse had the plain entirely to himself. Then a Stag intruded into his domain and shared his pasture. The Horse, desiring to revenge himself on the stranger, asked a man if he were willing to help him in punishing the Stag. The man replied that if the Horse would receive a bit in his mouth and agree to carry him, he would contrive effective weapons against the Stag. The Horse consented and allowed the man to mount him. From that hour he found that instead of obtaining revenge on the Stag, he had enslaved himself to the service of man.
translated_paragraphs: 从前，整片平原都归马独享。后来有头雄鹿闯入，分吃它的牧草。马一心要报复这个不速之客，问一个人肯不肯帮忙惩罚雄鹿。那人回答，只要马同意嘴里套上嚼子，背上驮着自己，他就能设法拿出对付雄鹿的有效武器。马应允了，让人骑到身上。自那刻起，它才发现，自己没能找雄鹿报仇，却先把自己变成了听人使唤的奴仆。

source_paragraphs: A JACKDAW, seeing some Doves in a cote abundantly provided with food, painted himself white and joined them in order to share their plentiful maintenance. The Doves, as long as he was silent, supposed him to be one of themselves and admitted him to their cote. But when one day he forgot himself and began to chatter, they discovered his true character and drove him forth, pecking him with their beaks. Failing to obtain food among the Doves, he returned to the Jackdaws. They too, not recognizing him on account of his color, expelled him from living with them. So desiring two ends, he obtained neither.
translated_paragraphs: 寒鸦看见鸽舍里的鸽子食物充足，便把自己刷白，混进去，好分享那里的丰盛供养。它一声不吭的时候，鸽子以为它是自己鸟群中的一员，便让它住进鸽舍。直到一天，它忘了遮掩，张嘴乱叫。鸽子识穿了它的本来面目，纷纷用嘴啄它，把它赶出去。鸽舍里既弄不来吃的，它又回到寒鸦群中。可它们也因羽色不对而不认得它，不肯同它一起生活。它一心想着两头好，到头来，两头都没有得到。

source_paragraphs: A FOX and a Monkey were traveling together on the same road. As they journeyed, they passed through a cemetery full of monuments. “All these monuments which you see,” said the Monkey, “are erected in honour of my ancestors, who were in their day freedmen and citizens of great renown.” The Fox replied, “You have chosen a most appropriate subject for your falsehoods, as I am sure none of your ancestors will be able to contradict you.”
A false tale often betrays itself.
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸和猴子结伴同行。路上经过一座墓地，里头满是纪念碑。猴子说：“你看到的所有这些碑，都是为了纪念我的祖先立起来的。他们在世时，都是获得自由、享有公民身份的名人。”狐狸答道：“你倒替你的谎话选了一个再合适不过的题目。因为我敢肯定，你的祖先没有一个能够起来反驳你。”
编出来的故事，常会自己露出马脚。

source_paragraphs: A MAN had a Wife who made herself hated by all the members of his household. Wishing to find out if she had the same effect on the persons in her father’s house, he made some excuse to send her home on a visit to her father. After a short time she returned, and when he inquired how she had got on and how the servants had treated her, she replied, “The herdsmen and shepherds cast on me looks of aversion.” He said, “O Wife, if you were disliked by those who go out early in the morning with their flocks and return late in the evening, what must have been felt towards you by those with whom you passed the whole day!”
Straws show how the wind blows.
translated_paragraphs: 有一个男人，他的妻子把家里所有人都得罪了。丈夫想知道，在她父亲家里，她是不是也一样惹人厌，于是找了个借口，请她回娘家探望父亲。过了不久，她回来了。丈夫问她这趟过得怎样，家里的佣人待她如何。她回答：“牧牛的和放羊的都朝我投来嫌恶的眼光。”丈夫说：“唉，我的妻子。那些一大早赶着牛羊出门、天晚才回来的人，都已经不喜欢你，那些整整一天同你待在一块儿的，对你又该作何感想啊！”
看一根稻草，也能知道风往哪儿吹。

sections.title_en: The Man, the Horse, the Ox, and the Dog
source_paragraphs: A HORSE, Ox, and Dog, driven to great straits by the cold, sought shelter and protection from Man. He received them kindly, lighted a fire, and warmed them. He let the Horse make free with his oats, gave the Ox an abundance of hay, and fed the Dog with meat from his own table. Grateful for these favours, the animals determined to repay him to the best of their ability. For this purpose, they divided the term of his life between them, and each endowed one portion of it with the qualities which chiefly characterized himself. The Horse chose his earliest years and gave them his own attributes: hence every man is in his youth impetuous, headstrong, and obstinate in maintaining his own opinion. The Ox took under his patronage the next term of life, and therefore man in his middle age is fond of work, devoted to labor, and resolute to amass wealth and to husband his resources. The end of life was reserved for the Dog, wherefore the old man is often snappish, irritable, hard to please, and selfish, tolerant only of his own household, but averse to strangers and to all who do not administer to his comfort or to his necessities.
translated_paragraphs: 一匹马、一头牛和一条狗，被严寒逼得无处可去，向人求个避难的地方。那人亲切收留它们，生起火，给它们取暖。自己的燕麦任由马吃，干草给牛备得足足的，他还把饭桌上的肉拿来喂狗。三个都很感激这些善待，商量要力所能及地报答。为这目的，它们把人这一生分成三段，各把自己身上最显著的品质送给其中一段。马挑了最初的年月，把自己的脾气给了那段时光。所以，人在年轻时冲动任性，固执地维护自己的意见。牛认领了接下去的岁月，因此，人到中年喜欢做事，专心劳作，决意积累财产，精心节用资源。人生最后一程留给了狗。因此，上年纪的人往往爱发火、好急躁、难讨好、只顾自己，只肯容忍自家人，却厌恶陌生人，厌恶那些不能为他的舒适和需要出力的人。

source_paragraphs: A THIEF came in the night to break into a house. He brought with him several slices of meat in order to pacify the Housedog, so that he would not alarm his master by barking. As the Thief threw him the pieces of meat, the Dog said, “If you think to stop my mouth, you will be greatly mistaken. This sudden kindness at your hands will only make me more watchful, lest under these unexpected favours to myself, you have some private ends to accomplish for your own benefit, and for my master’s injury.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个小偷趁夜前来，要闯进一所房子。他带上好几片肉，想讨好看家狗，不让它吠叫着惊醒主人。小偷把肉片丢过来时，狗说：“你指望这样能堵住我的嘴，可大错特错了。你突然向我示好，只会叫我更加警惕。谁知道你特意送我这些想不到的好处，背后是不是另有盘算，好为自己谋利，却叫我的主人吃亏？”

sections.title_en: The Apes and the Two Travelers
source_paragraphs: TWO MEN, one who always spoke the truth and the other who told nothing but lies, were traveling together and by chance came to the land of Apes. One of the Apes, who had raised himself to be king, commanded them to be seized and brought before him, that he might know what was said of him among men. He ordered at the same time that all the Apes be arranged in a long row on his right hand and on his left, and that a throne be placed for him, as was the custom among men. After these preparations he signified that the two men should be brought before him, and greeted them with this salutation: “What sort of a king do I seem to you to be, O strangers?” The Lying Traveler replied, “You seem to me a most mighty king.” “And what is your estimate of those you see around me?” “These,” he made answer, “are worthy companions of yourself, fit at least to be ambassadors and leaders of armies.” The Ape and all his court, gratified with the lie, commanded that a handsome present be given to the flatterer. On this the truthful Traveler thought to himself, “If so great a reward be given for a lie, with what gift may not I be rewarded, if, according to my custom, I tell the truth?” The Ape quickly turned to him. “And pray how do I and these my friends around me seem to you?” “Thou art,” he said, “a most excellent Ape, and all these thy companions after thy example are excellent Apes too.” The King of the Apes, enraged at hearing these truths, gave him over to the teeth and claws of his companions.
translated_paragraphs: 两个男人结伴旅行，一个总是说实话，另一个除了谎言，别的什么也不说。他们碰巧来到了猿猴之邦。有一只猿猴自己爬到了国王的位置，很想知道人类中间怎样议论它，便下令擒住两人，带到面前。它又下令让所有猿猴在自己左右排成长列，仿照人类的规矩，为它安放一张王座。这些排场都备好了，它示意带人上前，用这样一句话招呼他们：“外乡人啊，依你们看来，我像是怎样的一位国王？”撒谎的旅人答：“您在我眼里，就是一位极其威武的大王。”“那你怎样评断我周围这些人呢？”“他们，”那人回答，“都是配得上您的伙伴，最起码也能出任使节，统领大军。”猿王和满朝官员都给这谎话哄得心花怒放，下令赠给奉承者一份丰厚礼物。说实话的旅人见了，便心想：“一句谎话尚且有这样厚的赏赐，我要是照往常说真话，那岂不是要得到更好的礼物？”猿王很快转向他：“那么请说说，在你眼里，我和身边这些朋友又是怎样呢？”“您是，”他说，“一只格外出色的猿猴。您身边这些伙伴拿您做榜样，也个个是出色的猿猴。”猿王听了这些真话勃然大怒，便把他交给众猿的爪牙处置。

source_paragraphs: WHEN A FOX who had never yet seen a Lion, fell in with him by chance for the first time in the forest, he was so frightened that he nearly died with fear. On meeting him for the second time, he was still much alarmed, but not to the same extent as at first. On seeing him the third time, he so increased in boldness that he went up to him and commenced a familiar conversation with him.
Acquaintance softens prejudices.
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸从出生以来，从没见过狮子。头一次偶然在林中相遇，它骇得几乎吓死。第二次遇见，仍然很是惊恐，却不再像头一回那样厉害了。到第三次见到狮子，它的胆子已大到径直走过去，随随便便攀谈起来。
彼此熟悉以后，成见便会减轻。

source_paragraphs: A WEASEL, inactive from age and infirmities, was not able to catch mice as he once did. He therefore rolled himself in flour and lay down in a dark corner. A Mouse, supposing him to be food, leaped upon him, and was instantly caught and squeezed to death. Another perished in a similar manner, and then a third, and still others after them. A very old Mouse, who had escaped many a trap and snare, observed from a safe distance the trick of his crafty foe and said, “Ah! you that lie there, may you prosper just in the same proportion as you are what you pretend to be!”
translated_paragraphs: 一只黄鼠狼老迈多病，行动迟缓，没法像从前那样捕鼠。于是它在面粉里打了几个滚，躺到幽暗的墙角。一只老鼠当它是可以吃的东西，纵身扑上去，立刻便被抓住捏死了。另一只也照样丧命，接着又是第三只，再往后还有好多只。有一只非常年老的鼠，逃过许许多多夹子和罗网，远远地待在安全处，识破了狡猾敌手的花招，说：“啊，你这个躺着的家伙！你扮的东西有几分是真的，我就祝你有几分好收成！”

source_paragraphs: A BOY bathing in a river was in danger of being drowned. He called out to a passing traveler for help, but instead of holding out a helping hand, the man stood by unconcernedly, and scolded the boy for his imprudence. “Oh, sir!” cried the youth, “pray help me now and scold me afterwards.”
Counsel without help is useless.
translated_paragraphs: 男孩在河里洗澡，眼看就要溺水。他向一名路过的旅人高声求救。那人却不肯伸手，满不在乎地站在旁边，责骂男孩做事不够谨慎。“哦，先生！”男孩叫道，“劳驾先帮我，过后再骂我吧。”
光给劝告却不肯帮忙，于事无补。

source_paragraphs: THE PEACOCK made complaint to Juno that, while the nightingale pleased every ear with his song, he himself no sooner opened his mouth than he became a laughingstock to all who heard him. The Goddess, to console him, said, “But you far excel in beauty and in size. The splendor of the emerald shines in your neck and you unfold a tail gorgeous with painted plumage.” “But for what purpose have I,” said the bird, “this dumb beauty so long as I am surpassed in song?” “The lot of each,” replied Juno, “has been assigned by the will of the Fates—to thee, beauty; to the eagle, strength; to the nightingale, song; to the raven, favourable, and to the crow, unfavourable auguries. These are all contented with the endowments allotted to them.”
translated_paragraphs: 孔雀去找朱诺诉苦，说夜莺只要开嗓唱歌，谁听了都喜欢，而它自己只须一张嘴，便成了所有听众的笑柄。女神安慰它说：“可你的美貌和身姿，远远胜过别的鸟。你的颈上闪着翡翠的光辉，尾屏展开，彩羽多么华丽。”“可只要我唱歌还输给别人，”孔雀说，“这不能出声的美丽于我有什么用呢？”朱诺回答：“每一位的所得，都依命运诸神的意志分定了。美貌给了你，力量给了鹰，歌喉给了夜莺。传报吉兆的本领给了渡鸦，传报凶兆的给了乌鸦。它们都满足于分给自己的天赋。”

source_paragraphs: A WOLF followed a flock of sheep for a long time and did not attempt to injure one of them. The Shepherd at first stood on his guard against him, as against an enemy, and kept a strict watch over his movements. But when the Wolf, day after day, kept in the company of the sheep and did not make the slightest effort to seize them, the Shepherd began to look upon him as a guardian of his flock rather than as a plotter of evil against it; and when occasion called him one day into the city, he left the sheep entirely in his charge. The Wolf, now that he had the opportunity, fell upon the sheep, and destroyed the greater part of the flock. When the Shepherd returned to find his flock destroyed, he exclaimed: “I have been rightly served; why did I trust my sheep to a Wolf?”
translated_paragraphs: 一头狼跟在羊群后面，跟了很久，从没试图伤害哪一只羊。起初牧羊人把它当作敌人防备，时时警觉地留意它的一举一动。可是狼一日又一日陪着羊群，从来没有一点扑羊的意思，牧羊人便渐渐把它看成护群者，而不看成伺机为恶的家伙。有一天他有事进城，竟把羊只完全交给它照管。狼得了机会，立即扑入羊群，扑死了大半。牧羊人回来，见羊群遭了殃，不由得喊：“我活该！我怎么能把羊交托给一头狼呢？”

source_paragraphs: THE HARES harangued the assembly, and argued that all should be equal. The Lions made this reply: “Your words, O Hares! are good; but they lack both claws and teeth such as we have.”
translated_paragraphs: 野兔们在大会上慷慨陈词，主张个个都该平等。狮子们答道：“啊，野兔，你们的话说得很好。可这些话缺少我们这样的爪子和牙齿。”

source_paragraphs: A CERTAIN MAN made a wooden image of Mercury and offered it for sale. When no one appeared willing to buy it, in order to attract purchasers, he cried out that he had the statue to sell of a benefactor who bestowed wealth and helped to heap up riches. One of the bystanders said to him, “My good fellow, why do you sell him, being such a one as you describe, when you may yourself enjoy the good things he has to give?” “Why,” he replied, “I am in need of immediate help, and he is wont to give his good gifts very slowly.”
translated_paragraphs: 有个人做了尊墨丘利木像，拿出来卖。眼看没有人愿意购买，他为招揽客人便吆喝，说自己所卖的是位大恩人的神像，会赐予人财富，助人积聚钱财。旁边一位便说：“我这好朋友，如果真像你说的那样，你大可以自己享用他送来的好处，干吗还要卖呢？”“哎，”那人答，“我眼下就等着钱救急，他老人家的好处却照例给得很慢。”

source_paragraphs: A NIGHTINGALE, sitting aloft upon an oak and singing according to his wont, was seen by a Hawk who, being in need of food, swooped down and seized him. The Nightingale, about to lose his life, earnestly begged the Hawk to let him go, saying that he was not big enough to satisfy the hunger of a Hawk who, if he wanted food, ought to pursue the larger birds. The Hawk, interrupting him, said: “I should indeed have lost my senses if I should let go food ready in my hand, for the sake of pursuing birds which are not yet even within sight.”
translated_paragraphs: 夜莺高高坐在橡树上，像往常一样唱歌。鹰看见了，正需要食物，便俯冲下来将它捉住。夜莺性命将要不保，苦苦哀求鹰放它走，说自己这么小，还不够鹰塞牙缝，要是对方想要食物，理应去追个头大一些的鸟。鹰打断它的话，说：“我若为追赶那些连影子还没瞧见的鸟，松开手里现成的食物，那才当真是失了理智。”

sections.title_en: The Lark and Her Young Ones
source_paragraphs: A LARK had made her nest in the early spring on the young green wheat. The brood had almost grown to their full strength and attained the use of their wings and the full plumage of their feathers, when the owner of the field, looking over his ripe crop, said, “The time has come when I must ask all my neighbors to help me with my harvest.” One of the young Larks heard his speech and related it to his mother, inquiring of her to what place they should move for safety. “There is no occasion to move yet, my son,” she replied; “the man who only sends to his friends to help him with his harvest is not really in earnest.” The owner of the field came again a few days later and saw the wheat shedding the grain from excess of ripeness. He said, “I will come myself tomorrow with my laborers, and with as many reapers as I can hire, and will get in the harvest.” The Lark on hearing these words said to her brood, “It is time now to be off, my little ones, for the man is in earnest this time; he no longer trusts his friends, but will reap the field himself.”
Self-help is the best help.
translated_paragraphs: 早春，云雀把窝筑在绿莹莹的麦苗上。等小鸟们长得差不多够强壮，会使翅膀，羽毛也快长齐了，田主人过来察看熟透的庄稼，说：“是时候了，我得请众位邻居帮我收麦子。”一只小云雀听见了，把这句话转告母亲，问她该搬去哪里才安全。她回答：“孩子，眼下还无须搬。一个人若只是托人去请朋友帮他割麦，那还不是当真的。”几天后，田主人又来，看见麦子已经熟过头，麦粒纷纷往下掉，便说：“明天我自己带上伙计，再把雇得到的收割人全雇来，一齐把麦子收进去。”云雀听了，立刻对小鸟们说：“孩子们，这就该走了。这回那人动了真格。他不再指望朋友，而要亲自来收割这片地啦。”
自助是最好的帮助。

sections.title_en: The Dog, the Cock, and the Fox
source_paragraphs: A DOG and a Cock being great friends, agreed to travel together. At nightfall they took shelter in a thick wood. The Cock flying up, perched himself on the branches of a tree, while the Dog found a bed beneath in the hollow trunk. When the morning dawned, the Cock, as usual, crowed very loudly several times. A Fox heard the sound, and wishing to make a breakfast on him, came and stood under the branches, saying how earnestly he desired to make the acquaintance of the owner of so magnificent a voice. The Cock, suspecting his civilities, said: “Sir, I wish you would do me the favour of going around to the hollow trunk below me, and waking my porter, so that he may open the door and let you in.” When the Fox approached the tree, the Dog sprang out and caught him, and tore him to pieces.
translated_paragraphs: 狗和公鸡是要好的朋友，约定一道出门旅行。天色将晚，他们到一片密林里投宿。公鸡飞上树枝落定，狗在树下空心的树干中找到了床。天一亮，公鸡照例放开嗓门，高声啼了几遍。狐狸听到，想拿它当早饭，便站到树下，表示自己实在非常渴望认识拥有这样一副绝妙歌喉的那位先生。公鸡对这些客套话存了疑，说：“先生，想请您帮个忙，绕到我脚下那棵空心树跟前，叫醒我的门房。他好替您开门，放您进来呀。”狐狸靠近树干，狗便一跃而出，捉住它，将它撕成了碎片。

source_paragraphs: THE GEESE and the Cranes were feeding in the same meadow, when a birdcatcher came to ensnare them in his nets. The Cranes, being light of wing, fled away at his approach; while the Geese, being slower of flight and heavier in their bodies, were captured.
translated_paragraphs: 鹅群和鹤群在同一片草地上觅食。这时，一个捕鸟人前来，要用网捉它们。鹤身轻翼捷，在他靠近时便已飞走。鹅飞得慢，身子又重，一只只落进了网。

source_paragraphs: AN ASS feeding in a meadow saw a Wolf approaching to seize him, and immediately pretended to be lame. The Wolf, coming up, inquired the cause of his lameness. The Ass replied that passing through a hedge he had trod with his foot upon a sharp thorn. He requested that the Wolf pull it out, lest when he ate him it should injure his throat. The Wolf consented and lifted up the foot, and was giving his whole mind to the discovery of the thorn, when the Ass, with his heels, kicked his teeth into his mouth and galloped away. The Wolf, being thus fearfully mauled, said, “I am rightly served, for why did I attempt the art of healing, when my father only taught me the trade of a butcher?”
translated_paragraphs: 一头驴正在草地上吃草，看见一只狼走过来要捉它，立即假装腿瘸。狼上前询问它为什么跛脚。驴说，穿过树篱的时候，脚底扎了一根尖刺，想请狼替它拔掉，免得等狼把它吃下去，那根刺会扎伤了狼的咽喉。狼答应了，抬起驴脚，正全神贯注地寻找尖刺。驴后蹄一踢，把狼的牙踹进它嘴里，拔腿飞奔而去。狼被踢得着实凄惨，说：“我这是活该。爸爸只教过我当屠夫，我又何必去试大夫的手艺？”

source_paragraphs: A MAN once kept a Goat and an Ass. The Goat, envying the Ass on account of his greater abundance of food, said, “How shamefully you are treated: at one time grinding in the mill, and at another carrying heavy burdens;” and he further advised him to pretend to be epileptic and fall into a ditch and so obtain rest. The Ass listened to his words, and falling into a ditch, was very much bruised. His master, sending for a leech, asked his advice. He bade him pour upon the wounds the lungs of a Goat. They at once killed the Goat, and so healed the Ass.
translated_paragraphs: 有个人养着一只山羊和一头驴。山羊嫉妒驴总能分到更充足的草料，便说：“人家待你多不像话！一会儿扔下你去推磨，一会儿又让你驮沉甸甸的货。”它进一步出主意，叫驴假装发了羊痫风，跌进沟里，从而就能得到休息。驴听信这话，果真倒进沟去，摔得遍体青紫。主人派人去请来医者，问该怎么治。医者嘱咐，要取一只山羊的肺浇敷伤口。他们立即杀了那只山羊，治好了驴。

source_paragraphs: A LION, greatly desiring to capture a Bull, and yet afraid to attack him on account of his great size, resorted to a trick to ensure his destruction. He approached the Bull and said, “I have slain a fine sheep, my friend; and if you will come home and partake of him with me, I shall be delighted to have your company.” The Lion said this in the hope that, as the Bull was in the act of reclining to eat, he might attack him to advantage, and make his meal on him. The Bull, on approaching the Lion’s den, saw the huge spits and giant caldrons, and no sign whatever of the sheep, and, without saying a word, quietly took his departure. The Lion inquired why he went off so abruptly without a word of salutation to his host, who had not given him any cause for offense. “I have reasons enough,” said the Bull. “I see no indication whatever of your having slaughtered a sheep, while I do see very plainly every preparation for your dining on a bull.”
translated_paragraphs: 一头狮子很想捉住公牛，却怕它身形高大，不敢硬碰，就打算用计置它于死地。它走到公牛身旁说：“朋友，我杀了一只肥羊。你要肯到我家来一起享用，我很高兴有你作伴。”狮子这样说，是希望公牛屈身进食时，自己可以趁机下手，用它饱餐一顿。公牛走近狮穴，看到巨大的烤肉叉、硕大的锅，却完全不见绵羊的踪影，便一言不发，悄悄离开。狮子问，主人并没冒犯你，怎么连声招呼也不打，便走得如此突然？“我有足够的理由。”公牛说，“我一点迹象都没瞧出，你曾杀过一只羊。倒看得清清楚楚，你为吃一头公牛，把东西都预备齐了。”

source_paragraphs: A FOX entered the house of an actor and, rummaging through all his properties, came upon a Mask, an admirable imitation of a human head. He placed his paws on it and said, “What a beautiful head! Yet it is of no value, as it entirely lacks brains.”
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸走进一位演员的房子，翻遍所有道具，找到一副面具，将人的头颅仿得极为逼真。它两爪捧着面具说：“多么漂亮的一颗头！可惜不值什么，因为里头全然没有脑子。”

source_paragraphs: AN OWL, accustomed to feed at night and to sleep during the day, was greatly disturbed by the noise of a Grasshopper and earnestly besought her to stop chirping. The Grasshopper refused to desist, and chirped louder and louder the more the Owl entreated. When she saw that she could get no redress and that her words were despised, the Owl attacked the chatterer by a stratagem. “Since I cannot sleep,” she said, “on account of your song which, believe me, is sweet as the lyre of Apollo, I shall indulge myself in drinking some nectar which Pallas lately gave me. If you do not dislike it, come to me and we will drink it together.” The Grasshopper, who was thirsty, and pleased with the praise of her voice, eagerly flew up. The Owl came forth from her hollow, seized her, and put her to death.
translated_paragraphs: 猫头鹰习惯夜里觅食、白日睡觉，给一只蚱蜢叫得十分烦恼，恳切地请求她停止鸣叫。可蚱蜢偏不肯停。猫头鹰越央求，她便叫得越响。眼见自己讨不到清静，所说的话又让对方不屑一顾，猫头鹰决定用计对付这位聒噪的家伙。“你的歌声弄得我睡不成觉，”它说，“请你相信，我觉得这声音跟阿波罗的七弦琴一样悦耳。既然睡不着，正好让我享受一点帕拉斯近来赐给我的神酒。你若不嫌弃，请到我这儿，我们一道饮用吧。”蚱蜢正口渴，又听人家赞美自己的歌喉，高高兴兴飞上前去。猫头鹰自树洞中出来，一把逮住了她，取了她的性命。

source_paragraphs: A FOWLER, taking his bird-lime and his twigs, went out to catch birds. Seeing a thrush sitting upon a tree, he wished to take it, and fitting his twigs to a proper length, watched intently, having his whole thoughts directed towards the sky. While thus looking upwards, he unknowingly trod upon a Viper asleep just before his feet. The Viper, turning about, stung him, and falling into a swoon, the man said to himself, “Woe is me! that while I purposed to hunt another, I am myself fallen unawares into the snares of death.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个捕鸟人带上黏鸟胶和细树枝，出门捕鸟。他瞧见一只鸫鸟歇在树上，想捉住它，便把细枝接到合适的长度，专心盯住目标，一门心思全放在天上。光顾着仰头，哪里晓得自己一脚踏中了脚边睡着的一条蝰蛇。蝰蛇转身咬了他一口。他昏倒之际，低声叹道：“我好惨哪！一心想猎取别人，没提防自己先跌进了死亡的圈套。”

source_paragraphs: A HORSE, proud of his fine trappings, met an Ass on the highway. The Ass, being heavily laden, moved slowly out of the way. “Hardly,” said the Horse, “can I resist kicking you with my heels.” The Ass held his peace, and made only a silent appeal to the justice of the gods. Not long afterwards the Horse, having become broken-winded, was sent by his owner to the farm. The Ass, seeing him drawing a dungcart, thus derided him: “Where, O boaster, are now all thy gay trappings, thou who are thyself reduced to the condition you so lately treated with contempt?”
translated_paragraphs: 一匹马为身上华丽的鞍辔十分自得，途中碰见一头驴。驴负载沉重，慢吞吞地让开了路。“我简直忍不住，”马说，“真想抬起后蹄踹你一下！”驴始终没有开口，只在心里默求诸神主持公道。过了不久，马得了喘病，主人把它送去农场。驴见它拉着粪车，便嘲笑道：“喂，爱夸口的家伙，你那身鲜亮的鞍辔现在都到哪儿去了？你如今自己沦落到的，不正是不久前你还瞧不起的境地吗？”

sections.title_en: The Lion and the Three Bulls
source_paragraphs: THREE BULLS for a long time pastured together. A Lion lay in ambush in the hope of making them his prey, but was afraid to attack them while they kept together. Having at last by guileful speeches succeeded in separating them, he attacked them without fear as they fed alone, and feasted on them one by one at his own leisure.
Union is strength.
translated_paragraphs: 三头公牛长久以来都在一起吃草。狮子躲在暗处，指望把他们当作猎物，可只要他们待在一起，狮子就不敢上前袭击。后来，他终于用花言巧语成功离间了他们。等三头牛分开吃草，他便放了心，随自己方便，一头一头地袭击，一头一头地吃掉了。
团结起来，就有力量。

source_paragraphs: A WOLF saw a Goat feeding at the summit of a steep precipice, where he had no chance of reaching her. He called to her and earnestly begged her to come lower down, lest she fall by some mishap; and he added that the meadows lay where he was standing, and that the herbage was most tender. She replied, “No, my friend, it is not for the pasture that you invite me, but for yourself, who are in want of food.”
translated_paragraphs: 狼看见山羊在高高的陡崖顶上吃草，自己一点儿也够不着。他向上呼喊，恳切地请山羊走到低处来，以免一不小心摔伤，又补充说，自己站的地方才是草场，青草尤其鲜嫩。山羊回答：“不，朋友。邀我下去，使你动心的不是草场，而是你自己。正缺吃的，是你呀。”

source_paragraphs: A FLY sat on the axle-tree of a chariot, and addressing the Draught-Mule said, “How slow you are! Why do you not go faster? See if I do not prick your neck with my sting.” The Draught-Mule replied, “I do not heed your threats; I only care for him who sits above you, and who quickens my pace with his whip, or holds me back with the reins. Away, therefore, with your insolence, for I know well when to go fast, and when to go slow.”
translated_paragraphs: 苍蝇坐在马车的车轴上，对拉车的骡子说：“你走得多慢！怎么不再快点？瞧我不用刺来扎一扎你的脖子！”骡子回答：“我不在意你的威胁。我只管你上头坐着的那个人。他一扬鞭，我就加快脚步；他一收缰绳，我就慢下来。收起你的傲慢吧，什么时候该快，什么时候该慢，我清楚得很。”

source_paragraphs: SOME FISHERMEN were out trawling their nets. Perceiving them to be very heavy, they danced about for joy and supposed that they had taken a large catch. When they had dragged the nets to the shore they found but few fish: the nets were full of sand and stones, and the men were beyond measure cast down so much at the disappointment which had befallen them, but because they had formed such very different expectations. One of their company, an old man, said, “Let us cease lamenting, my mates, for, as it seems to me, sorrow is always the twin sister of joy; and it was only to be looked for that we, who just now were over-rejoiced, should next have something to make us sad.”
translated_paragraphs: 几个渔夫出海拖网，觉得网沉甸甸的，以为准捞到了好多鱼，高兴得手舞足蹈。可把网拖上岸，里头只有几尾鱼，倒满是沙子和石块。大家垂头丧气，伤心到了极点。与其说是这趟落空本身叫人沮丧，倒不如说先前盼的跟眼前所见差得太远。同行的一位老人说：“伙计们，别再叹气了。依我看来，悲和喜原就是孪生姐妹。我们刚才高兴过了头，接下来该遇见点叫人伤心的事，这也在意料之中。”

sections.title_en: The Town Mouse and the Country Mouse
source_paragraphs: A COUNTRY MOUSE invited a Town Mouse, an intimate friend, to pay him a visit and partake of his country fare. As they were on the bare plowlands, eating there wheat-stocks and roots pulled up from the hedgerow, the Town Mouse said to his friend, “You live here the life of the ants, while in my house is the horn of plenty. I am surrounded by every luxury, and if you will come with me, as I wish you would, you shall have an ample share of my dainties.” The Country Mouse was easily persuaded, and returned to town with his friend. On his arrival, the Town Mouse placed before him bread, barley, beans, dried figs, honey, raisins, and, last of all, brought a dainty piece of cheese from a basket. The Country Mouse, being much delighted at the sight of such good cheer, expressed his satisfaction in warm terms and lamented his own hard fate. Just as they were beginning to eat, someone opened the door, and they both ran off squeaking, as fast as they could, to a hole so narrow that two could only find room in it by squeezing. They had scarcely begun their repast again when someone else entered to take something out of a cupboard, whereupon the two Mice, more frightened than before, ran away and hid themselves. At last the Country Mouse, almost famished, said to his friend: “Although you have prepared for me so dainty a feast, I must leave you to enjoy it by yourself. It is surrounded by too many dangers to please me. I prefer my bare plowlands and roots from the hedgerow, where I can live in safety, and without fear.”
translated_paragraphs: 乡下鼠邀来好友城里鼠，请他来作客，吃一顿乡间饭菜。他们待在光秃秃的耕地上，吃的只是麦秆和从树篱边拔来的草根。城里鼠对朋友说：“你在这里，过的是蚂蚁一般的生活，我家却有个取之不尽的丰饶之角。我身旁样样奢华。你若肯遂我的心愿跟我走，我那些美食必定有你一大份。”乡下鼠很容易便被说动，跟朋友一同进了城。一到家，城里鼠就摆上了面包、大麦、豆子、无花果干、蜂蜜和葡萄干，最后又从篮子里取出一块可口的奶酪。乡下鼠看见这样一桌好菜，十分高兴，热情地赞不绝口，又感叹自己的命运辛苦。两位才动口，忽然有人推开房门。他们吱吱叫着，撒开腿逃进一个洞，洞窄得必须用力挤才塞得下两位。刚刚重新开吃，另一个人又进来，打开橱柜拿东西。两位比刚才吓得更厉害，又慌忙逃走躲好。最后，乡下鼠已经饿得要命，他对朋友说：“虽然你替我备下这么精致的盛宴，我也只能留下你自己享用了。这顿饭周围的危险太多，我实在喜欢不来。我宁愿回到我那光秃秃的耕地，吃树篱旁的草根。那里能安安稳稳，不用担惊受怕地过日子。”

sections.title_en: The Wolf, the Fox, and the Ape
source_paragraphs: A WOLF accused a Fox of theft, but the Fox entirely denied the charge. An Ape undertook to adjudge the matter between them. When each had fully stated his case the Ape announced this sentence: “I do not think you, Wolf, ever lost what you claim; and I do believe you, Fox, to have stolen what you so stoutly deny.”
The dishonest, if they act honestly, get no credit.
translated_paragraphs: 狼控告狐狸偷了东西，狐狸却把指控否认得干干净净。猿答应替他们断案。等两边各自把事情述说完毕，猿宣判：“狼，我不信你真丢过你声称丢掉的东西；狐狸，我倒是相信，你这样一口咬定没有偷过的东西，就是你偷的。”
惯于欺骗的人，即使做了诚实的事，也难得到信任。

sections.title_en: The Wasps, the Partridges, and the Farmer
source_paragraphs: THE WASPS and the Partridges, overcome with thirst, came to a Farmer and besought him to give them some water to drink. They promised amply to repay him the favour which they asked. The Partridges declared that they would dig around his vines and make them produce finer grapes. The Wasps said that they would keep guard and drive off thieves with their stings. But the Farmer interrupted them, saying: “I have already two oxen, who, without making any promises, do all these things. It is surely better for me to give the water to them than to you.”
translated_paragraphs: 黄蜂和鹧鸪口渴得难受，前来恳求农夫给它们一点水喝。它们保证，一定会厚报他的好意。鹧鸪表示，愿意松一松他那葡萄藤周围的土，好叫葡萄长得更好；黄蜂说，它们可以替他站岗，用尾针赶跑小偷。农夫却打断它们：“我早已有两头牛，什么也没答应过，照样把这些活儿全做了。照理，还是把水给他们喝比给你们更好。”

source_paragraphs: A FATHER had one son and one daughter, the former remarkable for his good looks, the latter for her extraordinary ugliness. While they were playing one day as children, they happened by chance to look together into a mirror that was placed on their mother’s chair. The boy congratulated himself on his good looks; the girl grew angry, and could not bear the self-praises of her Brother, interpreting all he said (and how could she do otherwise?) into reflection on herself. She ran off to her father, to be avenged on her Brother, and spitefully accused him of having, as a boy, made use of that which belonged only to girls. The father embraced them both, and bestowing his kisses and affection impartially on each, said, “I wish you both would look into the mirror every day: you, my son, that you may not spoil your beauty by evil conduct; and you, my daughter, that you may make up for your lack of beauty by your virtues.”
translated_paragraphs: 父亲有一儿一女。哥哥相貌十分俊美，妹妹却长得格外丑。一天，两个孩子一同玩耍，无意间往母亲椅子上摆的一面镜子里望去。男孩为自己的好相貌而得意，女孩却生了气。她听不得哥哥一再自夸，觉得他每句话都在挖苦自己（她又怎能不这样想呢？）。她跑去找父亲，要他替自己报复哥哥，还气呼呼地告状，说哥哥一个男孩，竟动用了只有女孩才该用的东西。父亲把他们一同搂在怀里，给两人一样多的亲吻和疼爱，说：“我倒愿你们天天照照镜子。儿子，你照一照，免得因举止不端损伤了自己的美貌。女儿，你也照一照，让自己的美德补足容貌的欠缺。”

source_paragraphs: SOME DOGS, finding the skin of a lion, began to tear it in pieces with their teeth. A Fox, seeing them, said, “If this lion were alive, you would soon find out that his claws were stronger than your teeth.”
It is easy to kick a man that is down.
translated_paragraphs: 几条狗找到一张狮子皮，便用牙齿撕扯起来。狐狸见了，说：“那头狮子要是还活着，你们很快就会知道，它的爪子比你们的牙齿更有力量。”
往已经跌倒的人身上再踹一脚，很容易。

sections.title_en: The Blind Man and the Whelp
source_paragraphs: A BLIND MAN was accustomed to distinguishing different animals by touching them with his hands. The whelp of a Wolf was brought him, with a request that he would feel it, and say what it was. He felt it, and being in doubt, said: “I do not quite know whether it is the cub of a Fox, or the whelp of a Wolf, but this I know full well. It would not be safe to admit him to the sheepfold.”
Evil tendencies are shown in early life.
translated_paragraphs: 一个盲人习惯用手去摸，辨认不同的动物。有人把一只狼崽带给他，请他摸摸，说出是什么。他摸了摸，心里仍有疑惑，说道：“我不大拿得准，这究竟是小狐狸，还是小狼。不过有一件事我很确定：让这小东西进羊圈，可不安全。”
有些有害的倾向，小时候就显露出来了。

source_paragraphs: A COBBLER unable to make a living by his trade and made desperate by poverty, began to practice medicine in a town in which he was not known. He sold a drug, pretending that it was an antidote to all poisons, and obtained a great name for himself by long-winded puffs and advertisements. When the Cobbler happened to fall sick himself of a serious illness, the Governor of the town determined to test his skill. For this purpose he called for a cup, and while filling it with water, pretended to mix poison with the Cobbler’s antidote, commanding him to drink it on the promise of a reward. The Cobbler, under the fear of death, confessed that he had no knowledge of medicine, and was only made famous by the stupid clamors of the crowd. The Governor then called a public assembly and addressed the citizens: “Of what folly have you been guilty? You have not hesitated to entrust your heads to a man, whom no one could employ to make even the shoes for their feet.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个鞋匠靠老本行养活不了自己，给贫穷逼得走投无路，便跑到一个谁也不认识他的小镇上行医。他售卖一种药物，声称能解百毒，又大做广告，夸得天花乱坠，因而名声大振。后来鞋匠碰巧生了重病，镇上的长官决意考验他的本领。长官让人取来杯子，往里注入清水，却装作在鞋匠的解毒药里掺了毒，又许下赏钱，命他喝下去。鞋匠生怕丢命，只好承认自己分毫不懂医术，全靠众人糊里糊涂地叫好，才出了名。长官于是召集公众，对镇民们说道：“你们这是犯了多大的糊涂啊！一个人，连脚上穿的鞋都没有谁愿意找他做，你们却毫不犹豫，把自己的脑袋都交给了他。”

source_paragraphs: A WOLF coming out of a field of oats met a Horse and thus addressed him: “I would advise you to go into that field. It is full of fine oats, which I have left untouched for you, as you are a friend whom I would love to hear enjoying good eating.” The Horse replied, “If oats had been the food of wolves, you would never have indulged your ears at the cost of your belly.”
Men of evil reputation, when they perform a good deed, fail to get credit for it.
translated_paragraphs: 一头狼从一块燕麦田里出来，遇见了马，便对他说：“我劝你到那田里去吧，里头满是上好的燕麦，我一粒没动，都给你留着呢。你是我的朋友，听着你吃得香甜，我就高兴。”马答道：“燕麦要是能给狼当饭吃，你就不会饿着自己的肚子，只为叫耳朵享清福了。”
名声不佳的人，即便做了件好事，也很难叫人相信他的好意。

sections.title_en: The Two Men Who Were Enemies
source_paragraphs: TWO MEN, deadly enemies to each other, were sailing in the same vessel. Determined to keep as far apart as possible, the one seated himself in the stem, and the other in the prow of the ship. A violent storm arose, and with the vessel in great danger of sinking, the one in the stern inquired of the pilot which of the two ends of the ship would go down first. On his replying that he supposed it would be the prow, the Man said, “Death would not be grievous to me, if I could only see my Enemy die before me.”
translated_paragraphs: 两个彼此仇恨、势不两立的人恰巧乘同一艘船。为了尽可能离得远些，一个坐在船尾，另一个坐到船头。风暴大作，船随时有沉没的危险。船尾那人问舵手，船的哪一头会先沉。舵手回答，大概是船头。他便说：“只要我亲眼见着仇人死在我前面，死也不算多伤心。”

source_paragraphs: A MAN had two Gamecocks in his poultry-yard. One day by chance he found a tame Partridge for sale. He purchased it and brought it home to be reared with his Gamecocks. When the Partridge was put into the poultry-yard, they struck at it and followed it about, so that the Partridge became grievously troubled and supposed that he was thus evilly treated because he was a stranger. Not long afterwards he saw the Cocks fighting together and not separating before one had well beaten the other. He then said to himself, “I shall no longer distress myself at being struck at by these Gamecocks, when I see that they cannot even refrain from quarreling with each other.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个人的家禽院里养着两只斗鸡。一天，他碰巧遇见有人卖一只驯熟的鹧鸪，就买回家，跟斗鸡一起养起来。鹧鸪一进院子，斗鸡们便向它扑打，还跟在它身后不肯罢休。鹧鸪十分烦恼，以为就因为自己是个外来户，才受到这样的欺凌。不久，它看见两只斗鸡彼此争斗，一定要一方把另一方狠狠揍一顿才肯分开。它便对自己说：“这两只斗鸡扑来打我，我用不着再放在心上了。我看见了，它们连彼此之间都忍不住打个不停。”

source_paragraphs: A FOX saw a Lion confined in a cage, and standing near him, bitterly reviled him. The Lion said to the Fox, “It is not thou who revilest me; but this mischance which has befallen me.”
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸见一头狮子被关在笼里，便站在近旁，恶狠狠地辱骂他。狮子对狐狸说：“骂我的并不是你，是眼下落到我头上的这场厄运。”

source_paragraphs: A FROG once upon a time came forth from his home in the marsh and proclaimed to all the beasts that he was a learned physician, skilled in the use of drugs and able to heal all diseases. A Fox asked him, “How can you pretend to prescribe for others, when you are unable to heal your own lame gait and wrinkled skin?”
translated_paragraphs: 从前有只青蛙从沼泽里的家中出来，向百兽宣布自己是位博学的医生，善用药物，百病包治。狐狸问他：“你自己的腿一瘸一拐，皮肤一层层打皱，这些毛病你还医不好，怎么就敢给旁人开药方呢？”

sections.title_en: The Lion, the Wolf, and the Fox
source_paragraphs: A LION, growing old, lay sick in his cave. All the beasts came to visit their king, except the Fox. The Wolf therefore, thinking that he had a capital opportunity, accused the Fox to the Lion of not paying any respect to him who had the rule over them all and of not coming to visit him. At that very moment the Fox came in and heard these last words of the Wolf. The Lion roaring out in a rage against him, the Fox sought an opportunity to defend himself and said, “And who of all those who have come to you have benefited you so much as I, who have traveled from place to place in every direction, and have sought and learnt from the physicians the means of healing you?” The Lion commanded him immediately to tell him the cure, when he replied, “You must flay a wolf alive and wrap his skin yet warm around you.” The Wolf was at once taken and flayed; whereon the Fox, turning to him, said with a smile, “You should have moved your master not to ill, but to good, will.”
translated_paragraphs: 狮子年老，患病卧在洞里。百兽都来看望它们的王，唯有狐狸没有来。狼觉得这是大好时机，便向狮子告状，说狐狸对统治众兽的大王毫无敬意，都不前来探望。恰在这时，狐狸走了进来，听到了狼最后几句话。狮子震怒，向它咆哮。狐狸瞅准机会，出言为自己辩护：“到您跟前来的这许多位，谁及得上我对您有益？我为您东奔西走，四处寻访医生，总算求得了治好您的法子。”狮子马上命他道出来。他答：“要活剥下一张狼皮，趁还温热裹在您的身上。”狼当场便被抓住，活活剥皮。狐狸向它转过脸，微微一笑：“你原该劝主人心生善意，不该教唆他动恶念才对。”

source_paragraphs: IN THE WINTERTIME, a Dog curled up in as small a space as possible on account of the cold, determined to make himself a house. However when the summer returned again, he lay asleep stretched at his full length and appeared to himself to be of a great size. Now he considered that it would be neither an easy nor a necessary work to make himself such a house as would accommodate him.
translated_paragraphs: 冬日，一条狗因为怕冷，把身子尽量缩小，蜷在一起，打定主意给自己造栋房子。可是等到夏天回来，他舒展开四肢睡大觉，便觉得自己长得好庞大。他如今想，要造一栋足够容得下自己的房子，既非容易的工作，也全无必要。

sections.title_en: The North Wind and the Sun
source_paragraphs: THE NORTH WIND and the Sun disputed as to which was the most powerful, and agreed that he should be declared the victor who could first strip a wayfaring man of his clothes. The North Wind first tried his power and blew with all his might, but the keener his blasts, the closer the Traveler wrapped his cloak around him, until at last, resigning all hope of victory, the Wind called upon the Sun to see what he could do. The Sun suddenly shone out with all his warmth. The Traveler no sooner felt his genial rays than he took off one garment after another, and at last, fairly overcome with heat, undressed and bathed in a stream that lay in his path.
Persuasion is better than Force.
translated_paragraphs: 北风和太阳争论谁更有力量，商定谁先叫一位过路人脱掉衣服，就算谁赢。北风先显本事，用尽全力吹。可它吹得越凌厉，旅人就把披风裹得越紧。最终，风彻底丧失了赢的希望，请太阳来试试。太阳忽然把全部暖意洒向大地。旅人一感觉到和煦的阳光，就一件接一件地脱下衣服。最后热到实在受不了，脱了个干净，跳进路旁的溪水去洗澡。
好言劝导，胜过强力逼迫。

source_paragraphs: A CROW caught in a snare prayed to Apollo to release him, making a vow to offer some frankincense at his shrine. But when rescued from his danger, he forgot his promise. Shortly afterwards, again caught in a snare, he passed by Apollo and made the same promise to offer frankincense to Mercury. Mercury soon appeared and said to him, “O thou most base fellow? how can I believe thee, who hast disowned and wronged thy former patron?”
translated_paragraphs: 乌鸦中了圈套，向阿波罗祷告，求他放了自己，还许诺要去他的神坛献上一些乳香。可刚刚获救脱险，它就把许下的诺言忘了。不久，它又一次中了圈套。这回它撇下阿波罗，转向墨丘利，照样许愿要献乳香。墨丘利很快现身，说：“你这卑劣透顶的家伙！从前的恩主，你转身就不认了，还亏负他，叫我如何信得过你？”

source_paragraphs: A FOX invited a Crane to supper and provided nothing for his entertainment but some soup made of pulse, which was poured out into a broad flat stone dish. The soup fell out of the long bill of the Crane at every mouthful, and his vexation at not being able to eat afforded the Fox much amusement. The Crane, in his turn, asked the Fox to sup with him, and set before her a flagon with a long narrow mouth, so that he could easily insert his neck and enjoy its contents at his leisure. The Fox, unable even to taste it, met with a fitting requital, after the fashion of her own hospitality.
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸邀鹤来用晚餐，招待他的却只有一些豆汤，还盛在一只宽阔而平坦的石盘里。鹤用长嘴一啜，汤就全漏了，一口也吃不着，心里烦恼。狐狸看在眼里，倒觉得十分好玩。轮到鹤请狐狸吃饭时，他在她跟前摆上一只颈口狭长的瓶子。鹤轻轻松松就能伸进脖子，慢慢享用瓶里的食物。狐狸连尝也尝不到，得到的这份报偿正合情理，因为这原是她自己待客的法子。

source_paragraphs: ROAMING BY the mountainside at sundown, a Wolf saw his own shadow become greatly extended and magnified, and he said to himself, “Why should I, being of such an immense size and extending nearly an acre in length, be afraid of the Lion? Ought I not to be acknowledged as King of all the collected beasts?” While he was indulging in these proud thoughts, a Lion fell upon him and killed him. He exclaimed with a too late repentance, “Wretched me! this overestimation of myself is the cause of my destruction.”
translated_paragraphs: 黄昏时，一头狼在山边游荡，看到自己的影子伸得好长好长，显得无比巨大，就对自己说：“我的个头这么庞大，伸展开来，差不多能横过一英亩地，为什么还得怕狮子？天下的百兽合在一起，难道不该推举我为王吗？”正当他沉醉在这些得意念头里的时候，一头狮子扑上来，要了他的命。狼这才懊悔地叫道：“我好悲惨！正是把自己估得太高，才送了自己的命。”可后悔已经迟了。

sections.title_en: The Birds, the Beasts, and the Bat
source_paragraphs: THE BIRDS waged war with the Beasts, and each were by turns the conquerors. A Bat, fearing the uncertain issues of the fight, always fought on the side which he felt was the strongest. When peace was proclaimed, his deceitful conduct was apparent to both combatants. Therefore being condemned by each for his treachery, he was driven forth from the light of day, and henceforth concealed himself in dark hiding-places, flying always alone and at night.
translated_paragraphs: 飞鸟和走兽开战，两边轮番占上风。蝙蝠害怕战局变幻莫测，觉得哪里强就替哪里打。等到两边宣告和平，它的欺瞒行径对双方都已昭然若揭。双方都谴责它的不忠，它因而被逐出了白日的阳光。从此，它只得藏身在黑暗隐秘的地方，总是孤零零一只，只在夜里出来飞行。

source_paragraphs: A YOUNG MAN, a great spendthrift, had run through all his patrimony and had but one good cloak left. One day he happened to see a Swallow, which had appeared before its season, skimming along a pool and twittering gaily. He supposed that summer had come, and went and sold his cloak. Not many days later, winter set in again with renewed frost and cold. When he found the unfortunate Swallow lifeless on the ground, he said, “Unhappy bird! what have you done? By thus appearing before the springtime you have not only killed yourself, but you have wrought my destruction also.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个年轻人极会挥霍，败光了继承的整份家产，只剩下一件好斗篷。有一天，他恰好看见一只来早了的燕子，贴着池塘轻轻掠过，快乐地啁啾。他当是夏天来了，便把斗篷拿去卖掉。不出几天，冬天竟又回转，再度降下严霜苦寒。他看见那只不幸的燕子死在地上，便说：“可怜的鸟，你都干了什么呀！春天还没到，你就抢先露面，不但断送了自己的性命，也把我一道害了。”

source_paragraphs: A TRUMPETER, bravely leading on the soldiers, was captured by the enemy. He cried out to his captors, “Pray spare me, and do not take my life without cause or without inquiry. I have not slain a single man of your troop. I have no arms, and carry nothing but this one brass trumpet.” “That is the very reason for which you should be put to death,” they said; “for, while you do not fight yourself, your trumpet stirs all the others to battle.”
translated_paragraphs: 号手勇敢地领着士兵冲锋，落到了敌人手里。他朝捉住他的人喊：“求各位饶我一命。别不查缘由、无凭无据就杀我。你们队伍里，没有一个人是我杀的。我不拿武器，手里只有这一把铜号。”那些人回答：“你该被处死，偏偏正是为了这个。你自己虽不交战，却是你的号角叫其他所有人都投入了战斗。”

source_paragraphs: AN OWL, in her wisdom, counseled the Birds that when the acorn first began to sprout, to pull it all up out of the ground and not allow it to grow. She said acorns would produce mistletoe, from which an irremediable poison, the bird-lime, would be extracted and by which they would be captured. The Owl next advised them to pluck up the seed of the flax, which men had sown, as it was a plant which boded no good to them. And, lastly, the Owl, seeing an archer approach, predicted that this man, being on foot, would contrive darts armed with feathers which would fly faster than the wings of the Birds themselves. The Birds gave no credence to these warning words, but considered the Owl to be beside herself and said that she was mad. But afterwards, finding her words were true, they wondered at her knowledge and deemed her to be the wisest of birds. Hence it is that when she appears they look to her as knowing all things, while she no longer gives them advice, but in solitude laments their past folly.
translated_paragraphs: 聪明的猫头鹰告诫群鸟，橡子一露芽，就该把它们连根拔起，不能任由它们生长。她说，橡子长出的树上会生槲寄生，人会从中提取对鸟儿无可挽救的毒物——黏鸟胶，用来把鸟捉住。接着，她又劝鸟儿拔除人们种下的亚麻籽，因为这种植物对它们不是什么好兆头。最后，猫头鹰见一个弓箭手正朝这里走来，就预言说，这人虽然只能在地上走，却会造出装了羽毛的箭，飞得比鸟儿自己的翅膀还快。群鸟全然不信这些警告，觉得猫头鹰失去理智，说她发疯了。后来，她的话句句应验，它们惊叹她的见识，认她为最聪明的鸟。所以，直到今天，她一出现，群鸟就盼着她无所不知，能有所指教。她却再也不给它们提建议，只独自为它们从前的愚行叹息。

source_paragraphs: ALL the Goods were once driven out by the Ills from that common share which they each had in the affairs of mankind; for the Ills by reason of their numbers had prevailed to possess the earth. The Goods wafted themselves to heaven and asked for a righteous vengeance on their persecutors. They entreated Jupiter that they might no longer be associated with the Ills, as they had nothing in common and could not live together, but were engaged in unceasing warfare; and that an indissoluble law might be laid down for their future protection. Jupiter granted their request and decreed that henceforth the Ills should visit the earth in company with each other, but that the Goods should one by one enter the habitations of men. Hence it arises that Ills abound, for they come not one by one, but in troops, and by no means singly: while the Goods proceed from Jupiter, and are given, not alike to all, but singly, and separately; and one by one to those who are able to discern them.
translated_paragraphs: 从前，福与祸共同参与人间万事，各占一份。后来祸患占着数量上的优势，夺得大地，把一切好事都挤了出去。好事们飘到了天上，求神主持公道，惩治迫害自己的对头。它们向朱庇特陈情，说自己和祸患毫无共同之处，既不能相处，又总在交战，请求不必再与祸患为伍，还望立下一条牢不可破的法则，保全它们今后安稳。朱庇特答应了它们，下令从此以后，祸患可以成群结伴地到人间去，好事却须逐一走进人的住处。这就是为什么祸事那么多：它们不肯一个接一个，而是成队到来，绝不单独行动。好事则由朱庇特那里出发，不会平均送给众人，只能个别、分散地赐予，一件件落到那些能认出它们的人手中。

sections.title_en: The Ass in the Lion’s Skin
source_paragraphs: AN ASS, having put on the Lion’s skin, roamed about in the forest and amused himself by frightening all the foolish animals he met in his wanderings. At last coming upon a Fox, he tried to frighten him also, but the Fox no sooner heard the sound of his voice than he exclaimed, “I might possibly have been frightened myself, if I had not heard your bray.”
translated_paragraphs: 驴披上狮皮，在森林里四处漫游，吓一吓途中碰到的傻动物，自得其乐。最后遇见一只狐狸，也想这样吓唬他。可狐狸一听驴开口，就叫道：“假如我没听见你那一声驴叫，连我也真可能被你吓着呢。”

source_paragraphs: A HARE pounced upon by an eagle sobbed very much and uttered cries like a child. A Sparrow upbraided her and said, “Where now is thy remarkable swiftness of foot? Why were your feet so slow?” While the Sparrow was thus speaking, a hawk suddenly seized him and killed him. The Hare was comforted in her death, and expiring said, “Ah! you who so lately, when you supposed yourself safe, exulted over my calamity, have now reason to deplore a similar misfortune.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只野兔被鹰扑住，伤心地抽泣，哭得像个孩子。麻雀数落她道：“你那了不起的飞毛腿，今天怎么啦？为什么脚步竟慢成这样？”麻雀话音未落，一只隼突然飞来，抓住它，取了它的性命。野兔在死前倒得到了一丝安慰，她咽气时说：“啊，刚才你还自以为安全，在我的不幸里幸灾乐祸。你现在倒该为自己遭遇了同样的灾祸而哀叹了。”

source_paragraphs: A FLEA thus questioned an Ox: “What ails you, that being so huge and strong, you submit to the wrongs you receive from men and slave for them day by day, while I, being so small a creature, mercilessly feed on their flesh and drink their blood without stint?” The Ox replied: “I do not wish to be ungrateful, for I am loved and well cared for by men, and they often pat my head and shoulders.” “Woe’s me!” said the flea; “this very patting which you like, whenever it happens to me, brings with it my inevitable destruction.”
