translated_paragraphs: 跳蚤问公牛：“你这是为什么呢？你长得那样高大有力，却忍受人类加给你的委屈，天天给他们做苦役。我这样小小一个生灵，倒可以毫不留情地吃他们的肉，尽情喝他们的血。”公牛答：“我并不愿忘恩负义。人爱护我，精心照料我，还常常轻拍我的脑袋和肩膀。”“哎呀，我真倒霉！”跳蚤说，“你喜欢别人拍你，可同样这一拍要是落到我头上，便是必死无疑啦。”

source_paragraphs: A MAN wished to purchase an Ass, and agreed with its owner that he should try out the animal before he bought him. He took the Ass home and put him in the straw-yard with his other Asses, upon which the new animal left all the others and at once joined the one that was most idle and the greatest eater of them all. Seeing this, the man put a halter on him and led him back to his owner. On being asked how, in so short a time, he could have made a trial of him, he answered, “I do not need a trial; I know that he will be just the same as the one he chose for his companion.”
A man is known by the company he keeps.
translated_paragraphs: 一个人想买头驴，同卖主说好，买之前先试一试。他把驴带回家，放进草料院，同自家其他的驴待在一处。这头新来的离开其他伙伴，一下子跑到了最懒、最能吃的那一头旁边。那人见状，便给驴系上笼头，又牵回卖主跟前。卖主问他，这么短的时间怎能试出好坏。他回答：“我不需要再试。它选了什么样的同伴，就足以让我明白它自己是什么样。”
看一个人常和谁做伴，也就知道了他的为人。

source_paragraphs: A DOVE shut up in a cage was boasting of the large number of young ones which she had hatched. A Crow hearing her, said: “My good friend, cease from this unseasonable boasting. The larger the number of your family, the greater your cause of sorrow, in seeing them shut up in this prison-house.”
translated_paragraphs: 关在笼子里的鸽子，正在夸口，自己已经孵出了多少多少孩子。乌鸦路过听见，说：“好朋友，收起这不合时宜的夸耀吧。眼看一家子全被锁在这座牢房里，家里成员越多，你该有的悲伤便越大。”

source_paragraphs: A MAN and a Satyr once drank together in token of a bond of alliance being formed between them. One very cold wintry day, as they talked, the Man put his fingers to his mouth and blew on them. When the Satyr asked the reason for this, he told him that he did it to warm his hands because they were so cold. Later on in the day they sat down to eat, and the food prepared was quite scalding. The Man raised one of the dishes a little towards his mouth and blew in it. When the Satyr again inquired the reason, he said that he did it to cool the meat, which was too hot. “I can no longer consider you as a friend,” said the Satyr, “a fellow who with the same breath blows hot and cold.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个人和一位半人半羊的林神萨堤尔曾举杯共饮，以示结盟。一个严寒的冬日，两人正讲话，那人把手指凑到嘴边，向上呵气。林神问他为什么这样做，他解释说，手实在冷，要这样暖一暖。过些时候，两人坐下来吃饭，端上的菜烫得要命。那人把一只盘子往嘴边举了举，又对着它吹气。林神追问缘故，他回答说，肉太热，要把它吹凉一点。林神说：“我不能再拿你当朋友了。同样一口气，能吹热又能吹冷，你这人真不可靠。”

sections.title_zh: 朱庇特、尼普顿、密涅瓦和摩摩斯
source_paragraphs: ACCORDING to an ancient legend, the first man was made by Jupiter, the first bull by Neptune, and the first house by Minerva. On the completion of their labours, a dispute arose as to which had made the most perfect work. They agreed to appoint Momus as judge, and to abide by his decision. Momus, however, being very envious of the handicraft of each, found fault with all. He first blamed the work of Neptune because he had not made the horns of the bull below his eyes, so he might better see where to strike. He then condemned the work of Jupiter, because he had not placed the heart of man on the outside, that everyone might read the thoughts of the evil disposed and take precautions against the intended mischief. And, lastly, he inveighed against Minerva because she had not contrived iron wheels in the foundation of her house, so its inhabitants might more easily remove if a neighbor proved unpleasant. Jupiter, indignant at such inveterate faultfinding, drove him from his office of judge, and expelled him from the mansions of Olympus.
translated_paragraphs: 据古老的传说，第一个人是朱庇特造的，第一头公牛是尼普顿造的，第一栋房屋则出自密涅瓦之手。他们各自收工以后，为谁做的东西最完美起了争执。他们同意请摩摩斯裁判，听从他的裁决。摩摩斯却很嫉妒各位的手艺，样样都要挑错。先批评尼普顿，说他没把牛角安在眼睛下方，那样公牛好看清楚该往哪里顶。又批评朱庇特，说他没把人心放在身体外边，好让人人都看清那些心怀恶念者的心思，提防他们预谋的祸事。最后，他指责密涅瓦没在屋基上安装铁轮子，若是邻居相处不来，屋里的人便能轻松搬走。朱庇特见他这样一味挑刺，愤慨之极，免了他的裁判职分，把他逐出了奥林匹斯的宫殿。

source_paragraphs: AN EAGLE, flying down from his perch on a lofty rock, seized upon a lamb and carried him aloft in his talons. A Jackdaw, who witnessed the capture of the lamb, was stirred with envy and determined to emulate the strength and flight of the Eagle. He flew around with a great whir of his wings and settled upon a large ram, with the intention of carrying him off, but his claws became entangled in the ram’s fleece and he was not able to release himself, although he fluttered with his feathers as much as he could. The shepherd, seeing what had happened, ran up and caught him. He at once clipped the Jackdaw’s wings, and taking him home at night, gave him to his children. On their saying, “Father, what kind of bird is it?” he replied, “To my certain knowledge he is a Daw; but he would like you to think an Eagle.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只鹰从栖身的高高岩壁上俯冲下来，抓住一头羊羔，用利爪把它带上高空。寒鸦亲眼见证了这次捕猎，心生羡慕，决心效仿老鹰有力的双翅和飞行的功夫。它把翅膀拍得哗哗作响，盘旋一圈，落在一头大公羊身上，想一举将它带走。可双爪却缠进羊毛里，任凭怎样拼命扑腾，寒鸦都挣脱不开。牧人看见出了什么事，赶上来抓住了它，当即剪短它的翅羽。夜里，他把寒鸦带回去送给了孩子。他们问：“爸爸，这是什么鸟呀？”他答：“据我确切知道，它是只寒鸦；可它大概很希望你们相信它是只鹰。”

source_paragraphs: AN EAGLE and a Fox formed an intimate friendship and decided to live near each other. The Eagle built her nest in the branches of a tall tree, while the Fox crept into the underwood and there produced her young. Not long after they had agreed upon this plan, the Eagle, being in want of provision for her young ones, swooped down while the Fox was out, seized upon one of the little cubs, and feasted herself and her brood. The Fox on her return, discovered what had happened, but was less grieved for the death of her young than for her inability to avenge them. A just retribution, however, quickly fell upon the Eagle. While hovering near an altar, on which some villagers were sacrificing a goat, she suddenly seized a piece of the flesh, and carried it, along with a burning cinder, to her nest. A strong breeze soon fanned the spark into a flame, and the eaglets, as yet unfledged and helpless, were roasted in their nest and dropped down dead at the bottom of the tree. There, in the sight of the Eagle, the Fox gobbled them up.
translated_paragraphs: 鹰与狐狸结成了亲密的朋友，决定比邻而居。鹰在高树枝间筑巢，狐狸则钻入树下的密丛，在那里生下幼崽。商量好这样的住处不久，鹰为了给雏鹰找食，竟趁着狐狸外出，俯冲下去，抓走一只小狐狸，自己带着小鹰饱餐了一顿。狐狸回来发现事情经过，失去孩子固然叫她悲伤，更叫她悲伤的，却是自己无力替孩子报仇。可是，鹰很快就遭到了应有的报应。一群村民正在祭坛上用山羊祭祀。鹰在旁边盘旋，猛地抓起一块肉，没留意到还带着一粒燃烧的炭，直接送回巢中。一阵强风吹过，火星很快蹿成火苗。小鹰们还没有长齐飞羽，帮不了自己，全被烧死在巢里，掉到树脚。就在鹰眼皮底下，狐狸把它们一只只吃下了肚。

source_paragraphs: EVERY MAN, according to an ancient legend, is born into the world with two bags suspended from his neck all bag in front full of his neighbors’ faults, and a large bag behind filled with his own faults. Hence it is that men are quick to see the faults of others, and yet are often blind to their own failings.
translated_paragraphs: 据古老的传说，每个人降生到世上，脖子上就挂着两只口袋。胸前那一只，装满了邻人的过错；背后那只大袋子，装的全是自己的过失。因此，人们对别人的错处眼睛特别尖，却常常看不见自己的缺点。

source_paragraphs: A BITCH, ready to whelp, earnestly begged a shepherd for a place where she might litter. When her request was granted, she besought permission to rear her puppies in the same spot. The shepherd again consented. But at last the Bitch, protected by the bodyguard of her Whelps, who had now grown up and were able to defend themselves, asserted her exclusive right to the place and would not permit the shepherd to approach.
translated_paragraphs: 一条快下崽的母狗恳求牧人，给她个地方产下小狗。牧人答应了，她又求他允许她就在那里养育孩子。牧人再度点了头。到了后来，小狗们长大了，有力气保护自己，又成了母亲的护卫。母狗仗着它们，竟宣称那地方只归她独占，不许牧人走近半步。

source_paragraphs: A STAG overpowered by heat came to a spring to drink. Seeing his own shadow reflected in the water, he greatly admired the size and variety of his horns, but felt angry with himself for having such slender and weak feet. While he was thus contemplating himself, a Lion appeared at the pool and crouched to spring upon him. The Stag immediately took to flight, and exerting his utmost speed, as long as the plain was smooth and open kept himself easily at a safe distance from the Lion. But entering a wood he became entangled by his horns, and the Lion quickly came up to him and caught him. When too late, he thus reproached himself: “Woe is me! How I have deceived myself! These feet which would have saved me I despised, and I gloried in these antlers which have proved my destruction.”
What is most truly valuable is often underrated.
translated_paragraphs: 雄鹿热得受不了，来到泉边饮水。它看见水里自己的倒影，十分欣赏头上一对鹿角又大又多分枝，却气自己几只脚纤细无力。正这样端详自己的时候，一头狮子现身池畔，伏低身子要向它扑来。雄鹿当即逃命，使出最快的速度。在平坦开阔的原野上，它轻轻松松同狮子保持着安全距离。可一进树林，鹿角就被枝条绊住，于是狮子很快赶上，把它抓住了。事到临头，雄鹿才责备自己：“我真惨哪！我把自己骗到了什么地步！能救我命的脚，我瞧不起；我得意洋洋的一对角，却断送了我的性命。”
真正最有价值的，往往最容易受到低估。

source_paragraphs: THE LARK (according to an ancient legend) was created before the earth itself, and when her father died, as there was no earth, she could find no place of burial for him. She let him lie uninterred for five days, and on the sixth day, not knowing what else to do, she buried him in her own head. Hence she obtained her crest, which is popularly said to be her father’s grave-hillock.
Youth’s first duty is reverence to parents.
translated_paragraphs: 据说，连大地本身都尚未造成时，云雀便已被造出来了。它的父亲死去，由于世上还没有泥土，它找不到一块地方安葬他。父亲的尸身停了五天仍未埋葬。第六天，她实在不知道怎么办才好，就把父亲埋进了自己的头顶。从此，云雀便长出了冠羽。按民间的说法，那是她父亲的坟丘。
年轻人的头一份责任，就是敬重父母。

source_paragraphs: A GNAT settled on the horn of a Bull, and sat there a long time. Just as he was about to fly off, he made a buzzing noise, and inquired of the Bull if he would like him to go. The Bull replied, “I did not know you had come, and I shall not miss you when you go away.”
Some men are of more consequence in their own eyes than in the eyes of their neighbors.
translated_paragraphs: 一只蚊子落到公牛的犄角上，一坐就是好久。临要飞走时，它嗡嗡响了几声，问公牛是不是希望它离开。公牛答：“你来的时候我都不知道，等你走了，我也不会挂念你。”
有些人在自己眼里要紧得很，在旁人眼里却不见得如此。

source_paragraphs: THE BEASTS of the forest gave a splendid entertainment at which the Monkey stood up and danced. Having vastly delighted the assembly, he sat down amidst universal applause. The Camel, envious of the praises bestowed on the Monkey and desiring to divert to himself the favour of the guests, proposed to stand up in his turn and dance for their amusement. He moved about in so utterly ridiculous a manner that the Beasts, in a fit of indignation, set upon him with clubs and drove him out of the assembly.
It is absurd to ape our betters.
translated_paragraphs: 林中百兽举行了一场盛会，猴子站起来跳舞，赢得了满堂欢喜，在大家的掌声中坐了下来。骆驼十分羡慕猴子所得的赞美，也想把宾客对它的喜爱转到自己身上，便提议轮到他起舞，给大家取乐。他扭动身体，模样荒唐可笑到了极点，惹得百兽一阵愤怒，纷纷举起棍棒，把他从集会上赶了出去。
见别人有真本领，就模仿他的做派来卖弄自己，实在可笑。

source_paragraphs: SOME DOGS famished with hunger saw a number of cowhides steeping in a river. Not being able to reach them, they agreed to drink up the river, but it happened that they burst themselves with drinking long before they reached the hides.
Attempt not impossibilities.
translated_paragraphs: 几条饿极了的狗看见几张牛皮泡在河里。它们够不到牛皮，就商量好把河水喝干。可离喝到皮还早，它们就已把自己肚子喝破了。
办不到的事，别硬去尝试。

source_paragraphs: A HALF-FAMISHED JACKDAW seated himself on a fig-tree, which had produced some fruit entirely out of season, and waited in the hope that the figs would ripen. A Fox seeing him sitting so long and learning the reason of his doing so, said to him, “You are indeed, sir, sadly deceiving yourself; you are indulging a hope strong enough to cheat you, but which will never reward you with enjoyment.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只半饿死的寒鸦坐上一棵无花果树。树上反季节结了几颗果子，它便守在那里，指望果子慢慢熟透。一只狐狸看见寒鸦坐了这么久，问清缘由，就对它说：“先生，你可把自己骗苦啦。你纵容心里的这份希望，它有足够的力量哄住你，却永远不会叫你享受到果实。”

source_paragraphs: A WORKMAN, felling wood by the side of a river, let his axe drop by accident into a deep pool. Being thus deprived of the means of his livelihood, he sat down on the bank and lamented his hard fate. Mercury appeared and demanded the cause of his tears. After he told him his misfortune, Mercury plunged into the stream, and, bringing up a golden axe, inquired if that were the one he had lost. On his saying that it was not his, Mercury disappeared beneath the water a second time, returned with a silver axe in his hand, and again asked the Workman if it were his. When the Workman said it was not, he dived into the pool for the third time and brought up the axe that had been lost. The Workman claimed it and expressed his joy at its recovery. Mercury, pleased with his honesty, gave him the golden and silver axes in addition to his own. The Workman, on his return to his house, related to his companions all that had happened. One of them at once resolved to try and secure the same good fortune for himself. He ran to the river and threw his axe on purpose into the pool at the same place, and sat down on the bank to weep. Mercury appeared to him just as he hoped he would; and having learned the cause of his grief, plunged into the stream and brought up a golden axe, inquiring if he had lost it. The Workman seized it greedily, and declared that truly it was the very same axe that he had lost. Mercury, displeased at his knavery, not only took away the golden axe, but refused to recover for him the axe he had thrown into the pool.
translated_paragraphs: 一个干活的人在河边砍木头，斧子不慎落入深潭。失去了赖以谋生的工具，他坐在岸上，哀叹自己命苦。墨丘利显现出来，问他为什么落泪。他说清自己的遭遇，墨丘利便潜入水中，带着一把金斧头出水，问丢的是不是这把。他答道，不是自己的。墨丘利第二次消失在水下，又举着一把银斧回来，再问这是不是他的。他仍回答说不是。墨丘利第三次潜入深潭，拿上来那把真正丢失的斧子。那人认出了自己的斧子，为失物复得大喜。墨丘利喜欢他的诚实，除了他自己的斧头，还把金斧、银斧也都送给了他。他回家以后，把整件事讲给同伴听。其中一位立即下定决心，也要给自己弄到同样的好运。他跑到河边，在同一个地方故意把自己的斧子扔进潭里，然后坐在岸边哭泣。墨丘利果然如他所愿现了身。得知他自称为何伤心，便潜入溪水，举起一把金斧，问他丢的是不是这一把。那人贪婪地一把接过，满口宣称，这正是他亲手弄丢的斧头。墨丘利恼怒他的欺骗，不但收走金斧，也拒绝替他找回他已扔进潭里的那一把。

source_paragraphs: A PEASANT had in his garden an Apple-Tree which bore no fruit but only served as a harbor for the sparrows and grasshoppers. He resolved to cut it down, and taking his axe in his hand, made a bold stroke at its roots. The grasshoppers and sparrows entreated him not to cut down the tree that sheltered them, but to spare it, and they would sing to him and lighten his labours. He paid no attention to their request, but gave the tree a second and a third blow with his axe. When he reached the hollow of the tree, he found a hive full of honey. Having tasted the honeycomb, he threw down his axe, and looking on the tree as sacred, took great care of it.
Self-interest alone moves some men.
translated_paragraphs: 一个农夫的园中有棵苹果树，从不结果，只给麻雀和蚂蚱提供栖身之地。他决意砍掉它，举起斧头，照树根重重来了一下。麻雀和蚂蚱求他别砍掉这棵为它们遮风的树，饶树一命，它们就唱歌给他听，叫他的劳作轻快些。他不理会它们的请求，又砍了第二斧、第三斧。等砍到树心的空处，却见里面有个蜂窝，满是蜂蜜。他尝过蜂巢，立刻放下斧子，把这棵树当成宝贝，悉心照料起来。
有些人只会为自己的利益所动。

sections.title_en: The Two Soldiers and the Robber
source_paragraphs: TWO SOLDIERS traveling together were set upon by a Robber. The one fled away; the other stood his ground and defended himself with his stout right hand. The Robber being slain, the timid companion ran up and drew his sword, and then, throwing back his traveling cloak said, “I’ll at him, and I’ll take care he shall learn whom he has attacked.” On this, he who had fought with the Robber made answer, “I only wish that you had helped me just now, even if it had been only with those words, for I should have been the more encouraged, believing them to be true; but now put up your sword in its sheath and hold your equally useless tongue, till you can deceive others who do not know you. I, indeed, who have experienced with what speed you run away, know right well that no dependence can be placed on your valor.”
translated_paragraphs: 两个士兵结伴赶路，忽然遭遇强盗袭击。一个转身逃了，另一个立在原地，凭自己强健的右手迎战自卫。等强盗已被杀死，胆怯的伙伴跑了回来，拔出长剑，把斗篷往背后一甩，说：“让我来对付他，我非让他知道他招惹的是什么人不可！”刚同强盗交过手的士兵回答：“我倒希望你刚才来帮我一把。哪怕只说上这几句话，我要是当了真，也能多几分胆气。可现在，收起你的剑，把它放回鞘里吧。你那张同样没用的嘴，也闭上吧，留着去哄弄别的不认得你的人吧。至于我，亲眼见过你逃跑得有多快，你的勇气有几分靠得住，我心里最清楚。”

source_paragraphs: A SHEPHERD driving his Sheep to a wood, saw an oak of unusual size full of acorns, and spreading his cloak under the branches, he climbed up into the tree and shook them down. The Sheep eating the acorns inadvertently frayed and tore the cloak. When the Shepherd came down and saw what was done, he said, “O you most ungrateful creatures! You provide wool to make garments for all other men, but you destroy the clothes of him who feeds you.”
translated_paragraphs: 牧人赶着羊群去树林，发现一棵格外高大的橡树，树上结满橡子。他把披风铺在树枝下面，亲自爬上树，把橡子摇下来。羊群吃橡子时，无意间把披风磨损撕破了。牧人爬下树看见这件事，说：“你们这些最不懂得感恩的家伙！你们供给旁人羊毛，叫人人都有衣服穿，却毁了那个给你们食物的人的衣裳。”

sections.title_en: The Trees Under the Protection of the Gods
source_paragraphs: THE GODS, according to an ancient legend, made choice of certain trees to be under their special protection. Jupiter chose the oak, Venus the myrtle, Apollo the laurel, Cybele the pine, and Hercules the poplar. Minerva, wondering why they had preferred trees not yielding fruit, inquired the reason for their choice. Jupiter replied, “It is lest we should seem to covet the honour for the fruit.” But said Minerva, “Let anyone say what he will the olive is more dear to me on account of its fruit.” Then said Jupiter, “My daughter, you are rightly called wise; for unless what we do is useful, the glory of it is vain.”
translated_paragraphs: 按古老传说，众神各自选了一种树，置于自己的特别庇护下。朱庇特选了橡树，维纳斯挑了香桃木，阿波罗选择月桂，库柏勒挑选松树，赫拉克勒斯则选中了白杨。密涅瓦奇怪他们怎么都偏爱那些不结果实的树，便询问缘故。朱庇特答：“是为了免得人以为，我们给树荣耀，是贪图它的果子。”密涅瓦却说：“任旁人怎样说，我格外爱橄榄树，正因为它的果实。”朱庇特于是说：“我的女儿，你叫作智慧女神，果然当之无愧。我们所做的事，若无益处，剩下的荣耀也不过是虚名。”

source_paragraphs: A FLEA settled upon the bare foot of a Wrestler and bit him, causing the man to call loudly upon Hercules for help. When the Flea a second time hopped upon his foot, he groaned and said, “O Hercules! if you will not help me against a Flea, how can I hope for your assistance against greater antagonists?”
translated_paragraphs: 一只跳蚤落在摔跤手光着的脚上，咬了他一口，那人便高声呼唤大力神赫拉克勒斯搭救。跳蚤第二次蹦到他脚上时，他呻吟道：“哦，赫拉克勒斯！连对付一只跳蚤你都不肯帮我，遇到更强的对手，我怎能指望你相助呢？”

source_paragraphs: A FOX entered into partnership with a Lion on the pretense of becoming his servant. Each undertook his proper duty in accordance with his own nature and powers. The Fox discovered and pointed out the prey; the Lion sprang on it and seized it. The Fox soon became jealous of the Lion carrying off the Lion’s share, and said that he would no longer find out the prey, but would capture it on his own account. The next day he attempted to snatch a lamb from the fold, but he himself fell prey to the huntsmen and hounds.
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸托称要做狮子的仆从，和他结成了伙伴。两位各按自己的性情和力气分担适当的任务。狐狸发现猎物，指给狮子看，狮子负责扑上去捉住。没多久，狐狸开始眼红狮子拿走的那份最大，宣称他不再替谁侦察猎物，要亲自动手去捕获，归自己所有。第二天，他试图从羊圈里抢走一只羊羔，却自己成了猎人和猎犬的猎物。

source_paragraphs: A WAYFARING MAN, traveling in the desert, met a woman standing alone and terribly dejected. He inquired of her, “Who art thou?” “My name is Truth,” she replied. “And for what cause,” he asked, “have you left the city to dwell alone here in the wilderness?” She made answer, “Because in former times, falsehood was with few, but is now with all men.”
translated_paragraphs: 一名旅人穿过荒漠，遇见一名独自站立的女子，神情极为沮丧。他问：“你是谁？”她回答：“我名叫真理。”他又问：“什么缘故，让你离开城市，到这荒野独自居住？”她说：“因为在从前，谎言只跟少数人结伴；到了现在，它却跟人人在一起。”

source_paragraphs: A MAN committed a murder, and was pursued by the relations of the man whom he murdered. On his reaching the river Nile he saw a Lion on its bank and being fearfully afraid, climbed up a tree. He found a serpent in the upper branches of the tree, and again being greatly alarmed, he threw himself into the river, where a crocodile caught him and ate him. Thus the earth, the air, and the water alike refused shelter to a murderer.
translated_paragraphs: 一个人杀了人，死者的亲属紧追不舍。凶手到了尼罗河边，看见岸上有狮子，害怕极了，赶快爬上树去。又看见树梢上有条蛇，他再度大惊，纵身跳进河里，一只鳄鱼捉住他，把他吃了。于是，地面、空中、水里，统统不肯给一个杀人凶手提供庇护。

source_paragraphs: AN EAGLE stayed his flight and entreated a Lion to make an alliance with him to their mutual advantage. The Lion replied, “I have no objection, but you must excuse me for requiring you to find surety for your good faith, for how can I trust anyone as a friend who is able to fly away from his bargain whenever he pleases?”
Try before you trust.
translated_paragraphs: 鹰停住飞行，请求狮子与它缔结同盟，好叫彼此都得好处。狮子回答：“我没有意见。不过，为了你的诚意能得个保障，还请原谅我，非要你找来担保才行。一个人爱什么时候飞走、抛下约定，就能什么时候飞走，又叫我如何信他是朋友？”
要相信，先考验。

source_paragraphs: AN ASS, being driven along a high road, suddenly started off and bolted to the brink of a deep precipice. While he was in the act of throwing himself over, his owner seized him by the tail, endeavoring to pull him back. When the Ass persisted in his effort, the man let him go and said, “Conquer, but conquer to your cost.”
translated_paragraphs: 驴在宽阔的大路上由主人赶着走，忽然离开正道，直奔深深的悬崖边。正要纵身跳下去时，主人揪住它的尾巴，使劲往回拉。驴却坚决往前挣。那人松开手，说：“好，你赢吧。不过，赢回来什么，你自己承担。”

source_paragraphs: A THRUSH was feeding on a myrtle-tree and did not move from it because its berries were so delicious. A Fowler observed her staying so long in one spot, and having well bird-limed his reeds, caught her. The Thrush, being at the point of death, exclaimed, “O foolish creature that I am! For the sake of a little pleasant food I have deprived myself of my life.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只画眉飞到香桃木上觅食。树上的浆果太鲜美了，它舍不得走。捕鸟人见它守着一处不动这么久，便在苇杆上厚厚涂了黏鸟胶，把它逮住。临死时，画眉叫道：“我这个傻家伙啊！为了一点可口的食物，我竟叫自己丢了性命。”

source_paragraphs: A FAMISHED WOLF was prowling about in the morning in search of food. As he passed the door of a cottage built in the forest, he heard a Mother say to her child, “Be quiet, or I will throw you out of the window, and the Wolf shall eat you.” The Wolf sat all day waiting at the door. In the evening he heard the same woman fondling her child and saying: “You are quiet now, and if the Wolf should come, we will kill him.” The Wolf, hearing these words, went home, gasping with cold and hunger. When he reached his den, Mistress Wolf inquired of him why he returned wearied and supperless, so contrary to his wont. He replied: “Why, forsooth! use I gave credence to the words of a woman!”
translated_paragraphs: 一只饿极了的狼在早晨出来找食，经过林中一座小屋门前，听见母亲对孩子说：“安静些，不然我把你从窗边扔出去，让狼吃你。”狼便在门口坐了一整天，专等这顿饭。到了傍晚，他听见同一个女人搂着孩子爱抚，说：“如今你安静了。狼要是敢来，我们就把它打死。”狼听了这些话，又冷又饿，气喘吁吁地回家去。到了洞穴，狼太太问为什么一反常态，弄得这么累，还没晚餐吃。他答：“还用问吗！只因我信了一个女人的话呀！”

source_paragraphs: A HEN finding the eggs of a viper and carefully keeping them warm, nourished them into life. A Swallow, observing what she had done, said, “You silly creature! why have you hatched these vipers which, when they shall have grown, will inflict injury on all, beginning with yourself?”
translated_paragraphs: 母鸡找到一窝蛇蛋，小心地给它们保暖，一直将它们孵出壳。燕子瞧着，说：“你这个傻家伙！为什么孵出这些毒蛇？它们一长大，就会从你自己开始，把大家全都害苦。”

source_paragraphs: AN AMARANTH planted in a garden near a Rose-Tree, thus addressed it: “What a lovely flower is the Rose, a favourite alike with Gods and with men. I envy you your beauty and your perfume.” The Rose replied, “I indeed, dear Amaranth, flourish but for a brief season! If no cruel hand pluck me from my stem, yet I must perish by an early doom. But thou art immortal and dost never fade, but bloomest for ever in renewed youth.”
translated_paragraphs: 一株不凋花长在花园的玫瑰旁边，对它说：“玫瑰开得多么美，众神和凡人同样喜爱它。我真羡慕你的容貌和芬芳。”玫瑰回答：“亲爱的不凋花啊，我开的花其实只有短短一季！就算没有残酷的手把我从枝头摘去，我也注定早早凋亡。可你长存而不朽，从不褪色，青春一次次重新焕发，永远开放。”

source_paragraphs: TWO TRAVELERS, worn out by the heat of the summer’s sun, laid themselves down at noon under the widespreading branches of a Plane-Tree. As they rested under its shade, one of the Travelers said to the other, “What a singularly useless tree is the Plane! It bears no fruit, and is not of the least service to man.” The Plane-Tree, interrupting him, said, “You ungrateful fellows! Do you, while receiving benefits from me and resting under my shade, dare to describe me as useless, and unprofitable?”
Some men underrate their best blessings.
translated_paragraphs: 夏天的太阳把两个旅行人晒得筋疲力尽。中午，他们便躺在一棵大悬铃木尽情伸展的枝条下，在树荫里休息。一个对另一个说：“这悬铃木真是出奇地没用！它不结果子，对人连一丁点儿好处都没有。”悬铃木打断他：“你们这些忘恩负义的家伙！一面受我的恩惠，一面在我的荫蔽下休息，竟还敢说我毫无用处，不能带来好处？”
有些人瞧低了自己得到的最好的恩惠。

source_paragraphs: AN ASS besought a Horse to spare him a small portion of his feed. “Yes,” said the Horse; “if any remains out of what I am now eating I will give it you for the sake of my own superior dignity, and if you will come when I reach my own stall in the evening, I will give you a little sack full of barley.” The Ass replied, “Thank you. But I can’t think that you, who refuse me a little matter now, will by and by confer on me a greater benefit.”
translated_paragraphs: 驴求马从自己的饲料里分一小部分给它。马答：“好啊。眼下我正吃的这份，要是剩下什么，我会看在我自己身份高贵的分上赏给你。晚上等我回了自己的马槽，你要肯来，我会给你满满一小袋大麦。”驴回答：“谢谢。可是眼前连一点点东西都不肯给我的人，过后倒会给我更大的好处，这我很难相信。”

source_paragraphs: A TROUBLESOME CROW seated herself on the back of a Sheep. The Sheep, much against his will, carried her backward and forward for a long time, and at last said, “If you had treated a dog in this way, you would have had your deserts from his sharp teeth.” To this the Crow replied, “I despise the weak and yield to the strong. I know whom I may bully and whom I must flatter; and I thus prolong my life to a good old age.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只招人烦的乌鸦坐在绵羊背上。绵羊极不愿意地驮着她来来回回走了许久，终于忍不住说：“你若拿这套来对付一条狗，它那口尖牙早该给你应得的下场了。”乌鸦回答：“我瞧不起弱者，在强者跟前就肯低头。我知道可以欺负谁，更知道必须奉承谁。正靠这法子，我才能长命百岁呀。”

source_paragraphs: A FOX was mounting a hedge when he lost his footing and caught hold of a Bramble to save himself. Having pricked and grievously torn the soles of his feet, he accused the Bramble because, when he had fled to her for assistance, she had used him worse than the hedge itself. The Bramble, interrupting him, said, “But you really must have been out of your senses to fasten yourself on me, who am myself always accustomed to fasten upon others.”
translated_paragraphs: 狐狸翻爬树篱时一脚踏空，顺手抓住一丛荆棘来救命。结果脚掌叫尖刺扎破，撕裂，受伤很重。狐狸责怪荆棘，说自己投奔她求助，她对待狐狸竟比树篱本身还坏。荆棘打断他：“不过，连我也要牢牢攀住，你的脑筋可真糊涂。攀住旁人牢牢不放，原本正是我的习性呀！”

source_paragraphs: AN ASS congratulated a Horse on being so ungrudgingly and carefully provided for, while he himself had scarcely enough to eat and not even that without hard work. But when war broke out, a heavily armed soldier mounted the Horse, and riding him to the charge, rushed into the very midst of the enemy. The Horse was wounded and fell dead on the battlefield. Then the Ass, seeing all these things, changed his mind, and commiserated the Horse.
translated_paragraphs: 驴恭喜马能得到那么周到、大方的供养，自己却辛苦劳作，都未必能吃得饱。可后来战争爆发了，一个全副武装的士兵骑上马，催它冲锋，直闯敌军中央。马受了伤，倒毙在战场。驴看见这一切，便改了先前的想法，转而怜惜起马来。

sections.title_en: The Lion, Jupiter, and the Elephant
source_paragraphs: THE LION wearied Jupiter with his frequent complaints. “It is true, O Jupiter!” he said, “that I am gigantic in strength, handsome in shape, and powerful in attack. I have jaws well provided with teeth, and feet furnished with claws, and I lord it over all the beasts of the forest, and what a disgrace it is, that being such as I am, I should be frightened by the crowing of a cock.” Jupiter replied, “Why do you blame me without a cause? I have given you all the attributes which I possess myself, and your courage never fails you except in this one instance.” On hearing this the Lion groaned and lamented very much and, reproaching himself with his cowardice, wished that he might die. As these thoughts passed through his mind, he met an Elephant and came close to hold a conversation with him. After a time he observed that the Elephant shook his ears very often, and he inquired what was the matter and why his ears moved with such a tremor every now and then. Just at that moment a Gnat settled on the head of the Elephant, and he replied, “Do you see that little buzzing insect? If it enters my ear, my fate is sealed. I should die presently.” The Lion said, “Well, since so huge a beast is afraid of a tiny gnat, I will no more complain, nor wish myself dead. I find myself, even as I am, better off than the Elephant.”
translated_paragraphs: 狮子三天两头抱怨，闹得朱庇特心烦。“哦，朱庇特，”它说，“不错，我力量惊人，形体英俊，出击有威。我颚上满是利齿，脚下生着利爪，森林百兽都听我号令。可我堂堂这副模样，竟被公鸡啼叫吓住，多丢脸呀！”朱庇特答：“为何无故怪罪于我？连我自己有的那些禀赋，都已给了你。除了这一桩，你的胆量哪一回叫你失望过？”狮子听了，呻吟叹息，好不难过，责怪自己懦弱，只恨不能死了算了。这样一路想着，遇见大象，便走上前攀谈。过了一阵，他发觉大象不停地抖耳朵，就问它出了什么事，两只耳朵为什么不时那样颤动。恰在这时，一只小蚊虫落在象的头顶。大象回答：“看见那只嗡嗡响的小虫了吗？它要是钻进我的耳朵，我就完了，马上便会死掉。”狮子说：“好吧，这么庞大的猛兽尚且害怕一只小小的蚊虫，我也不再抱怨，不再盼着自己去死。就照我眼下这副样子，我发现自己还比大象幸运呢。”

source_paragraphs: A DOG, used to eating eggs, saw an Oyster and, opening his mouth to its widest extent, swallowed it down with the utmost relish, supposing it to be an egg. Soon afterwards suffering great pain in his stomach, he said, “I deserve all this torment, for my folly in thinking that everything round must be an egg.”
They who act without sufficient thought, will often fall into unsuspected danger.
translated_paragraphs: 一条吃惯鸡蛋的狗见到一只牡蛎，以为是鸡蛋，就把嘴张到最大，津津有味地整个吞下。没过多久，他的肚子痛得厉害，便说：“这些痛苦是我应得的，谁叫我这样糊涂，以为凡是圆乎乎的东西就必定是蛋。”
不肯想清楚就行事的人，常常会落入意想不到的危险。

source_paragraphs: TWO MULES well-laden with packs were trudging along. One carried panniers filled with money, the other sacks weighted with grain. The Mule carrying the treasure walked with head erect, as if conscious of the value of his burden, and tossed up and down the clear-toned bells fastened to his neck. His companion followed with quiet and easy step. All of a sudden Robbers rushed upon them from their hiding-places, and in the scuffle with their owners, wounded with a sword the Mule carrying the treasure, which they greedily seized while taking no notice of the grain. The Mule which had been robbed and wounded bewailed his misfortunes. The other replied, “I am indeed glad that I was thought so little of, for I have lost nothing, nor am I hurt with any wound.”
translated_paragraphs: 两头骡子驮着沉甸甸的货，一步步往前跋涉。一头两侧的驮筐装满金钱，另一头背着沉重的粮袋。驮宝物的那一头昂首前进，仿佛十分清楚自己的货物值多少钱，还把脖子上的铃铛抖得叮当脆响。同伴却走得轻松而安静，跟在后头。忽然，一伙强盗从藏身处向它们扑来。与主人们扭打时，强盗拿剑刺伤了驮金钱的骡子，贪婪地抢走财宝，连眼角都没扫一眼粮袋。既遭抢劫又受伤的骡子哀叹自己的不幸。另一头说：“我倒真庆幸没人瞧得上我。东西一件没丢，身上也半处伤都没有。”

source_paragraphs: A WOLF pursued a Lamb, which fled for refuge to a certain Temple. The Wolf called out to him and said, “The Priest will slay you in sacrifice, if he should catch you.” On which the Lamb replied, “It would be better for me to be sacrificed in the Temple than to be eaten by you.”
translated_paragraphs: 狼追逐小羊，小羊逃进一座神庙求庇护。狼向里高喊：“祭司要是逮住你，可会宰了你做祭品！”羊答：“我宁愿在庙里做祭品，也比让你吃掉好。”

source_paragraphs: A FOWLER caught a Partridge and was about to kill it. The Partridge earnestly begged him to spare his life, saying, “Pray, master, permit me to live and I will entice many Partridges to you in recompense for your mercy to me.” The Fowler replied, “I shall now with less scruple take your life, because you are willing to save it at the cost of betraying your friends and relations.”
translated_paragraphs: 捕鸟人捉住一只鹧鸪，正要杀了它。鹧鸪恳切地求他饶命：“好主人，容我活下去，我愿意引诱好多鹧鸪到您手里，报答您今天的慈悲。”捕鸟人答：“听了这话，我杀你倒更没什么顾忌了。你竟肯出卖亲戚朋友，拿他们的命换自己活。”

source_paragraphs: A MAN, very much annoyed with a Flea, caught him at last, and said, “Who are you who dare to feed on my limbs, and to cost me so much trouble in catching you?” The Flea replied, “O my dear sir, pray spare my life, and destroy me not, for I cannot possibly do you much harm.” The Man, laughing, replied, “Now you shall certainly die by mine own hands, for no evil, whether it be small or large, ought to be tolerated.”
translated_paragraphs: 一个人被跳蚤叮得烦透了，终于将它抓住，便说：“你是个什么东西，敢在我的四肢上吸血，还叫我费了那么大的力气才抓到你？”跳蚤答：“亲爱的先生，求您饶我一命，不要杀我。无论如何，我也不能给您多大的伤害。”那人笑着回答：“这下你可定要死在我手上了。因为无论作的恶是小是大，都不该姑息。”

sections.title_en: The Rich Man and the Tanner
source_paragraphs: A RICH MAN lived near a Tanner, and not being able to bear the unpleasant smell of the tan-yard, he pressed his neighbor to go away. The Tanner put off his departure from time to time, saying that he would leave soon. But as he still continued to stay, as time went on, the rich man became accustomed to the smell, and feeling no manner of inconvenience, made no further complaints.
translated_paragraphs: 一位富翁同皮匠毗邻而居，受不了鞣皮场里那股刺鼻的气味，一再催邻居搬家。皮匠总说很快就走，却一回回将搬迁往后推。等他一住再住，时光渐长，富翁慢慢习惯了那股味道，再也不觉得有什么不便，也就不再出声抱怨。

source_paragraphs: A VIPER, entering the workshop of a smith, sought from the tools the means of satisfying his hunger. He more particularly addressed himself to a File, and asked of him the favour of a meal. The File replied, “You must indeed be a simple-minded fellow if you expect to get anything from me, who am accustomed to take from everyone, and never to give anything in return.”
The covetous are  poor givers.
translated_paragraphs: 一条蝰蛇钻进铁匠的作坊，想向工具们谋取一顿饭吃。它尤其看中了锉刀，向它讨这一餐人情。锉刀回答：“你若指望从我这里得到什么，可真是个头脑简单的家伙。我的习惯一向是从人人那里锉下一些，绝不回给谁一点东西。”
贪得无厌的人难得慷慨。

source_paragraphs: A LION, roaming through a forest, trod upon a thorn. Soon afterward he came up to a Shepherd and fawned upon him, wagging his tail as if to say, “I am a suppliant, and seek your aid.” The Shepherd boldly examined the beast, discovered the thorn, and placing his paw upon his lap, pulled it out; thus relieved of his pain, the Lion returned into the forest. Some time after, the Shepherd, being imprisoned on a false accusation, was condemned “to be cast to the Lions” as the punishment for his imputed crime. But when the Lion was released from his cage, he recognized the Shepherd as the man who healed him, and instead of attacking him, approached and placed his foot upon his lap. The King, as soon as he heard the tale, ordered the Lion to be set free again in the forest, and the Shepherd to be pardoned and restored to his friends.
translated_paragraphs: 一头狮子在林中游荡，踩中一根尖刺。不久，它来到牧羊人跟前，摇着尾巴，显得十分温顺，仿佛在说：“我是来恳求你的，请你帮帮我。”牧羊人大着胆子检查它的身体，找到尖刺，又把爪子放在自己膝上，将刺拔了出来。痛苦解除，狮子便回到森林中。过些时候，牧人被人诬告下狱。为了那桩莫须有的罪名，他被判处“投给狮子”。狮子从笼里放出来，认出那人正是医好自己的牧羊人，非但没有攻击，还主动凑过去，把爪子又放在他膝上。国王听完原委，当即下令，放狮子重回森林，赦免牧人，让他回到友人身边。

source_paragraphs: THE CAMEL, when he saw the Bull adorned with horns, envied him and wished that he himself could obtain the same honours. He went to Jupiter, and besought him to give him horns. Jupiter, vexed at his request because he was not satisfied with his size and strength of body, and desired yet more, not only refused to give him horns, but even deprived him of a portion of his ears.
translated_paragraphs: 骆驼看到公牛的头有犄角装点，心里羡慕，盼自己也能得到同样的体面。它前去恳求朱庇特，请赐一对角给它。朱庇特恼它有如此庞大的身躯和力气仍不知足，还想多要，不但不肯给它一对角，反而从它的耳朵上削去了两截。

source_paragraphs: A PANTHER, by some mischance, fell into a pit. The Shepherds discovered him, and some threw sticks at him and pelted him with stones, while others, moved with compassion towards one about to die even though no one should hurt him, threw in some food to prolong his life. At night they returned home, not dreaming of any danger, but supposing that on the morrow they would find him dead. The Panther, however, when he had recruited his feeble strength, freed himself with a sudden bound from the pit, and hastened to his den with rapid steps. After a few days he came forth and slaughtered the cattle, and, killing the Shepherds who had attacked him, raged with angry fury. Then they who had spared his life, fearing for their safety, surrendered to him their flocks and begged only for their lives. To them the Panther made this reply: “I remember alike those who sought my life with stones, and those who gave me food aside, therefore, your fears. I return as an enemy only to those who injured me.”
translated_paragraphs: 豹子不慎掉进一个坑。牧羊人们发现了它，有些拿木棍和石块砸它，也有一些见它哪怕没人加害也眼看要死，动了恻隐之心，投下几样吃的，想让它多活些时候。天晚了，大伙儿各自回家，都以为次日来时，豹子必定已经死了，丝毫不曾想到会有危险。然而，豹子借此恢复了一点气力，忽地往上一蹿，逃出土坑，迅速回到自己的巢穴。过了几天，它出来宰杀牲畜，把那些攻击过它的牧人杀死，大肆发泄怒火。先前让它活下来的牧人们担心自己的安危，便交出羊群，只求留得性命。豹子对他们说：“谁想拿石头打死我，谁给了我食物，两种人我都记得。放下你们的恐惧吧。我回来只同那些伤害过我的人为敌。”

source_paragraphs: AN EAGLE, overwhelmed with sorrow, sat upon the branches of a tree in company with a Kite. “Why,” said the Kite, “do I see you with such a rueful look?” “I seek,” she replied, “a mate suitable for me, and am not able to find one.” “Take me,” returned the Kite, “I am much stronger than you are.” “Why, are you able to secure the means of living by your plunder?” “Well, I have often caught and carried away an ostrich in my talons.” The Eagle, persuaded by these words, accepted him as her mate. Shortly after the nuptials, the Eagle said, “Fly off and bring me back the ostrich you promised me.” The Kite, soaring aloft into the air, brought back the shabbiest possible mouse, stinking from the length of time it had lain about the fields. “Is this,” said the Eagle, “the faithful fulfillment of your promise to me?” The Kite replied, “That I might attain your royal hand, there is nothing that I would not have promised, however much I knew that I must fail in the performance.”
translated_paragraphs: 鹰忧心忡忡，和一只鸢一起歇在树枝上。鸢说：“我怎么看着你这样愁容满面呢？”鹰答：“我想找一个配得上我的伴侣，却找不着。”“选我吧，”鸢答，“我的力气比你大得多。”“哦，你当真能靠掠取猎物维持生计吗？”“我可不是头一回用爪子捉住鸵鸟，把它整个儿拎走啦。”鹰给这些话说动，接受了它做伴。婚后不久，鹰说：“飞出去，把答应给我捉来的鸵鸟带回来吧。”鸢高高飞走，却只带回一只破烂到不能再破烂的老鼠，早在田间躺了太久，已臭不可闻。“你就这样，”鹰说，“忠实履行给我的诺言吗？”鸢回答：“为了赢得高贵的你与我成婚，我没有什么事不肯答应。哪怕明知绝不可能兑现，也不例外。”

source_paragraphs: AN EAGLE was once captured by a man, who immediately clipped his wings and put him into his poultry-yard with the other birds, at which treatment the Eagle was weighed down with grief. Later, another neighbor purchased him and allowed his feathers to grow again. The Eagle took flight, and pouncing upon a hare, brought it at once as an offering to his benefactor. A Fox, seeing this, exclaimed, “Do not cultivate the favour of this man, but of your former owner, lest he should again hunt for you and deprive you a second time of your wings.”
translated_paragraphs: 有只鹰落到一个人手里，那人立即剪短它的飞羽，把它同家禽院里的群鸟关在一起。受了这般对待，鹰倍感悲伤。后来，另一个邻居把它买下，放任它的羽毛重新长齐。鹰展翅飞去，扑到一只野兔，立刻送回来，献给自己的恩人。狐狸见状，叫道：“你别费心讨好这个人，该讨好的是你原先那个主人。免得他又来打猎，把你捉去，第二次夺走你的翅膀。”

sections.title_en: The King’s Son and the Painted Lion
source_paragraphs: A KING, whose only son was fond of martial exercises, had a dream in which he was warned that his son would be killed by a lion. Afraid the dream should prove true, he built for his son a pleasant palace and adorned its walls for his amusement with all kinds of life-sized animals, among which was the picture of a lion. When the young Prince saw this, his grief at being thus confined burst out afresh, and, standing near the lion, he said: “O you most detestable of animals! through a lying dream of my father’s, which he saw in his sleep, I am shut up on your account in this palace as if I had been a girl: what shall I now do to you?” With these words he stretched out his hands toward a thorn-tree, meaning to cut a stick from its branches so that he might beat the lion. But one of the tree’s prickles pierced his finger and caused great pain and inflammation, so that the young Prince fell down in a fainting fit. A violent fever suddenly set in, from which he died not many days later.
We had better bear our troubles bravely than try to escape them.
translated_paragraphs: 一位国王只有一个儿子，王子酷爱操练武艺。国王做了个梦，梦里有人警告说，他的儿子会死于狮子之手。国王怕梦境成真，就给儿子盖了一座美丽的宫殿，为了给他消遣，还在墙上画了各种与真身一样大的动物，其中就画了一头狮子。年轻的王子看见这幅画，受拘禁的悲愤重新发作。他站到狮子跟前，说：“你这最可恨的畜生！就因为你，因为父亲睡梦中做了个骗人的梦，我便像个女孩子似的关在这宫殿里。我该怎么收拾你才好？”说完，他伸手去拉旁边一棵荆棘树，想折下根木棍来打那狮子。不料一根尖刺扎进手指，伤处剧烈疼痛，起了炎症，年轻的王子竟倒地昏厥。随后他突然发起了厉害的热病，没有几天就死了。
与其千方百计躲避忧患，不如勇敢承受。

source_paragraphs: A CAT fell in love with a handsome young man, and entreated Venus to change her into the form of a woman. Venus consented to her request and transformed her into a beautiful damsel, so that the youth saw her and loved her, and took her home as his bride. While the two were reclining in their chamber, Venus wishing to discover if the Cat in her change of shape had also altered her habits of life, let down a mouse in the middle of the room. The Cat, quite forgetting her present condition, started up from the couch and pursued the mouse, wishing to eat it. Venus was much disappointed and again caused her to return to her former shape.
Nature exceeds nurture.
translated_paragraphs: 猫爱上一位英俊的青年，恳求维纳斯把自己变成一个女人。维纳斯同意了，将她变作俊美的少女。青年见了她便生爱意，娶她回家做了新娘。两人正并卧房中，维纳斯想知道猫改变形貌以后，连生活习性是否也改了，便放下一只老鼠在房中间。猫完全忘记了自己此时的身份，从卧榻上猛然跳起，追逐老鼠，一心要把它吃掉。维纳斯很失望，又叫她恢复了原本的模样。
天性比后来的教养更有力量。

source_paragraphs: THE EAGLE and the Beetle were at enmity together, and they destroyed one another’s nests. The Eagle gave the first provocation in seizing upon and in eating the young ones of the Beetle. The Beetle got by stealth at the Eagle’s eggs, and rolled them out of the nest, and followed the Eagle even into the presence of Jupiter. On the Eagle making his complaint, Jupiter ordered him to make his nest in his lap; and while Jupiter had the eggs in his lap, the Beetle came flying about him, and Jupiter rising up unawares, to drive him away from his head, threw down the eggs, and broke them.
The weak often revenge themselves on those who use them ill, even though they be more powerful.
translated_paragraphs: 鹰和甲虫结下了仇怨，彼此毁坏对方的巢。是鹰先行挑衅，捉去吃了甲虫的孩子。甲虫偷偷接近鹰巢，把鹰蛋滚出窝去，随后甚至一路追着鹰到了朱庇特面前。鹰向朱庇特申诉，朱庇特便命它在自己的膝头安巢。等他把蛋放在膝上，甲虫又绕着他飞起来。朱庇特一时不察，站起来，想把甲虫从头边赶开，膝上的鹰蛋就掉到地上摔碎了。
即便对方比自己强大，弱者也常能报复那些虐待它们的人。

source_paragraphs: THE SHE-GOATS having obtained a beard by request to Jupiter, the He-Goats were sorely displeased and made complaint that the females equaled them in dignity. “Allow them,” said Jupiter, “to enjoy an empty honour and to assume the badge of your nobler sex, so long as they are not your equals in strength or courage.”
It matters little if those who are inferior to us in merit should be like us in outside appearances.
translated_paragraphs: 母山羊向朱庇特请求，也得了胡须。公山羊极不高兴，前去抱怨，说雌羊竟与自己一样威风了。朱庇特答：“只要她们的力气与胆量还比不上你们，就随她们去享用这点空名，也带上你们雄性这更高贵的一方的标志吧。”
本领不及我们的人，若只是外观看起来跟我们相似，那并没有多大关系。

sections.title_en: The Bald Man and the Fly
source_paragraphs: A FLY bit the bare head of a Bald Man who, endeavoring to destroy it, gave himself a heavy slap. Escaping, the Fly said mockingly, “You who have wished to revenge, even with death, the Prick of a tiny insect, see what you have done to yourself to add insult to injury?” The Bald Man replied, “I can easily make peace with myself, because I know there was no intention to hurt. But you, an ill-favoured and contemptible insect who delights in sucking human blood, I wish that I could have killed you even if I had incurred a heavier penalty.”
translated_paragraphs: 一只苍蝇叮了秃头人的脑袋。那人想拍死它，却在自己的光头上结结实实打了一巴掌。苍蝇逃走以后，嘲笑他说：“一只小虫稍微叮一下，你就想要它的命来报复。看看你自己做的事，吃了这一叮，难道还要再添一记耳光？”秃头人回答：“我可以轻易同自己和解，因为我知道，我没有存心要伤害自己。至于你，这么一个丑陋可鄙、专爱吸人血的虫子，哪怕要付出比这更重的代价，我也盼自己刚才把你打死了。”

sections.title_en: The Shipwrecked Man and the Sea
source_paragraphs: A SHIPWRECKED MAN, having been cast upon a certain shore, slept after his buffetings with the deep. After a while he awoke, and looking upon the Sea, loaded it with reproaches. He argued that it enticed men with the calmness of its looks, but when it had induced them to plow its waters, it grew rough and destroyed them. The Sea, assuming the form of a woman, replied to him: “Blame not me, my good sir, but the winds, for I am by my own nature as calm and firm even as this earth; but the winds suddenly falling on me create these waves, and lash me into fury.”
translated_paragraphs: 一位遭了海难的人被冲上岸边，在大海的折腾之后沉沉睡去。醒来面对海水，他连声责备，说海总是以平静的外貌诱人，等引得人们驾着船在它上面耕犁似的破浪前行，它却猛然翻腾，毁掉他们。大海化作一位女子，回答他说：“好先生，别怪我，去怪风吧。我生性平静踏实，一如眼前的大地。是风突然落到我身上，掀起这些波浪，把我抽打得暴怒起来。”

source_paragraphs: A RICH NOBLEMAN once opened the theaters without charge to the people, and gave a public notice that he would handsomely reward any person who invented a new amusement for the occasion. Various public performers contended for the prize. Among them came a Buffoon well known among the populace for his jokes, and said that he had a kind of entertainment which had never been brought out on any stage before. This report being spread about made a great stir, and the theater was crowded in every part. The Buffoon appeared alone upon the platform, without any apparatus or confederates, and the very sense of expectation caused an intense silence. He suddenly bent his head towards his bosom and imitated the squeaking of a little pig so admirably with his voice that the audience declared he had a porker under his cloak, and demanded that it should be shaken out. When that was done and nothing was found, they cheered the actor, and loaded him with the loudest applause. A Countryman in the crowd, observing all that has passed, said, “So help me, Hercules, he shall not beat me at that trick!” and at once proclaimed that he would do the same thing on the next day, though in a much more natural way. On the morrow a still larger crowd assembled in the theater, but now partiality for their favourite actor very generally prevailed, and the audience came rather to ridicule the Countryman than to see the spectacle. Both of the performers appeared on the stage. The Buffoon grunted and squeaked away first, and obtained, as on the preceding day, the applause and cheers of the spectators. Next the Countryman commenced, and pretending that he concealed a little pig beneath his clothes (which in truth he did, but not suspected by the audience ) contrived to take hold of and to pull his ear causing the pig to squeak. The Crowd, however, cried out with one consent that the Buffoon had given a far more exact imitation, and clamored for the Countryman to be kicked out of the theater. On this the rustic produced the little pig from his cloak and showed by the most positive proof the greatness of their mistake. “Look here,” he said, “this shows what sort of judges you are.”
translated_paragraphs: 一位富有的贵族免费开放剧场，请民众看戏，又张贴告示，谁若能为此发明新奇的玩意儿，他便重重有赏。各行表演艺人纷纷争夺奖金。有位以笑话闻名于百姓之中的小丑前来，说他有一样消遣，先前任何舞台都没演出过。这消息一传，引起好大的轰动，剧场里挤得满满当当。小丑独自登台，没带道具，也没带帮手。全场只因期待，已经安静得落针可闻。他突然朝胸前一低头，学起小猪尖叫。声音惟妙惟肖，观众们断言他斗篷里一定藏着一只活猪，非让他抖出来不可。他果然抖了斗篷，里头什么也没有。人们欢呼喝彩，为他献上最热烈的掌声。一个乡下人在人群中看完这一切，说：“赫拉克勒斯助我，我绝不能叫他这点把戏比下去！”他当场宣布次日再来，他也要表演同一种声音，而且会更自然得多。第二天，剧院聚起了更多的观众。不过，偏爱熟悉的小丑的人占了大半，多数过来与其说是看节目，不如说想看乡下人的笑话。两位表演者登上舞台。小丑先出场，哼哼唧唧，尖声叫唤，又同前一天一样，赢得了欢呼与掌声。接着，乡下人开始了。他做出衣服底下藏着小猪的模样（其实还真的有一只，但观众们完全不疑心）。他设法把小猪耳朵抓住，一拉，小猪便叫了起来。然而，众人竟异口同声地嚷，还是小丑模仿得像得多，叫嚣着要把乡下人踢出剧场。乡下人这才从斗篷里面抱出小猪，叫大家亲眼确证，他们的判断究竟错得多厉害。“瞧瞧吧，”他说，“这就看得出你们是怎样的裁判了。”

source_paragraphs: A CROW in great want of food saw a Serpent asleep in a sunny nook, and flying down, greedily seized him. The Serpent, turning about, bit the Crow with a mortal wound. In the agony of death, the bird exclaimed: “O unhappy me! who have found in that which I deemed a happy windfall the source of my destruction.”
translated_paragraphs: 乌鸦饿得急需食物，看见一条蛇睡在向阳的角落，立即飞下去，贪婪地抓住它。蛇一转身，给了乌鸦致命的一口。乌鸦在濒死的痛苦中叫道：“我可真不幸！原本以为是意外落到嘴边的好东西，到头来竟成了断送我性命的祸根。”

source_paragraphs: A CERTAIN HUNTER, having snared a hare, placed it upon his shoulders and set out homewards. On his way he met a man on horseback who begged the hare of him, under the pretense of purchasing it. However, when the Horseman got the hare, he rode off as fast as he could. The Hunter ran after him, as if he was sure of overtaking him, but the Horseman increased more and more the distance between them. The Hunter, sorely against his will, called out to him and said, “Get along with you! for I will now make you a present of the hare.”
translated_paragraphs: 猎人用圈套捉了一只野兔，往肩上一搭，动身回家。路上遇见一个骑马的人，托说要买那只兔子，向猎人讨来先看。可兔子一到手，骑马人便纵马飞驰而去。猎人撒腿追赶，好像很有把握能追上，可两人的距离却越来越远。猎人万般不愿，只得向他喊道：“拿去吧！这只兔子，此刻便算是我送给你的礼物好了。”

source_paragraphs: THE OLIVE-TREE ridiculed the Fig-Tree because, while she was green all the year round, the Fig-Tree changed its leaves with the seasons. A shower of snow fell upon them, and, finding the Olive full of foliage, it settled upon its branches and broke them down with its weight, at once despoiling it of its beauty and killing the tree. But finding the Fig-Tree denuded of leaves, the snow fell through to the ground, and did not injure it at all.
translated_paragraphs: 橄榄树取笑无花果树，说自己四季常青，而无花果树的叶子却跟着季节更替。一场雪落到两棵树上。橄榄树枝头满是叶子，积雪便停驻其上，压折了枝条，一下子剥夺了它的美貌，也要了它的命。无花果树却已经落了叶，于是雪从枝间漏过去，落到地上，树本身毫发未损。

sections.title_en: The Frogs’ Complaint Against the Sun
source_paragraphs: ONCE UPON A TIME, when the Sun announced his intention to take a wife, the Frogs lifted up their voices in clamor to the sky. Jupiter, disturbed by the noise of their croaking, inquired the cause of their complaint. One of them said, “The Sun, now while he is single, parches up the marsh, and compels us to die miserably in our arid homes. What will be our future condition if he should beget other suns?”
translated_paragraphs: 从前有一次，太阳宣布打算娶妻，青蛙们便冲着天上高声喧嚷。它们的呱噪声打搅了朱庇特，他问它们在抱怨什么。一只青蛙回答：“太阳还没娶妻，只他一个，就已经能烤干沼泽，让我们不得不在干涸的家中悲惨地等死。若他再生下别的小太阳，往后咱们可怎么活呢？”

source_paragraphs: A BRAZIER had a little Dog, which was a great favourite with his master, and his constant companion. While he hammered away at his metals the Dog slept; but when, on the other hand, he went to dinner and began to eat, the Dog woke up and wagged his tail, as if he would ask for a share of his meal. His master one day, pretending to be angry and shaking his stick at him, said, “You wretched little sluggard! what shall I do to you? While I am hammering on the anvil, you sleep on the mat; and when I begin to eat after my toil, you wake up and wag your tail for food. Do you not know that labor is the source of every blessing, and that none but those who work are entitled to eat?”
translated_paragraphs: 有个铜匠养了条小狗，十分疼它，走到哪儿都有它作伴。铜匠拿铁锤叮叮当当捶打金属，小狗便睡觉。可主人一去吃饭，刚把食物往嘴里送，狗就醒来摇尾巴，仿佛在讨一口主人的饭。一日，主人故意装作生气，拿棍子朝它一晃，说：“你这不像话的小懒虫！拿你怎么办才好？我在铁砧上捶打时，你倒在垫子上美美睡觉。等我辛苦一阵，坐下来开吃，你就醒来摇尾巴讨东西。你难道不懂，一切好处都得靠干活才有，只有干活的才有资格吃饭吗？”

source_paragraphs: 1 (return) [ A History of the Literature of Ancient Greece, by K. O. Mueller. Vol. i, p. 191. _London_, Parker, 1858.]
2 (return) [ Select Fables of Æsop, and other Fabulists. In three books, translated by Robert Dodsley, accompanied with a selection of notes, and an Essay on Fable. _Birmingham_, 1864. P. 60.]

3 (return) [ Some of these fables had, no doubt, in the first instance, a primary and private interpretation. On the first occasion of their being composed they were intended to refer to some passing event, or to some individual acts of wrong-doing. Thus, the fables of the “Eagle and the Fox” and of the “Fox and Monkey” are supposed to have been written by Archilochus, to avenge the injuries done him by Lycambes. So also the fables of the “Swollen Fox” and of the “Frogs asking a King” were spoken by Æsop for the immediate purpose of reconciling the inhabitants of Samos and Athens to their respective rulers, Periander and Pisistratus; while the fable of the “Horse and Stag” was composed to caution the inhabitants of Himera against granting a bodyguard to Phalaris. In a similar manner, the fable from Phædrus, the “Marriage of the Sun,” is supposed to have reference to the contemplated union of Livia, the daughter of Drusus, with Sejanus the favourite, and minister of Trajan. These fables, however, though thus originating in special events, and designed at first to meet special circumstances, are so admirably constructed as to be fraught with lessons of general utility, and of universal application.]
4 (return) [ Hesiod. Opera et Dies, verse 202.]

5 (return) [ Æschylus. Fragment of the Myrmidons. Æschylus speaks of this fable as existing before his day. ὡς δ’ ἐστὶ μύθων τῶν Διβυστικῶν λογος. See Scholiast on the Aves of Aristophanes, line 808.]
6 (return) [ Fragment. 38, ed. Gaisford. See also Mueller’s History of the Literature of Ancient Greece, vol. i. pp. 190–193.]

7 (return) [ M. Bayle has well put this in his account of Æsop. “Il n’y a point d’apparence que les fables qui portent aujourd’hui son nom soient les mêmes qu’il avait faites; elles viennent bien de lui pour la plupart, quant à la matière et la pensée; mais les paroles sont d’un autre.” And again, “C’est donc à Hésiode, que j’aimerais mieux attribuer la gloire de l’invention; mais sans doute il laissa la chose très imparfaite. Esope la perfectionne si heureusement, qu’on l’a regarde comme le vrai père de cette sorte de production.”—_Bayle. Dictionnaire Historique_.]
8 (return) [ Plato in Phædone.]

9 (return)
[ Apologos en! misit tibi
Ab usque Rheni limite
Ausonius nomen Italum
Præceptor Augusti tui
Æsopiam trimetriam;
Quam vertit exili stylo
Pedestre concinnans opus
Fandi Titianus artifex.
_Ausonii Epistola_, xvi. 75–80.]
10 (return) [ Both these publications are in the British Museum, and are placed in the library in cases under glass, for the inspection of the curious.]

11 (return) [ Fables may possibly have been not entirely unknown to the mediæval scholars. There are two celebrated works which might by some be classed amongst works of this description. The one is the “Speculum Sapientiæ,” attributed to St. Cyril, Archbishop of Jerusalem, but of a considerably later origin, and existing only in Latin. It is divided into four books, and consists of long conversations conducted by fictitious characters under the figures the beasts of the field and forest, and aimed at the rebuke of particular classes of men, the boastful, the proud, the luxurious, the wrathful, &c. None of the stories are precisely those of Æsop, and none have the concinnity, terseness, and unmistakable deduction of the lesson intended to be taught by the fable, so conspicuous in the great Greek fabulist. The exact title of the book is this: “Speculum Sapientiæ, B. Cyrilli Episcopi: alias quadripartitus apologeticus vocatus, in cujus quidem proverbiis omnis et totius sapientiæ speculum claret et feliciter incipit.” The other is a larger work in two volumes, published in the fourteenth century by Cæsar Heisterbach, a Cistercian monk, under the title of “Dialogus Miraculorum,” reprinted in 1851. This work consists of conversations in which many stories are interwoven on all kinds of subjects. It has no correspondence with the pure Æsopian fable.]
12 (return) [ Post-mediæval Preachers, by S. Baring-Gould. Rivingtons, 1865.]
13 (return) [ For an account of this work see the Life of Poggio Bracciolini, by the Rev. William Shepherd. Liverpool, 1801.]
14 (return) [ Professor Theodore Bergh. See Classical Museum, No. viii. July, 1849.]

15 (return) [ Vavassor’s treatise, entitled “De Ludicrâ Dictione” was written A.D. 1658, at the request of the celebrated M. Balzac (though published after his death), for the purpose of showing that the burlesque style of writing adopted by Scarron and D’Assouci, and at that time so popular in France, had no sanction from the ancient classic writers. _Francisci Vavassoris opera omnia_. Amsterdam. 1709.]

16 (return) [ The claims of Babrias also found a warm advocate in the learned Frenchman, M. Bayle, who, in his admirable Dictionary, (_Dictionnaire Historique et Critique de Pierre Bayle_. Paris, 1820,) gives additional arguments in confirmation of the opinions of his learned predecessors, Nevelet and Vavassor.]

17 (return) [ Scazonic, or halting, iambics; a choliambic (a lame, halting iambic) differs from the iambic Senarius in always having a spondee or trochee for its last foot; the fifth foot, to avoid shortness of metre, being generally an iambic. See Fables of Babrias, translated by Rev. James Davies. Lockwood, 1860. Preface, p. 27.]
18 (return) [ See Dr. Bentley’s Dissertations upon the Epistles of Phalaris.]
19 (return) [ Dr. Bentley’s Dissertations on the Epistles of Phalaris, and Fables of Æsop examined. By the Honourable Charles Boyle.]

20 (return) [ M. Bayle thus characterises this Life of Æsop by Planudes, “Tous les habiles gens conviennent que c’est un roman, et que les absurdités grossières qui l’on y trouve le rendent indigne de toute créance.” _Dictionnaire Historique_. Art. _Esope_.]
translated_paragraphs: 〔1〕K. O. 缪勒《古希腊文学史》，第一卷，第191页。伦敦帕克出版社，1858年。
〔2〕《伊索与其他寓言家寓言选》，三卷，罗伯特·多兹利译，附若干注释和《论寓言》一文。伯明翰，1864年，第60页。

〔3〕某些寓言初时无疑有其明确而特定的意思。当初写作，针对的是一桩一时的事件，或某个人做的一件错事。譬如，据说阿尔基洛科斯写《鹰和狐狸》与《狐狸和猴子》，是为了回敬吕坎贝斯对他的伤害。又如，伊索讲《肚子胀大的狐狸》和《请求国王的青蛙》，直接目的分别是劝萨摩斯和雅典的居民接受佩里安德和庇西特拉图的统治。《马和雄鹿》则是要告诫希梅拉人，不要把一支卫队配给法拉里斯。同样，费德鲁斯的《太阳结婚》据说暗指德鲁苏斯之女莉维娅与受宠的大臣塞扬努斯所筹议的结合，底本称塞扬努斯是图拉真的大臣。这些寓言固然起于个别事件，原为应对特定环境而作，可是构思如此精巧，以至于其中蕴含的教益足以广泛而普遍地运用。
〔4〕赫西俄德《工作与时日》，第202行。
〔5〕埃斯库罗斯《密耳弥冬人》残篇。他提到这则寓言在他之前就已存在，所谓“如利比亚故事所言”（ὡς δ’ ἐστὶ μύθων τῶν Διβυστικῶν λογος）。又见阿里斯托芬《鸟》的古注，第808行。
〔6〕盖斯福德编本，残篇38。另见缪勒《古希腊文学史》，第一卷，第190至193页。
〔7〕贝尔先生在谈到伊索时说得好：“今天以伊索为名的寓言，看来不可能就是他当年所写的那些。多数篇的材料和思想应当源自他，措辞却出自别人。”他又说：“所以，我宁愿把开创的荣誉归给赫西俄德，不过他留下的东西无疑还很不完备。伊索将它完善得如此成功，人们便视他为这种作品真正的父亲。”见贝尔《历史词典》。
〔8〕柏拉图《斐多篇》。

〔9〕“看呀，从遥远的莱茵河边境，
奥索尼乌斯，带着意大利的名字，
你的奥古斯都的老师，
送来这些伊索的三音步寓言。
辞章之士提提亚努斯
以朴素的笔调翻写，
将它们写成了散文。”
见《奥索尼乌斯书信集》，第十六封，第75至80行。
〔10〕这两个出版物当时都藏在大英博物馆，陈列于图书馆的玻璃展柜里，供好奇的读者观看。

〔11〕中世纪学者也许并非全然不知道寓言。有两部著名作品，一些人或许会将其归入这类。其一是《智慧之镜》，署名为耶路撒冷大主教圣西里尔，实际成书晚得多，只有拉丁文传本。书分四卷，借田野和林中禽兽虚构角色，让它们长篇对谈，针对的分别是好夸口的人、傲慢的人、奢靡的人、易怒的人等。这些故事没有一则恰是伊索的某一篇，也不具备那位伟大希腊寓言家最醒目的和谐、简洁，以及那种读来无可误认的寓意。书的全题为《主教圣西里尔的智慧之镜，又名四部寓言辩说，于其箴言中一切智慧之镜明照，今欣然开卷》（Speculum Sapientiæ, B. Cyrilli Episcopi: alias quadripartitus apologeticus vocatus, in cujus quidem proverbiis omnis et totius sapientiæ speculum claret et feliciter incipit）。其二是篇幅更大的两卷本，据底本所述为熙笃会修士海斯特巴赫的凯撒在十四世纪刊行，名为《奇迹对话录》，1851年重印。书中以交谈为体，穿插各类题目的许多故事，与纯粹的伊索式寓言并不相合。
〔12〕S. 巴林-古尔德《中世纪以后的布道家》，里文顿出版社，1865年。
〔13〕关于这部书，参见威廉·谢泼德牧师《波焦·布拉乔利尼传》，利物浦，1801年。
〔14〕西奥多·贝格教授。见《古典博物馆》第八期，1849年7月。
〔15〕瓦瓦瑟的论著《论诙谐的文辞》写于公元1658年，是应著名的巴尔扎克先生之请，虽在后者去世后才出版。该书要表明，斯卡龙和达苏西采用、当时风行于法国的滑稽仿作笔法，没有古代经典作家的先例作为依据。见《弗朗索瓦·瓦瓦瑟全集》，阿姆斯特丹，1709年。
〔16〕主张巴布里阿斯为作者的一方，还在法国学者贝尔先生那里找到了热心的支持。贝尔在他出色的词典《皮埃尔·贝尔历史与批判词典》（巴黎，1820年）中提出补充论据，佐证此前学者内韦莱和瓦瓦瑟的看法。
〔17〕Scazonic 即“跛行的”短长格。跛行短长格与一般的六音步短长格不同，末音步必用长长格或长短格；为避免音律过短，第五音步一般取短长格。参见詹姆斯·戴维斯牧师译《巴布里阿斯寓言》，洛克伍德出版，1860年，序言第27页。
〔18〕见本特利博士《论法拉里斯书信》。
〔19〕查尔斯·博伊尔阁下著《本特利博士论法拉里斯书信与伊索寓言的论文辨考》。
〔20〕贝尔先生这样评论普拉努德斯的《伊索传》：“一切明达的人都同意，这是一部小说，而其中种种粗陋荒诞之处，使它不值得丝毫信任。”见《历史词典》“伊索”条。
